text:
A federal judge in California blocked the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) from re-arresting immigrants during their routine check-in appointments, in a decision that does not directly protect Cubans in Florida but marks a growing legal stance against that tactic.

In parallel, a class action lawsuit filed in Georgia is progressing within the same federal circuit that covers Florida and could, if successful, compel ICE to change its behavior in that state as well.

Judge Dana M. Sabraw of the Southern District of California certified the class action suit Fanfan et al. v. Noem et al. and ordered that ICE cannot re-detain individuals who have already been released with open court cases during their check-in appointments without first conducting an individual assessment that demonstrates a significant change in circumstances.

The order applies only to San Diego and Imperial counties.

The case was brought forward by the Center for Human Rights and Constitutional Law and the UCLA School of Law.

"ICE was drawing those people in for check-ins or ICE appointments and detaining them without reason," said Monika Langarica, legal director of that organization.

Las redetenciones de ICE en citas de control y sus implicaciones legales para cubanos en Florida forman parte de un panorama migratorio en constante cambio. Sigue los últimos desarrollos en nuestra sección de

This is not the first order of its kind: in December 2025, Judge Sabraw had already granted a temporary restriction in the case, and a court in San Francisco blocked the same practice for Northern California.

Georgia's Lawsuit: Why It Matters to Florida

The most significant legal front for Cubans in Florida opened on November 12 in the Northern District of Georgia.

The ACLU of Georgia, North Carolina, and South Carolina, along with the law firm Foley Hoag, filed a class action lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security, Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Acting ICE Director David Venturella, and the Acting ICE Office Director in Atlanta, Kristen Sullivan.

The lawsuit challenges the "re-detention policy" that DHS adopted around May 2025, when it abandoned the "change of circumstances policy" that the ICE office in Atlanta had followed for over four decades.

Under that previous policy, ICE could not arrest someone who had been released again without first determining that their circumstances had materially changed.

"Our clients have complied with the rules imposed by the government. They have appeared at court hearings, attended check-in appointments, and adhered to the conditions of their release," said Corina Scott, attorney for the ACLU of North Carolina.

The key for Florida is that Georgia is part of the 11th Circuit, the same one that covers Florida and Alabama. If the lawsuit succeeds and goes to appeal, a ruling from that court would be binding throughout the circuit.

At the close of this edition, the court has not yet issued a decision on the suspension and class certification motions filed on November 17.

What changes —and what doesn't— for Cubans in Miramar

Thousands of Cubans with the I-220A form periodically visit the ICE office in Miramar, in South Florida, where arrests have been documented during these appointments and alleged abuses that led to a federal complaint filed by the SPLC and Americans for Immigrant Justice.

None of the judicial decisions from California or Georgia have any direct effect in Florida today.

However, the legal line they outline—requiring individual evaluation before re-detaining—is already being used by lawyers in habeas corpus petitions in the Southern District of Florida, where more than 97,000 detainees have resorted to this route since Trump’s return.

The legal landscape for Cubans with I-220A is mixed: last May, the 11th Circuit recognized the right to bail hearings for detainees within the country, but on November 17, that same court ruled that the I-220A is not equivalent to the parole required by the Cuban Adjustment Act, closing that path to residency for many.

While the courts determine the extent of these protections, experts advise continuing to attend appointments in Miramar: failing to appear increases the risk of detention. It is recommended to always have an immigration lawyer readily available before any appointment with ICE.

title: Green Card Update: USCIS Tightens Rules for Abused Migrant Children - Newsweek
description:

The second focuses on the green card process, including when USCIS can review or revoke an earlier SIJ approval and potentially begin removal proceedings.
Read More on News Those with approved SIJ petitions may ultimately be eligible to apply for lawful permanent residence, commonly known as a green card.
The two USCIS policy updates were issued on November 20, took effect immediately, and apply to pending and future cases.

text:
The Trump administration has tightened rules for some young immigrants seeking green cards after experiencing parental abuse, neglect, or abandonment, according to two new policy updates from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS).

The changes affect the Special Immigrant Juvenile (SIJ) program, which provides immigration protection to certain unmarried immigrants under 21 who have been subject to state juvenile court proceedings related to parental abuse, neglect, abandonment, or a similar basis under state law.

The first policy focuses on who qualifies for SIJ protection, giving USCIS officers more scope to examine the circumstances behind a juvenile court order. The second focuses on the green card process, including when USCIS can review or revoke an earlier SIJ approval and potentially begin removal proceedings.

Read More on News

Those with approved SIJ petitions may ultimately be eligible to apply for lawful permanent residence, commonly known as a green card.

Newsweek has contacted USCIS for comment via email outside working hours.

USCIS primarily administers immigration benefits, including green cards, asylum, work authorization, and citizenship, but has taken a more active role in immigration enforcement under the Trump administration. In October, the agency said it had taken enforcement actions affecting about 2.2 million people since President Donald Trump returned to office.

The two USCIS policy updates were issued on November 20, took effect immediately, and apply to pending and future cases.

Under PA-2026-17, USCIS said immigration officers will independently determine whether an applicant qualifies for SIJ classification and whether the request is bona fide. Officers can interview applicants, seek additional evidence about the factual basis for juvenile court findings, and consider information from government databases.

The same policy directs officers to give additional scrutiny to certain cases involving claims that one parent abandoned the applicant. USCIS said officers should assess whether a primary purpose for seeking the juvenile court order was protection from parental maltreatment rather than obtaining an immigration benefit.

The second policy, PA-2026-18, applies when people with SIJ classification seek green cards. USCIS said applicants must meet the legal requirements for permanent residence and merit a favorable exercise of discretion.

Under the policy, USCIS may revoke an approved SIJ petition for "good and sufficient cause" if it later finds the petition was not bona fide, involved fraud or willful misrepresentation, or was approved in error.

USCIS may also place applicants in deportation proceedings if their green card application is denied or their SIJ petition is revoked.

USCIS said the changes are intended to address fraud, national security, and public safety concerns in the SIJ program.

In a July 2025 report, the agency analyzed more than 300,000 SIJ petitions filed from the beginning of fiscal 2013 through February 2025. It identified 853 known or suspected gang members who had filed SIJ petitions and said most of those petitions were approved. The agency said more than 600 known or suspected MS-13 members had filed SIJ petitions and more than 500 had been approved.

The report also said nearly 19,000 SIJ petitioners had criminal arrests, including at least 120 arrested for murder. The figures have not been independently verified by Newsweek.

"The Special Immigrant Juvenile visa program is infected with fraud and abuse," James Percival, DHS general counsel, wrote in a post on X.

SIJ filings increased from 18,711 in fiscal 2020 to 78,156 in fiscal 2025, a 317 percent increase. USCIS said the growth contributed to a visa backlog that has left applicants waiting about five years after SIJ approval for a visa to become available.

The National Immigration Project and End SIJS Backlog Coalition have criticized the changes, saying they could make it harder for young people who have experienced abuse, neglect, or abandonment to secure permanent protection. The groups said they are considering possible legal action.

"The law Congress wrote hasn't changed. USCIS changed the rules anyway, in the middle of young people’s cases, and told its officers to treat a child who survived neglect, abuse, and abandonment like a suspect," Rebecca Scholtz, supervising attorney at the National Immigration Project and a member of the steering committee of the End SIJS Backlog Coalition, said in a statement.

"Singling out children Congress chose to shield, who lack the power to fight back, is cruelty by design. We will keep fighting to protect the rights of SIJS youth, alongside the young people these dangerous policies target."

Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, senior fellow at the American Immigration Council, wrote in a post on X, "The Trump admin’s war on migrant children continues; under this very major change in policy, the government is likely going to begin mass rejecting applications for Special Immigrant Juvenile Status and moving to deport as many migrant teens and young adults as they can."

title: Federal Tort Claims Act Suit Tests Chicago Border Patrol Arrest - Immigration Analytics
description:

The suit pleads false arrest and imprisonment, battery, intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligent denial of medical care.

text:
A U.S. citizen pulled from her car by federal agents during Chicago’s Operation Midway Blitz has filed a Federal Tort Claims Act lawsuit against the United States, seeking up to $1 million. Dayanne Figueroa, 31, a paralegal, sued on Nov. 23 in federal court in Chicago over her Oct. 10, 2025, arrest in the West Town neighborhood, Newsweek reported, and the case is an early test of what damages law still offers people hurt in immigration operations.

A tort claim against the government cannot reach court until the agency has had six months to answer an administrative claim, and the operation’s first arrests are now past that mark. More suits like this one are likely to follow.

Two accounts of one traffic lane

According to the complaint as described by Newsweek, Figueroa had just dropped her son at school when an unmarked SUV driven by a Customs and Border Protection agent moved into her lane and struck her car. Agents pulled her out by the legs, handcuffed her and held her for hours without a warrant or probable cause, first at the Broadview processing facility and then at a site in Lombard, the filing says. Recovering from kidney-related surgery, she was initially refused medical help and later taken to a hospital by ambulance, according to the complaint, which lists internal bleeding, a torn muscle and a broken dental crown among her injuries. The suit pleads false arrest and imprisonment, battery, intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligent denial of medical care. Democracy Forward, a progressive legal group, represents her, Newsmax reported.

The government’s version is the opposite. A DHS spokesperson told Newsweek the driver used her vehicle to “ram” the agents’ vehicle and “violently resisted.” Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., quoted DHS in a November 2025 floor speech as saying she “crashed into an unmarked government vehicle and violently resisted arrest, injuring two officers”; Durbin called that false and said she was released with no charges. A Justice Department spokesperson said agents “are protected by long-established legal immunities and defenses” and that filing a claim “does not mean it has merit,” Newsmax reported.

Why the Federal Tort Claims Act carries the load

People injured by federal officers once could also sue the officers personally under Bivens. In Egbert v. Boule (2022), the Supreme Court refused to recognize such a claim against a Border Patrol agent, citing national security concerns at the border that it said belong to Congress. The practical effect is that the Federal Tort Claims Act, which makes the United States itself liable for certain wrongs of its employees, is now nearly the only damages route after an immigration enforcement encounter.

The act runs on a fixed sequence. Under 28 U.S.C. 2675, a claimant first presents a written claim to the agency, usually on Standard Form 95, and may sue only after a denial or six months of silence, which counts as a denial. Figueroa filed an administrative complaint with DHS and received no response within six months, according to Newsmax and other outlets. The same section generally caps recovery at the sum demanded in that claim, which is why these suits name a fixed ceiling. Claims must be presented within two years under 28 U.S.C. 2401(b), so people hurt in the fall 2025 Chicago operation have until roughly fall 2027.

Assault, battery and false arrest are normally excluded, but 28 U.S.C. 2680(h) restores them when the actor is a federal “investigative or law enforcement officer,” which covers CBP and ICE agents. Figueroa’s claims are the kind Congress expressly allowed.

Where the government is likely to fight

The main battleground is likely to be the discretionary function exception in Section 2680(a), which shields government choices involving judgment or policy. In Martin v. United States (June 2025), a suit over an FBI raid on the wrong house, a unanimous Supreme Court held that the law enforcement proviso overrides only the intentional-tort exception, not the discretionary function exception, and sent the case back for that analysis. That leaves the open question here: whether how agents box in a car and remove a driver is a protected judgment call. Many lower courts have refused to treat unconstitutional conduct as discretionary, so the probable cause allegation is likely to carry real weight.

Two other features shape the stakes. These cases are tried to a judge, not a jury, under 28 U.S.C. 2402, and liability turns on Illinois tort law. Punitive damages are barred, and any award is paid by the government, not the agents, who are not defendants.

More claims in the same pipeline

DHS has said its Illinois operation produced more than 4,500 arrests, Newsweek reported. No public dataset counts how many people stopped were U.S. citizens or how many administrative claims followed. What is visible is a steady run of related disputes, including a $25 million claim by a U.S. citizen shot in Ontario, Calif., the deportation of a Texas man whose citizenship DOJ later conceded, the arrest of U.S. citizens in Oakland and a CBP shooting in Portland.

Next comes the government’s answer, generally due 60 days after the United States is served, and a likely motion to dismiss on discretionary function grounds. How the Northern District of Illinois rules will tell other Midway Blitz claimants how much the act can deliver after Martin.

This article is for general information and is not legal advice.

Sources

Newsweek, “US Citizen Dragged From Car by Border Patrol Sues Trump Admin” (Nov. 25, 2026)

Newsmax, report on the Figueroa lawsuit (Nov. 25, 2026)

Sen. Dick Durbin, floor remarks on the Figueroa arrest (Nov. 4, 2025)

28 U.S.C. 2675, 28 U.S.C. 2680, 28 U.S.C. 2401 and 28 U.S.C. 2402

Egbert v. Boule, 596 U.S. 482 (2022)

Martin v. United States, No. 24-362 (June 12, 2025)

text:
New Congress, New Investigations

In a November 18 letter to congressional leaders, the coalition urged lawmakers to investigate Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

MORE NEWS: Michigan Veterans Benefit From $1.3 Billion in VA-Funded Local Healthcare

The coalition wants testimony from people who say they were harmed by immigration enforcement, immigrant advocates and state attorneys general who have fought what they call “abuse.”

“Americans deserve not only oversight, but accountability,” Nessel said in a recent press release about the letter, accusing federal immigration agencies of having “antagonized and terrorized communities across the country.”

In the coalition’s letter, it states, “In the face of immigration enforcement conduct that is both immoral and unlawful, the outgoing House and Senate majorities were content to look the other way. The incoming majorities need to confront this head-on. The American people voted for real, serious oversight – with teeth and consequences for any agency or individual who would ignore the rule of law.”

The coalition also questions billions in federal spending on detention facilities, including a reported $2.2 billion purchase of four prisons from CoreCivic, a company they claim has donated to Trump-related political committees.

Accountability or Political Showdown?

The coalition argues in the letter that the outgoing congressional majorities failed to hold the Trump administration accountable. With Democrats preparing to take control, the attorneys general clearly have a lengthy investigative wish list.

The attorneys general want Congress to investigate alleged excessive force, deaths in immigration custody and potential waste of taxpayer dollars among other things. Their accusations remain allegations requiring examination, not established findings of congressional wrongdoing. For Nessel, who has repeatedly challenged Trump administration policies in court, the letter opens another avenue for scrutiny.

text:
A renewed federal push to convert commercial warehouses into mass immigration detention facilities is colliding with fierce opposition from courts, state attorneys general, local governments and Congress's own nonpartisan auditor — each raising alarms about a program critics argue is both legally compromised and financially reckless.

The controversy is sharpened by a glaring contradiction at its core: even as the federal government prepares to sell seven of the eleven warehouses it already purchased, it is simultaneously directing hundreds of millions of dollars toward new construction at contested sites.

A Billion-Dollar Spree That Bought Mostly Empty Buildings

At the center of a bruising oversight fight are two GAO audits published in September and November 2026 warning that ICE's warehouse acquisition drive was implemented rapidly and risks significant taxpayer waste. Between January and March 2026, ICE purchased eleven warehouses for roughly $1.07 billion—paying at least 50 percent above local tax-assessed values on nine of them, according to data compiled in the November 19 report. While the watchdog noted that tax assessments do not always reflect fair market value, the purchase prices exceeded total assessed values by roughly $532 million. Among the starkest examples: an Oakwood, Georgia, facility tax-assessed at approximately $15 million for which ICE paid more than $68 million.

The government now plans to sell seven of the eleven properties, spending more than $20 million on costs it cannot recover — such as security and zoning assessments — in the process. Meanwhile, construction is moving forward at other sites.

The purchasing frenzy drew on the $45 billion Congress earmarked for immigration enforcement detention under a 2025 law. ICE launched what it called the Detention Reengineering Initiative with a sweeping blueprint: a national network of processing centers capable of holding 7,000 to 10,000 detainees at a time for stays of up to 60 days. By mid-January 2026, ICE's detained population had surpassed 73,000 — the highest figure in the agency's history — as the administration drove toward an eventual target of 100,000 beds.

Cities and Towns Refuse to Stand Aside

The plan ignited immediate and unusually broad resistance. In Romulus, Michigan, residents locked officials out of a city council meeting in protest. High school students rallied outside a warehouse in Surprise, Arizona. Salt Lake City saw street demonstrations the same week ICE finalized its purchase there.

Kansas City, Missouri, moved swiftly, passing a five-year moratorium on permits for non-municipal detention facilities in January — a measure that inspired similar actions in neighboring Jackson County and Wyandotte County, Kansas. Plans for a large facility in Socorro, Texas, were scaled back after sustained community pressure. In at least one additional state, federal officials announced they were searching for alternative locations after local opposition took hold.

Facing litigation and mounting political headwinds, ICE paused further warehouse acquisitions on March 31.

New Jersey: Federal Deception Alleged in Open Court

That pause has since collapsed — most dramatically in New Jersey, where the case has escalated into a direct courtroom confrontation between state authorities and federal immigration officials.

The 470,000-square-foot warehouse at 1879 Route 46 in Roxbury Township — purchased by ICE in February for approximately $129 million, more than twice its assessed value — was initially placed on the agency's list of properties for sale. Federal attorneys told a New Jersey court the government intended to sell the site entirely. That assurance has since proven false.

In November, ICE reversed course. The agency awarded a $31.8 million construction contract on November 5 to begin converting the warehouse into a facility capable of housing up to 1,500 immigration detainees. The full contract carries optional provisions that could push the total commitment to nearly $1 billion over five years.

In an emergency motion filed November 23, Attorney General Jennifer Davenport argued the contract violates a May federal court order prohibiting ICE from taking any steps to convert the site until a legally required environmental assessment is completed. Davenport charged that ICE solicited construction bids as early as August and received at least one bid in September — all while assuring the court it had made no decision and had no timeline. The court has not yet ruled on the state's motion.

"That was false," Davenport's motion states. "It is completely unacceptable that DHS and ICE are flouting this court order — which is why we're going back to court today to stop their lawbreaking conduct."

Standing with Davenport is a coalition that defies easy political categorization. The all-Republican Roxbury Township Council and Mayor Shawn Potillo have aligned with Democratic Governor Mikie Sherrill in opposing the project. Potillo described information coming from DHS as "vague, incomplete," while Sherrill put it plainly: "This isn't a partisan issue." Protesters disrupted a November 10 council meeting, forcing an early adjournment.

A Rising Death Toll Adds Moral Urgency

The legal and financial disputes are amplified by a grim human toll. ICE's own reporting lists 36 deaths in its custody for fiscal year 2026 — the highest total on the agency's public death-reporting page, which goes back to fiscal 2018, and a 50 percent increase over the previous fiscal year. As of late October, at least 32 people had died in calendar year 2026 alone. Immigrant advocates argue the warehouse detention model, which prioritizes throughput and scale above all else, is structurally incompatible with any meaningful standard of detainee care.

In April, Representative Rashida Tlaib introduced the Ban Warehouse Detention Act, which would legally prohibit converting non-traditional properties into ICE facilities. The bill has yet to advance in the Republican-controlled Congress.

The Trump administration has not publicly responded to the GAO's findings or to New Jersey's latest court motion. What is clear is that a program designed to expand rapidly and at scale has instead generated one of the most geographically and politically diverse resistance coalitions of the second Trump term — with no straightforward path forward.

name: Human Rights
title: The Danish prime minister's coarse language about migrants has no place in a European democracy
description:
Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, who calls herself a social democrat, now alludes to the “great replacement” migration conspiracy theory in rejecting multiculturalism.
But such criticism can be brushed aside when even Denmark’s supreme court appears to support the government’s anti-migrant stance.
The shock-and-awe manner of these announcements, and the coarse anti-migrant and anti-Muslim language that European leaders now use, are disturbing enough.
It’s the deliberate manufacturing of moral panic about migrants through choreographed, headline-grabbing announcements, coded language and dog whistles that invoke far-right tropes once considered beyond the pale in mainstream European politics.
In other words, yet more cash and other benefits offered to global-south governments that agree to stop migrants from reaching Europe.
text:
With the notable exception of Spain’s Pedro Sánchez, who may soon be out of office, EU leaders appear most united when promoting one clear aim: reinforcing the already heavily guarded borders of Fortress Europe against unwanted migrants.

Policymakers who once criticised Donald Trump’s immigration policies as inhumane now enact measures that increasingly resemble Washington’s ugly playbook of ICE home raids, family separations, deportations and offshore detention deals.

Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, who calls herself a social democrat, now alludes to the “great replacement” migration conspiracy theory in rejecting multiculturalism. On a podcast last week, she said: “We are a Danish society, and we form an ethnically Danish indigenous tribe.” For good measure, she added: “We do not have religious equality. We are a Christian country. We shall continue to be so.”

Just a day earlier, the Danish PM joined leaders of four other EU countries – Austria, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands –in unveiling the first ever European “return hub” in Rwanda for people whose asylum claims are rejected in the EU. Frederiksen called the deportation deal “gamechanging”. Given Rwanda’s dismal human rights record, the pact – under which the first transfers of about 100 people are due in 2027 – is more accurately described by rights groups as “disgraceful”.

But such criticism can be brushed aside when even Denmark’s supreme court appears to support the government’s anti-migrant stance. The court ruled this week that the eviction of “non-western” tenants from a social housing estate in Copenhagen under the country’s controversial “ghetto law” is not discriminatory.

Belgium, meanwhile, has approved legislation allowing police to forcibly enter properties to remove people deemed to be undocumented, an abhorrent measure that conflates lack of legal residence status with criminality.

The shock-and-awe manner of these announcements, and the coarse anti-migrant and anti-Muslim language that European leaders now use, are disturbing enough. What frightens me even more is their cumulative effect: the normalisation of hate, fear and discrimination, which makes the dehumanisation and exclusion of particular categories of people – migrants and by extension also Black, brown and Muslim European citizens – appear ordinary, orderly and even necessary.

The deportation scheme and police raid legislation may ultimately be challenged in courts and perhaps even overturned. But the purpose of the fanfare is to shift public norms, and widen the Overton window – make previously unacceptable ideas appear a legitimate part of public debate.

What we are witnessing, I believe, is pure spectacle, courtesy of politicians who face growing public anger over such things as inflation and housing, to give the illusion that they are “taking back control”. It’s the deliberate manufacturing of moral panic about migrants through choreographed, headline-grabbing announcements, coded language and dog whistles that invoke far-right tropes once considered beyond the pale in mainstream European politics.

The political theatre serves an even deeper purpose: it turns extreme ideas into everyday conversations. It creates fear, chills solidarity and deters people from offering shelter.

In his book Chain of Ideas, the American scholar Ibram X Kendi explains how the great replacement theory, which claims that Europe is being “invaded” by people from the global south, moved from a fringe conspiracy into Europe’s everyday consciousness. And here it is, seeping into the discourse of Denmark’s Frederiksen and embedded in the Rwanda plan.

When politicians face little or no pushback for violating longstanding taboos – and are instead invited on to TV chatshows and podcasts to repeat their toxic messages – both their words and actions can become even more inflammatory. And this, in turn, allows EU institutions to quietly start crossing their own red lines by using coded technocratic and neutral-sounding language about “risk management”, “burden sharing”, “returns” and finding “innovative solutions” to control migration.

Brussels could push back against the Rwanda plan but instead of doing that, Magnus Brunner, the most senior EU official on migration policy, has doubled down on the discredited strategy of “migration diplomacy”. In other words, yet more cash and other benefits offered to global-south governments that agree to stop migrants from reaching Europe.

The latest headline-grabbing announcements also serve to divert and distract from Europe’s real problems. Student protests over education shortfalls, failing public services and unaffordable housing are sidelined – and blamed on foreigners.

Despite politicians’ alarmist drumbeat, however, the European parliament’s spring Eurobarometer shows that almost 50% of Europeans see inflation and the cost of living, not migration, as their principal concern. And despite the sense of permanent crisis conveyed by EU leaders, latest data by Frontex, the EU’s increasingly powerful border-control agency, shows the number of “irregular” border crossings into the EU fell by 29% in the first 10 months of this year.

In fact, many of the countries with the toughest public discourse on migration, including Denmark, are quietly bringing in workers from India, the Philippines, Bangladesh and other states to fill labour shortages, often on short-term contracts that can leave workers vulnerable to exploitation.

Elections in the coming days and months could see the installation of even more hardline anti-migration governments across Europe, including in France, where Marine Le Pen, the unapologetically anti-Muslim and anti-migrant leader of the far-right National Rally, is hoping to become president next year.

I watch all this in sadness and fear but retain hope that Europe’s progressive politicians become more vocal in ensuring a more humane European migration policy and a more responsible and equitable policy towards racialised and Muslim citizens.

Europe’s history should have taught us the dangers of scapegoating, hate-mongering and dehumanising people. And yet here we are again, hurtling down a dangerously slippery slope.

title: A complex network: Trump's 'Third Country' Deportations deals with African countries. Part 1
description: Donald Trump’s administration is striking deals with African governments to accept migrants expelled from the United States. These ‘third-country deportations’ raise questions over diplomatic incentives, legal protections and the fate of those caught in the middle. Now, the case is being taken to the US Supreme Court. Jamila Versi spoke to some of the leading investigators and litigation experts on the case.
text:
Rabbiatu Kuyateh, a Sierra Leonean woman, had spent three decades living in the US. She worked as a nurse in Maryland for more than 20 years, raised an American-born son, and regularly reported to US immigration authorities. An immigration judge had granted her protection against deportation to Sierra Leone, which she had fled fearing persecution.

But in November 2025, her life changed in an instant. After being detained during a regular US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) check-in in July, she was unexpectedly deported to Accra, Ghana.

Stark footage published by the investigative journalism consortium Forbidden Stories shows her struggling as she is dragged by officials across the lobby of a hotel in the Ghanaian capital.

From Ghana, she was forcibly repatriated – back to Sierra Leone, the very country she had fled.

Kuyateh is one of 536 identified people deported from the US to African countries between January 2025 and August 2026, according to a Human Rights Watch report published in October 2026, based on ICE data.

Under Trump’s immigration crackdown, at least 25,000 people have been deported to third countries through an extensive network of so-called ‘third-country deportation agreements’. These allow the US to remove migrants to countries other than their own, including individuals whom American courts have found would face persecution or torture if returned home.

Africa has become an important focus of this diplomatic operation. According to internal US State Department documents obtained by the Forbidden Stories investigation, Washington had approached 49 of the continent’s 54 countries about receiving deportees by March 2026.

Yet behind the growing network of bilateral agreements lies a troubling contradiction. Many of those being transferred have already been recognised by US courts as facing persecution or torture in their home countries. Now, they find themselves passed between governments, sometimes detained indefinitely, sometimes returned to the very places they fled.

The situation raises significant questions about African sovereignty, diplomatic bargaining – and who is responsible for protecting people once they arrive.

For Édouard Perrin, editor-in-chief at Forbidden Stories , investigating the agreements has revealed a vast diplomatic operation stretching far beyond immigration enforcement inside the United States.

Their investigation began with the arrest of Salvadoran journalist Mario Guevara, who, while covering a demonstration in Atlanta (US), was taken into custody by ICE.

Forbidden Stories , whose mission is to continue investigations when journalists are threatened or silenced, began examining the wider treatment of journalists reporting on immigration enforcement, which led them to the complicated case in Cameroon.

Four journalists attempting to investigate a facility holding US deportees in Yaoundé were themselves detained. Forbidden Stories and its partners subsequently continued their reporting, tracking down two women who had been interviewed by the journalists before their detention.

“We saw the potential for a collaboration nearly instantly because we are talking about a global policy with multiple countries that are taking part of this,” Perrin tells me.

The Deportation Project , as they call it, became an investigation involving 72 journalists from 26 different global news organisations.

Journalists examined diplomatic documents and memorandums of understanding, tracked flights, and worked with data-collecting NGOs and local reporters to establish what happened to people after they reached their destinations.

Some agreements were publicly acknowledged; others remained secret. Even where documents were available, they frequently offered little detail about their implementation, making the system difficult to understand and scrutinise.

“Some of them were never made public. Some of them were not acknowledged. For instance, in the case of Mexico, which is where the largest number of people were expelled, Mexico adamantly denies having been in any kind of agreement with the US.”

The investigation identified agreements with at least 35 countries, predominantly in Africa and the Americas, but also extending to Europe and Asia.

The investigation identified that the US government “flagged and dedicated” at least $410m to the third-country deportation project, including direct payments to governments and funding for international organisations.

Perrin emphasises the distinction between money earmarked and money spent. Not all planned expenditure could be verified as having been disbursed.

The State Department’s new Office of Remigration, which oversees negotiations with foreign governments, is playing a substantial role. The office forms part of a striking transformation within a department historically responsible for refugee assistance and resettlement.

The term remigration has strong associations with Europe’s far-right movements, where it has been used to advocate the mass removal of migrants, including people with citizenship rights.

The adoption of such terminology within an official US government office marks a significant departure from the State Department’s previous emphasis on refugee protection.

Yael Schacher, director for the Americas and Europe at Refugees International, argues that understanding the third-country deportation policy requires looking at it through precisely that lens.

“The Trump administration is very clear about this. It’s an ethnic purge. There were a lot of African asylum seekers that came to the United States during the Biden administration, same thing with the Latin Americans, and those people are being targeted for sure.

“The Trump administration really wants to portray what it’s doing as fixing all the wrong things that the Biden administration did.”

Although a State Department policy, Schacher argues that immigration enforcement must be thought of as the driving element behind it. “It’s the first time in US history that the State Department has made deportation its top priority,” argues Schacher.

“It’s a department that used to provide humanitarian support for refugees in third countries; the purpose of that money has been flipped on its head.”

Schacher helped establish Third Country Deportation Watch, a joint project with Human Rights First that monitors the agreements, deportations and associated legal challenges.

She identifies two overlapping dimensions of the policy: immigration enforcement and foreign policy. Beyond physically removing people, she argues, the threat of deportation to an unfamiliar country can discourage others from pursuing asylum claims.

“It’s using the threat to induce fear in the immigrant population in the United States, and to get people to give up their claims and self-deport. So it’s not only being used as a very real deportation tool but as a threat,” says Schacher.

Alma David, a US immigration lawyer representing people subjected to third-country deportations, highlights how the portrayal of African destinations can also undermine deportees’ credibility.

“Part of it is deliberately making it very clear that the reason why people are afraid is that they’re being sent to a place that’s less developed than where they want to be.

“It plays into this whole idea to undermine their credibility in terms of how afraid they really are. Like, if you were really that afraid, wouldn’t you just want to be anywhere where you weren’t in your own country?”

The policy’s impact has the potential to extend far beyond the relatively small number actually transferred to African countries.

text:
On Saturday, November 21, 2026, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detained two individuals as they boarded a flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA), as many have seen both on video and in the news.

Our position remains clear: ICE immigration enforcement does not belong in our airports. These enforcement actions disrupt airport and airline operations, undermine public trust, spread fear among travelers and workers, and place local law enforcement in a difficult position between federal actions outside their control and their responsibility to protect public safety.

Following Saturday's incident, Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal informed the Commission that Port staff had received advance notification of federal immigration enforcement activity. The Commission immediately requested a review of relevant records and communications.

We confirmed that Transportation Security Administration (TSA) officials provided limited notice of enforcement operations to federal and Port personnel. This information did not include identifying information of individuals. Today, November 25th 2026, Port leadership informed the Commission that these were one-way notifications for situational awareness, that no action was taken in response, and that staff complied with Keep Washington Working Act and Commission policy.

However, the Commission was not informed of these notifications, their frequency, or their contents.

The Commission is taking two immediate steps:

Developing an order establishing an independent investigation with full access to relevant records, communications, and personnel. The Commission will retain outside legal counsel to provide guidance and support the independent investigative process.

Engaging our congressional delegation to pursue federal accountability, strengthen congressional oversight, and advance legislative and policy measures to end ICE immigration enforcement at airports.

The Port is also continuing its internal review and will plan to provide an update to the Commission at its next meeting. Our commitment to accountability within the Port does not diminish our opposition to ICE enforcement at SEA. Being a welcoming Port is more than a policy on paper. It must be reflected in our operations, decisions, and actions. We will hold our own institution accountable while continuing to demand accountability from federal agencies. The traveling public, our workforce, and the people of King County deserve nothing less.

title: Federal Court Blocks Trump's Attempt to Restrict Birthright Citizenship | Ratopati
description:
A federal court has blocked President Donald Trump's latest attempt to ban birthright citizenship for children born in America.
The federal court in Washington has stayed the implementation of the Trump administration's new executive order, ruling that children born in America cannot be deprived of birthright citizenship based on their parents' citizenship or immigration status.
The US administration argued that individuals in these groups do not fall under the category of receiving birthright citizenship under the US Constitution.
Another Blow After Supreme Court's Old Ruling This decision, which came on Wednesday, is another legal defeat for the Trump administration's citizenship policy.
The new ruling has created further obstacles for the Trump administration's efforts to limit the right to birthright citizenship in America.
text:
Washington. A federal court has blocked President Donald Trump's latest attempt to ban birthright citizenship for children born in America. The court clarified that the President cannot arbitrarily add new conditions or exceptions to the right to citizenship guaranteed by the US Constitution.

The federal court in Washington has stayed the implementation of the Trump administration's new executive order, ruling that children born in America cannot be deprived of birthright citizenship based on their parents' citizenship or immigration status.

The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) filed a lawsuit in court on behalf of affected families.

New Measure After Old Order Was Blocked

On August 6, Trump issued a new executive order attempting to exclude some children born in America from the right to citizenship by birth.

Previously, in June, the US Supreme Court had blocked Trump's old order regarding citizenship. Following that, the administration attempted to deprive more categories of children of citizenship rights through a new order.

Citizenship of Which Children Was at Risk?

Trump's new order targeted children born in America to families where neither parent is a US citizen. This primarily included the following groups:

– Children of individuals whom the administration considered 'foreign nationals of enemy nations'.

– Children of foreign government officials and individuals residing in America due to official responsibilities.

– Children of foreign nationals who come to America with the intention of obtaining citizenship by giving birth.

– Children born in America through paid commercial surrogacy.

This order also included children of some employees of foreign embassies and consular offices. The US administration argued that individuals in these groups do not fall under the category of receiving birthright citizenship under the US Constitution.

What Did the Court Say?

The court rejected the administration's argument, clarifying that the President cannot create new exceptions to citizenship at his own discretion for children born in America.

According to the ACLU, the court ruled that children falling under US law cannot be deprived of their birthright citizenship based on their parents' citizenship or immigration status.

Joint Legal Challenge by Various Organizations

The ACLU and other organizations filed a lawsuit against Trump's new order in a Washington court on September 28. Organizations including the Asian Law Caucus, NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund, and Democracy Defenders Fund participated in this legal campaign.

These organizations had previously attempted to challenge the new order issued in August through an old citizenship case. However, a separate lawsuit was later filed against the new order.

Another Blow After Supreme Court's Old Ruling

This decision, which came on Wednesday, is another legal defeat for the Trump administration's citizenship policy. Previously, in June, the Supreme Court had ruled to protect the rights of children at risk of losing citizenship due to Trump's first order.

The new ruling has created further obstacles for the Trump administration's efforts to limit the right to birthright citizenship in America.

text:
A new report from the Government Accountability Office reveals that Immigration and Customs Enforcement paid more than four times the assessed value of a Georgia warehouse that it planned to use as a detention center.

Earlier this year, the Department of Homeland Security bought two warehouses in Social Circle and Oakwood as part of a national plan to convert facilities across the county into centers that would hold ICE detainees.

In documents obtained by CBS News Atlanta, the two sites were part of a plan by the federal agency to create new large-scale "hubs" across the country that would hold thousands of detainees by the end of the year.

Social Circle's facility was expected to house between 7,500 and 10,000 detainees. Oakwood was to be designated a "processing site," where detainees would stay for some time between three to seven days. The facility was expected to house an average daily population of 1,000 to 1,500 detainees.

Officials in both cities pushed back against the plan, citing concerns over the lack of communication and fears that the large-scale projects would severely impact infrastructure like water and sewage systems. Social Circle Social Circle officials cut off water to site of planned Georgia ICE detention "mega-center" in March, saying that the water shutoff wouldn't be removed until ICE showed how it would prevent the facility from exceeding its limited water and sewer capacity.

In a report released this month, the GAO said that it visited the warehouse ICE purchased in Social Circle to interview officials overseeing the project and observe the site as part of an examination into how the agency used its funds.

The GAO found that ICE spent around $128 million on the Social Circle warehouse, more than double its 2026 assessed value of more than $58 million. In Oakwood, the GAO said ICE spent more than $68 million compared to its assessed value of slightly less than $14 million.

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin put a pause on the $38-billion plan to scrutinize all contracts signed under former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem. The agency estimated ICE acquired 11 warehouses in total for about $1.07 billion before scaling down the initiative.

In September, ICE notified cities that they were looking into selling the Georgia properties. Earlier this month, both Social Circle and Oakwood were put up as part of a portfolio of properties by commercial real estate company Cushman & Wakefield. The other properties include warehouses in Salt Lake City, Detroit, El Paso, and Central Pennsylvania. The deadline for bids on the properties has now passed.

GAO recommended that ICE update its spending plan for detention funding and develop cost estimates with DHS before making any new investments in its detention plans. DHS officials agreed to those recommendations, the agency said.

text:
On Thursday, November 19, activists led by the Gainesville Immigrant Neighbor Inclusion Initiative (GINI) urged city commissioners to stand against the Gainesville Police Department (GPD) general order that requires officers to report suspected undocumented immigrants to the state.

This came one day after GINI held a protest outside GPD. It also comes amid efforts from student activists at the University of Florida who want to remove the UF Police Department’s 287(g) agreement with ICE.

GPD Chief Nelson Moya has argued that he’s not required to sign a 287(g) agreement, but that the law requires he and his officers to report suspected undocumented immigrants if there is “reasonable suspicion” to believe they are in the country without legal authorization.

UF student Carlos Giglio told city commissioners that the policy makes victims and witnesses scared to report. “If they can’t go to GPD, where are they supposed to go?” he said

Registered nurse Abigail Toulman said the fear of ICE is a barrier to healthcare, pointing out the reduction in urgent care usage during Operation Metro Surge in Minnesota. She said she is aware of pregnant women who are afraid to go to the hospital because of ICE. She said GPD’s policy leads to a similar result, including in cases of domestic violence and child abuse.

GINI coordinator Ethan Maia de Needell said that after first passing the policy, GPD said it was required due to Florida Statute 908.1031. He said, “When GINI and the community showed how that statute does not apply to 82.4, and countless calls demanded an explanation, Gainesville residents were then told that the city’s hands were tied because of Florida Administrative Code 11Q-2.”

Maia de Needell said city leaders were informed that Code 11Q-2 has not been adopted by the state. “Yet the order remains in place and there has been no public acknowledgment from anyone on the dais,” he said. “Your hands are not tied by any state statute, administrative code, rule or law, and your continued refusal to not call for the end of a policy that institutionalizes racial profiling, destroys public trust, and harms community safety, is unacceptable. Now that we see the state is moving to formally adopt a drafted data collection rule, are you all waiting for your decision to be made for you? We do not know when it will be passed, how long the process may take or what the final language will look like. But you all have the power today to cancel the policy and prevent more of our neighbors, including victims and witnesses, from having targets placed on their backs for ICE.”

Maia de Needell said General Order 82.4 opens the city up to liability by “requiring unauthorized GPD officers, who are not legally able to determine whether someone is unlawfully present… to investigate an individual's immigration status… " He said, "GINI is watching how this order is being implemented and working with legal organizations, such as the Community Justice Project, to explore legal action if and when appropriate… GPD’s order is also currently putting the safety and trust of victims and witnesses needlessly at risk. It is completely within your ability to carve out protections for this critical and vulnerable population by following what Florida law already actually does have in place, according to statute 908.104, Section 7. It is stated that cooperation with federal authorities does not apply to victims and witnesses of a crime if they are assisting law enforcement.”

Supervising attorney with the National Immigration Project, Tess Helgren, said she regularly engages in federal and class-action litigation to challenge unlawful immigration detention. She said the statute cited by GPD does not require them to implement the policy, and affirmed the proposed administrative rule has not been finalized or adopted.

“The GPD policy is about what officers should do when they encounter an individual they believe to be quote an unauthorized non-citizen,” said Helgren. “It provides no clear definition of who such individuals are, nor clear guidance of how officers should be conducting these stops in accordance with law, and the policy recognizes that GPD officers are not delegated to enforce federal immigration law, or trained in its application. This invitation to guess about an individual's immigration status will become an invitation to racially profile...”

Helgren went on to say, “Information collected through this policy is in service of federal immigration enforcement that has consistently and egregiously violated the law. I have personally worked with many Florida residents, including in Gainesville, who have had to challenge their unlawful immigration detention in court. Single parents separated from children, elderly individuals, people with medical needs… Since July 2025, federal courts have ruled against the government in over 22,000 cases challenging unlawful immigration detention. GPD should not adopt policies that make it more likely for our neighbors to join these statistics.”

Venezuelan-American Abigail Parrott spoke about a young and homeless Central American woman whom she advocated for.

“There were no available beds at the shelter, and at the time, a sizable encampment still existed on the surrounding land," Parrott said. "She didn't speak any English, making it even more difficult to support her or gather information, especially with about 300 other people needing crisis support in an under-resourced environment. She was understandably scared and timid. She went into the woods with the other campers who had nowhere else to go. Unfortunately, as is often the case in this line of work, men were waiting, claiming to help her, keep her safe or show her the ropes, but ultimately exploiting her vulnerability. She looked like a child and was inevitably sexually exploited. For several days, she was treated like property, much like how our current immigrant detention center treats innocent people. It didn't take long for us to notice her situation, and once we did, we worked urgently to find a safer place for her. Immigrant women face sexual abuse and violence at a rate of about 50%, nearly three times the national average. Furthermore, statistics show that women who are sexually assaulted are about 35 times more likely to be assaulted again. I cannot even imagine how much harder it is for so many immigrant women in our region who have lost their breadwinners. Wherever this young woman is now, she is likely still at risk. Yet, under policies like GPD’s Show Me Your Papers policy, she will never feel safe asking for help, and neither will other victims.”

Following public comment, Mayor Harvey Ward did not acknowledge the speakers and moved on to the next agenda item.

Commissioner Bryan Eastman spoke up to address the advocates, stating, “We as a city have worked very hard to ensure that we have that relationship between our police department and folks within our community. I am very sensitive to the topic, particularly—of anyone who is within our community, and with the resources, that we are under utilizing GPD resources for federal immigration work in the first place, much less, doing it in a community that, it's not our role. It's not our responsibility. We're also under state law... We have had our city attorney look at it... We're sort of in this funny gray area between where—between what is required and where we want to go, and where we can be. I have heard, and I would like staff to look at witnesses and victims of crime. I thought that was a very important point.”

Commissioner Casey Willits asked if an existing policy overlays all policy regarding victims and witnesses.

City Attorney Daniel Nee said GPD is “fully aware” of the provisions of the law that protect victims and witnesses from immigration-related investigations.

Willits suggested there be a higher threshold than “reasonable suspicion.”

City Manager Andrew Persons said they’ll follow up on Willits’ comments. Persons added that Moya signs U-visas for victims and witnesses to protect them from deportation.

“I think everyone is doing their best here to provide the protection we can for our immigrant community...” said Commissioner James Ingle. “If we've got good policies that people don't know about, those policies don't give any comfort to the people that need to come forward... If we can take a look at what we can do to make that more explicit... or make sure those protections are there, or if they're not, to the extent that we can."

NY, UNITED STATES, November 26, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ —

Raisa Cohen, Retired U.S. Immigration Judge and Principal of Cohen Immigration Law Group, P.C., Draws on Experience Across Government, the Bench, and Private Practice to Guide Clients Through Complex Immigration Matters

Queens, New York – Raisa Cohen is a retired U.S. Immigration Judge and accomplished immigration attorney with more than two decades of experience across government service, the judiciary, and private practice. Today she serves as Principal of Cohen Immigration Law Group, P.C., where she represents individuals and families in complex, high-stakes immigration matters nationwide. She also advises fellow attorneys on litigation strategy, motions, appeals, removal defense, and federal court cases. Her areas of focus include complex immigration law, immigration litigation, and immigration court proceedings. An immigrant and former refugee from Uzbekistan, Raisa brings both professional depth and personal understanding to her work.

Raisa’s passion for immigration law took shape at St. John’s University School of Law, where she participated in the Immigrants’ Rights Clinic. After earning her Juris Doctor, she began her legal career with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security as an Assistant Chief Counsel and ICE prosecutor. In that role, she represented the government in complex removal proceedings and handled matters involving national security, human rights violations, immigration fraud, and other high-stakes issues. She went on to serve as a U.S. Immigration Judge with the U.S. Department of Justice. From the bench, she presided over removal proceedings and adjudicated cases involving asylum, withholding of removal, cancellation of removal, waivers, adjustment of status, human trafficking, persecution, and unaccompanied minors.

Having worked on both sides of the courtroom, Raisa offers a distinctive 360-degree perspective on the immigration system. That experience has given her a deep understanding of litigation strategy, courtroom dynamics, evidentiary standards, and due process. She retired from the immigration bench at the end of 2024 and opened a new chapter in private practice. Her professional recognition includes being named a Super Lawyer and one of the Top 50 Lawyers.

Raisa attributes her success to hard work, determination, and an immigrant mindset of gratitude and resilience. She sees success as the product of seizing every opportunity to build a better life, staying committed to one’s goals, and giving back to the community. The best career advice she has received came from the many professors, judges, and legal professionals who mentored and inspired her along the way. Their guidance, leadership, and example helped her develop the confidence and skills that have shaped her career.

For young women entering the legal profession, Raisa recommends stepping outside their comfort zones and blocking out the noise of self-doubt. She encourages them to believe in themselves and to keep trying, learning, growing, and evolving. She also urges them to celebrate their achievements and to measure progress against where they started. Comparing oneself to an ideal or to someone else’s journey, she cautions, only distracts from genuine growth.

Raisa observes that immigration law is evolving rapidly, creating significant challenges alongside meaningful opportunities. As policies and legal landscapes shift, she sees a growing need for experienced advocates who can provide knowledgeable representation. Such advocates, in her view, also play an important role in educating communities and promoting fairness throughout the immigration system.

Integrity, justice, compassion, perseverance, and service are the values most important to Raisa. She holds that everyone deserves to be treated with dignity and that true success comes from using knowledge and experience to help others. Family, philanthropy, mentorship, and giving back to the community also matter deeply to her. Beyond her practice, she is an active speaker, educator, and mentor within the immigration and broader legal communities. She regularly takes part in professional conferences, continuing legal education programs, moot court competitions, and panels on immigration law, courtroom advocacy, criminal-immigration intersections, and enforcement developments. She is involved with the American Immigration Lawyers Association, the Roundtable of Former Immigration Judges, the New York State Trial Lawyers Association, and the American Bar Association.

From refugee to prosecutor, judge, and advocate, Raisa has devoted her career to a system she understands from every angle. Her work remains grounded in fairness and compassion, offering steady guidance to individuals and families facing an often overwhelming process. Through her advocacy, teaching, and mentorship, Raisa Cohen continues to help others find their footing and to strengthen the integrity of immigration justice.

text:
On Monday, a federal judge permanently barred the Trump administration from penalizing individuals and organizations who submit evidence to the International Criminal Court (ICC), in a victory for organizations that have faced sanctions for their efforts to bring accountability for the genocide in Gaza.

Monday’s ruling by Judge Jesse M. Furman expanded and made permanent a previous court order, issued in October, that blocked the Trump administration from imposing civil or criminal liability on the organizations Democracy for the Arab World Now and Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide.

The two groups had sued the Trump administration in July after President Donald Trump issued an executive order in February threatening fines and up to 20 years in prison for individuals or groups that share evidence with the ICC, UN Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territories Francesca Albanese, or Palestinian human rights groups Al-Haq, Al Mezan, and the Palestinian Center for Human Rights.

This week’s court order extended protections to all Americans who provide evidence to or advocate before the ICC, stating that bringing evidence to the ICC is First Amendment-protected speech. The ruling also rejected the Trump administration’s claims that the U.S. must be protected from the ICC, declaring that the government has failed to establish why it is necessary to penalize every instance of evidence provision to the court.

The ruling is a victory against Trump’s long-standing effort to undermine and attack the ICC for its investigations into war crimes committed in Gaza, which culminated in institutional sanctions against the entire court last month. The Trump administration had already sanctioned 11 ICC judges and prosecutors, preventing them from traveling to the U.S., freezing their U.S.-based assets, and severely limiting their ability to undertake financial transactions.

Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and even former Secretary of State Antony Blinken have all decried the ICC for its attempts to investigate and issue arrest warrants for Israeli officials over the genocide in Gaza.

“This landmark ruling dismantles a core part of Trump’s ICC draconian sanctions regime,” said Omar Shakir, executive director at Democracy for the Arab World Now. “The court has affirmed that every American has the constitutional right to advocate for justice on Palestine without fear of reprisal.”

Joseph Pace, attorney for Democracy for the Arab World Now and Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide, spoke to the weight of the victory.

“Typically, courts can now only offer relief to the plaintiffs — no matter how many thousands of nonparties are being victimized by an unconstitutional policy,” he said. “This decision is a major victory, not just because it invalidates a key part of the ICC sanctions’ regime, but because it universally bars the Trump Administration from using the sanctions to penalize anyone, anywhere in the country, for exercising their First Amendment rights.”

As a result of the decision, rights groups and individuals will be able to work with Albanese and Palestinian rights groups once again.

While the ruling protects evidence submission and advocacy, it leaves intact previously-applied sanctions that have frozen ICC members’ assets, funds, and financial transactions, including on individuals like Albanese.

In a separate ruling on Monday, Furman ruled against three ICC judges who asked to be removed from Trump’s sanctions list and for their frozen assets to be unblocked. The judge denied a preliminary injunction in their favor, stating that “deference here is owed not only to the president but also to Congress.” Furman also gave weight to Trump’s use of an International Emergency Economic Powers Act when he declared a national emergency over the ICC’s actions.

text:
Immigration & Customs Enforcement said a former Le Moyne swimmer overstayed his permitted visit, leading to his detainment.

In a statement sent to CNY Central, ICE said 23-year-old Belal Mahmoud Saeed Hamad Aly was detained on Nov. 23. The federal agency said Aly was admitted to the United States in February 2018 on a "temporary basis" and that it expired in August 2018.

The full statement by ICE, as it was sent to CNY Central, is posted below:

On November 23, ICE arrested 23-year-old Belal Mahmoud Saeed Hamad Aly, an illegal alien from Egypt.

Aly was admitted to visit the United States in February 2018 on a temporary basis, with authorization that expired 8 years ago in August 2018. Against our nation’s laws, Aly overstayed his welcome and failed to depart once his permission to be in the United States ended. He will remain in ICE custody pending the outcome of his removal proceedings.

To be clear, a pending case does NOT confer legal status in this country, and the expiration of status is NOT a suggestion—you must leave our country when your authorization expires. If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return.

We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the CBP Home App. The United States is offering illegal aliens $3,000 and a free flight to self-deport now. We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream. If not, our message is clear: we will find you, we will arrest you, and we will deport you.

A GoFundMe campaign was launched to help cover legal expenses and support the family of Aly.

The campaign, titled “Standing with Belal Aly and His Family,” was organized by Yusef Amer on behalf of Aly’s family and friends. It says they have received few answers about why Aly was detained or what happens next.

Aly’s mother-in-law, Kathy Rumney, also addressed his detention in a Facebook post. She identified Aly as her son-in-law and said he was taken by ICE on Monday, adding that the family is working to get him released. She asked people to support or share the fundraiser.

The GoFundMe seeks donations to cover an immigration attorney, legal and court fees, possible bond, and living expenses for Aly’s wife, Aya. It also lists travel and phone costs to help the family stay in contact with him.

In a statement sent to CNY Central, Le Moyne College President Joseph Della Posta said he "can confirm that Belal did graduate with a bachelor's in physics in 2025 and was a member of our swim team while he was a student at Le Moyne. The College is aware of his detainment."

According to Le Moyne College, Aly attended PSLA at Fowler High School in Syracuse, graduating in 2021 with an advanced Regents diploma and a New York State Seal of Biliteracy in Arabic. He was a physics major and competed on Le Moyne’s men’s swimming and diving team.

During his freshman season in 2021-22, Aly finished fourth in the 200-yard freestyle, fifth in the 500-yard freestyle and seventh in the 100-yard freestyle at the NE10 Championship. He also won regular-season competitions in the 50-yard freestyle, 100-yard freestyle, 200-yard freestyle and 100-yard butterfly.

The GoFundMe says Aly works as a technical engineer at Indium and is pursuing a master’s degree in mechanical engineering at Clarkson University.

CNY Central has reached out to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement for additional information and comment. This story will be updated if they respond.

text:
Kampala — The National Citizenship and Immigration Control (NCIC) has denied that human rights activist Praise Aloikin Opoloje was abducted at Entebbe International Airport, saying immigration officers involved in the incident were carrying out their lawful duties in coordination with security agencies.

However, the immigration authority has not explained why Opoloje was detained, which security agencies were involved in the operation, or where she was taken after the airport encounter, leaving questions about the circumstances surrounding her detention. A statement issued by the Ministry of Internal Affairs Public Relations Office on Wednesday, November 25, said: "NCIC clarifies that no abduction took place.

The officers were carrying out their lawful duties in coordination with relevant government institutions, including security agencies, in accordance with established procedures. " The statement followed widespread concern on social media after Opoloje reported being held at the airport shortly after returning to Uganda. In a post on X, formerly Twitter, the activist said immigration officials had confiscated her national identity card without explaining why she was being held.

She also said the officers were making telephone calls to another officer expected to collect her.

Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines

"On a serious note though, I am being abducted at Entebbe International Airport. They have confiscated my ID with no explanation, but they are making calls with a certain afande supposed to pick me up from the airport," Opoloje wrote. In a video recorded at the airport and circulated online, Opoloje questioned the officials about the reason for holding her.

"I'm trying to find out what my offence is. I'm just coming back home, and I'm not getting an answer," she said. The incident prompted civil society organisation Agora Discourse to issue an abduction alert, saying it had been unable to establish her whereabouts several hours after she recorded the encounter.

The organisation called for an explanation from the airport authorities, while activists amplified the hashtag #FreePraiseAloikin and demanded information about her whereabouts and safety.

In its response, the immigration authority criticised what it described as sensationalised and misleading accounts circulating on social media. It warned that unverified narratives could cause unnecessary alarm, damage the reputations of officers and undermine their work. The NCIC also urged members of the public to refrain from photographing or recording immigration officers while they are performing official duties.

"While public accountability and the right to seek information are recognised, recording officers with the intention of intimidating, provoking, harassing or misrepresenting them, or subsequently circulating such footage in a misleading or disparaging manner, is unacceptable," the statement reads.

The authority said it had instituted legal action against individuals who had deliberately published defamatory, malicious or otherwise unlawful content targeting immigration officers. It, however, did not identify those facing legal action or disclose the nature of the cases.

The statement also acknowledged the public's right to question government institutions and demand accountability, but said this should be exercised with respect for the rights and dignity of others.

"Being in public service does not make them targets for harassment, intimidation or online humiliation," the statement said.

Opoloje's latest reported detention comes about six weeks after she was granted bail by Buganda Road Chief Magistrate's Court following her arrest in September. On September 28, she was charged with unlawfully using a SIM card registered in another person's name, contrary to Regulation 29 of the Regulation of Interception of Communications Regulations, 2024. She denied the charge and was remanded to Luzira Women's Prison.

The court granted her bail on October 14, with conditions that included restrictions on travelling outside Uganda without court permission. Her September arrest had also attracted criticism from human rights defenders after associates alleged that armed security operatives took her from Namungoona Police Station, where she had initially been held.

The Uganda Law Society subsequently demanded her release and questioned the circumstances surrounding her disappearance from police custody. It remains unclear whether Wednesday's airport detention is connected to her earlier case or a separate security operation. The latest incident has also attracted political attention because Opoloje had announced plans to unveil the logo of a new political party, Anti-Cabbages, on Thursday, November 26.

The activist has used her social media platforms to criticise Chief of Defence Forces General Muhoozi Kainerugaba and his political ambitions. However, neither the immigration authority nor other government agencies have publicly linked the airport incident to her political activities.

The immigration authority concluded by urging the public to verify information before sharing it and to allow relevant authorities to carry out their work without unnecessary interference.

It said it remained committed to lawful, professional and humane immigration management while safeguarding the rights, dignity and safety of both the public and its officers.
