text:
Even when it comes to pregnant immigrants, the Trump administration has proven itself indifferent. In the first 16 months of the Republican’s second term, 733 pregnant women remained in the custody of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), most of them for extended periods. One of them was detained for seven months. Among those facing high-risk pregnancies, few had access to specialized medical care and were not released immediately.

These revelations appear in a report published Tuesday by the Women’s Refugee Commission (WRC), which questions the federal administration’s lack of empathy toward a particularly vulnerable population — both in ICE detention centers, which have been repeatedly cited for mistreating immigrants — and in local jail facilities that held contracts with the government and where most of these women were held.

The report accompanies a lawsuit that the WRC and organizations such as the Venezuelan Association of Massachusetts and the Workers’ Center of Central New York filed in a District of Columbia court. In it, they demand that ICE and the Department of Homeland Security put an end to the ordeal suffered by these women, who are caught up in Trump’s immigration crackdown.

“Immigration detention has become a black box of impunity,” said Zain Lakhani, director of the WRC’s Migrant Rights and Justice Program, in a statement. This organization, Lakhani said, has documented “a substantial increase in the number of pregnant women in detention and brought to light grave concerns about their treatment and care.” “Now, this data shows that these abuses are happening at scale,” he added.

Among these abuses, it is notable that of some 128 women diagnosed with high-risk pregnancies, only four were transferred to a “higher level of care.” The report details at least 16 cases of miscarriages recorded between January 2025 and February 2026.

Malnourished and sleeping on the floor

During Joe Biden’s administration, between 2021 and 2024, ICE released most of the pregnant women it had detained — either on parole or under a promise to appear in court.

But at the start of Trump’s second term, the number of women in detention began to rise as the president’s immigration crackdown intensified. From nine pregnant women in ICE custody in January 2025, the number rose to 128 last March, representing a 1,320% increase. Most of them — about 75% — were held in state or local facilities under contract with the government, which, according to the WRC report, “have lower medical standards and higher taxpayer costs.”

The report estimates that ICE spent at least $4 million on the detention of 557 pregnant women, not including the costs of medical care.

The Department of Homeland Security has not commented on this report and lawsuit, but in the summer of 2025, in response to an investigation by the office of Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff — which documented 14 credible reports of mistreatment of pregnant women in ICE custody — the agency denied having neglected these migrants.

The reports compiled by Ossoff’s office point to deficiencies such as a lack of adequate medical care and timely checkups, the absence of emergency care when needed, the denial of adequate snacks and meals, and the requirement to sleep on the floor due to overcrowding.

In its response, DHS stated that these women received medical care and nutritional support, and maintained that “the detention of pregnant women is rare and subject to rigorous oversight and review.” It added that “no pregnant woman has been forced to sleep on the floor.”

Seven months in custody

Human rights advocates, Democratic members of Congress, and journalistic investigations have documented an alarming increase in the number of pregnant women detained by ICE during the current administration, which is determined to deport as many undocumented immigrants as possible.

“Advocates interviewed more than a dozen women, and in their letter, also describe disturbing accounts of shackling and use of restraint during transport, solitary confinement, denial of prenatal vitamins, inadequate food, delayed or substandard medical care, and lack of interpretation during medical visits. One woman experienced a dangerous infection after a miscarriage due to ICE’s medical neglect,” states a letter sent by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) to ICE in October 2025.

The indiscriminate detention of these women demonstrates that ICE has failed to comply with its own directive, established in 2021, which stipulates that, except in exceptional circumstances or for other legally justified reasons, pregnant women, women in the postpartum period, or breastfeeding women should not remain in the agency’s custody.

In its recent report, the WRC places special emphasis on the length of time these women spend in detention. During the Biden administration, the average was about five days. Under the Trump administration, that figure skyrocketed to 43 days — a 750% increase.

At least 145 women were held in custody for 90 days or more. The report highlights the case of one woman who was detained for 219 days — nearly seven months into her pregnancy.

To collect reports from these migrants, the WRC launched a tool called the Detention Pregnancy Tracker in September 2025. Through this tool, it gathered testimonies from women who suffered miscarriages, were malnourished, or did not receive specialized medical care.

The organization even traveled to Honduras to interview recently deported individuals. “There, we heard testimonies from women with life-threatening conditions who were denied medical care,” the group notes.

text:
Over the weekend, the Massachusetts Lottery shared a picture of Ariel Velasquez-Morales smiling gently as he gripped an oversized check for US$1 million in winnings. On social media, commenters congratulated him, with one person writing they hoped he would be able to “make any dreams come true.”

But Velasquez-Morales was arrested Tuesday by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in East Boston, the same neighborhood where he bought the $10 winning scratch-off ticket from a local market.

He now faces deportation as ICE says the Salvadoran national has been in the country illegally for more than a decade.

“Looks like his luck ran out,” said ICE Assistant Director of Public Affairs Micah Bock in a release announcing the arrest.

It is unclear whether the publication of his lottery winnings attracted ICE’s attention. ICE declined to answer questions from CNN about what led to the arrest or where Velasquez-Morales is being detained.

Velasquez-Morales illegally entered the United States in 2013, during the Obama administration, in the Rio Grande Valley in Texas. Border Patrol agents issued him a notice to appear before an immigration judge, and he was released into the country with a list of free legal service providers, the agency said.

“A Department of Justice immigration judge ordered Velasquez-Morales removed in 2014, but he illegally remained in the country,” the ICE release said.

He will remain in ICE custody pending his removal from the U.S.. CNN has been unable to determine whether he has legal representation.

U.S. President Donald Trump has overseen a massive immigration crackdown after promising to lead the largest deportation operation in U.S. history. In his second term, arrests have shifted away from the border and focused more on the interior of the country, where aggressive tactics have become a hallmark of ICE’s ramped-up detention efforts.

By July 2026, there were nearly 66,000 detainees in ICE custody, an increase of nearly 70 per cent from the total detained when Trump took office the year prior.

But after a Republican wipeout in the midterms, Trump has publicly questioned whether the tactics were too hard-line and unpopular. It remains to be seen, though, whether he is considering significant changes to his immigration policies.

“Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the United States and will be removed as quickly as possible,” ICE said in its release on Velasquez-Morales. “Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin’s leadership, ICE is delivering on its mission to enforce our nation’s immigration laws, restore accountability and protect American communities.”

Velasquez-Morales was playing the lottery’s “$2,000,000 50X Cashword,” in which players scratch cards resembling crossword puzzles to try to reveal complete words. It was the first puzzle he had scratched, the lottery said, and he matched 11 words.

He chose to accept his winnings in cash, which would give him a one-time lump sum of $650,000 before taxes, according to ICE. It is not clear what will happen to his winnings.

Massachusetts lottery participants do not need to be legal residents of the state to play, but they must be 21 or older and be located in the state at the time they purchase or play.

CNN has sought comment from the Massachusetts State Lottery Commission.

The Supreme Court agreed to review the case on June 29.

text:
The United States Supreme Court will examine next Monday a case that could determine the immigration future of Cubans and other immigrants who obtained asylum in the country but later lost that protection without having secured permanent residency.

According to the official Supreme Court record, the justices will hear oral arguments in the case Wassily v. Blanche (No. 25-842), in which two immigrants are claiming the ability to obtain permanent residency despite having their asylum status terminated due to criminal convictions.

The legal controversy revolves around whether a foreigner who received asylum retains the ability to apply for a green card through that avenue after losing such protection.

The ruling could have consequences for both the primary beneficiaries of asylum and their spouses and children, when these have obtained their immigration status derivatively.

What is at stake before the Supreme Court?

The dispute centers on the interpretation of section 209(b) of the United States Immigration and Nationality Act, which allows for permanent residency to be granted to foreign nationals who have been granted asylum and meet certain requirements.

Among those conditions are having accumulated at least one year of physical presence in the United States after receiving asylum, continuing to meet the corresponding legal requirements, and being admissible as an immigrant, except for the exceptions provided by law.

The federal courts of appeals for the Second and Fourth Circuits have determined that those who lose their asylum are automatically excluded from the possibility of adjusting their status through that route.

The Fifth Circuit, on the other hand, has considered that the termination of asylum does not necessarily prevent one from applying for permanent residency.

In its submission made on October 2, the Department of Justice argued that the legislation reserves that possibility for immigrants who maintain their asylum status.

The plaintiffs' lawyers argued in their reply on November 2 that the law does not explicitly establish that restriction and that the prior grant of asylum can still serve as a legal basis to apply for status adjustment.

A favorable ruling for the plaintiffs would not guarantee the acquisition of permanent residency, but it would allow for the individual evaluation of applications from those who have lost their asylum and meet the other legal requirements.

The cases that reached the Supreme Court

The protagonists of the litigation are Tamer S. Wassily, an Egyptian citizen who obtained asylum in the United States in 2000, and Byron E. Velasquez Arreaga, a Guatemalan citizen who received that protection in 1996.

Wassily lost his status after being convicted of harassment and endangering the welfare of a minor. An immigration judge initially granted him permanent residency, but that decision was later overturned by the Board of Immigration Appeals.

Velasquez Arreaga, for his part, lost his asylum after convictions related to driving under the influence of alcohol and also saw his opportunity to adjust his immigration status thwarted.

Both appealed to the Second Circuit Court of Appeals, which ruled against them on August 7, 2025. The Supreme Court agreed to review the case on June 29.

Why could family members also be affected?

One of the most sensitive aspects of litigation is that its consequences could extend to people who have not committed any crime.

The U.S. federal regulations stipulate that the termination of the principal beneficiary's asylum also means the loss of derivative asylum for their spouse and children.

If the Supreme Court supports the Government's interpretation, those relatives could also be prevented from applying for permanent residency through asylum, even if they are not responsible for the circumstances that led to the loss of the holder's status.

The plaintiffs' lawyers even warned about the potential consequences for victims of domestic violence who obtained immigration protection through the asylum granted to their aggressors.

The regulations allow, however, that affected family members can submit their own asylum applications if they meet the legal requirements.

How could the decision affect Cubans?

The upcoming ruling is particularly important for Cuban immigrants who have already received asylum in the United States but have not yet obtained permanent residency, as well as for those who have relatives protected by derivative asylum.

However, Cubans have a migratory alternative that sets them apart from most foreigners: the Cuban Adjustment Act of 1966.

This legislation allows nationals or naturalized citizens of Cuba who have been inspected and admitted or have received a temporary stay permit known as parole, to apply for permanent residency after accumulating at least one year of physical presence in the United States and meeting the other legal requirements.

Therefore, losing asylum does not necessarily mean that a Cuban is deprived of the possibility of obtaining permanent residency through other means.

The impact of the future ruling could be greater for those Cubans who obtained asylum but do not meet the requirements of the Cuban Adjustment Act, as well as for those with criminal records that hinder their access to residency.

Among those potentially affected are certain holders of Form I-220A who have been granted asylum but lack a valid admission or parole to qualify for Cuban adjustment.

The case that the Supreme Court will examine does not directly challenge the Cuban Adjustment Act nor alter the requirements of that legislation.

It also does not represent an immediate change for those with pending asylum applications, as the controversy specifically concerns immigrants who were granted that protection and subsequently had it revoked.

What can Cubans do who are still waiting for their residency?

Those who already have approved asylum can check if they meet the requirements to apply for permanent residency using Form I-485 and determine which of the available pathways is most suitable for their circumstances.

It is advisable to consult an immigration attorney, especially if there are criminal records, ongoing deportation proceedings, or notifications regarding a potential termination of asylum.

Submitting an application for permanent residency does not, by itself, prevent authorities from initiating a procedure to revoke that immigration protection.

Other pending migration cases before the Supreme Court

The hearing next Monday will take place while the U.S. Supreme Court examines other immigration controversies that could have implications for the Cuban community.

The Supreme Court has already agreed to review whether Donald Trump can ban asylum applications at the southern border of the United States.

title: What so many people got wrong about the Kilmar Abrego Garcia case - Reason Magazine
authors: Billy Binion, Christian Britschgi, Agustina Vergara Cid, Charles Oliver, Veronique de Rugy, Meagan O'Rourke
description:
Who is Kilmar Abrego Garcia?
So why was Abrego Garcia still here until just this week?
This was in August 2025; Abrego Garcia said he was willing to go.
This is relevant here, because the African countries the Trump administration set its sights on for Abrego Garcia—Uganda, Eswatini, and Ghana—did not agree.
Put differently, Abrego Garcia could have been gone long ago.
text:
Who is Kilmar Abrego Garcia? For the last year and a half, that question has animated the fight over the Trump administration's approach to immigration. Is he most accurately a "Maryland man" whose American wife, family, and work grounded him in the community? Or is he merely an illegal immigrant whose removal from the country was long overdue?

As of today, he is technically neither. The Salvadoran national is now a tourist in Madrid, having just self-deported to Spain.

His departure from the U.S. caps off a saga that became a microcosm for the immigration debate. It was, in some ways, an apt case for that. But often not in the way people thought.

Abrego Garcia catapulted to a subject of national discussion and derision in March 2025 after the government deported him to CECOT, the notorious megaprison in El Salvador. This was complicated, most notably because a court had granted him a withholding of removal to that very country. (Abrego Garcia came to the U.S. illegally in 2012 at 16 years old because, he says, the Barrio 18 gang had threatened him and his family.)

His deportation was only the first domino. The Trump administration subsequently said it had sent him to El Salvador as the result of an "administrative error." In turn, the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland ruled that the executive branch was obligated to "facilitate" Abrego Garcia's return, which the Supreme Court affirmed unanimously.

After many protestations, the administration facilitated that return in June of the same year. So why was Abrego Garcia still here until just this week? The answer to that question does tell you something, yet it is also where this controversy has been the most confused.

When Abrego Garcia arrived back in the U.S., the Department of Justice brought a criminal indictment against him for allegedly participating in a scheme to transport undocumented immigrants. "We got him out of here," Todd Blanche, then the deputy attorney general, told Fox News' Laura Ingraham in June 2025. "And a judge in Maryland and many members of Congress…questioned that decision" to deport him. So the government "started…investigating him."

Wrapped up among those charges was an offer: The government had solicited Costa Rica to accept Abrego Garcia, and the country—which has a standing agreement with the U.S. to take deportees who cannot go to their home countries—had accepted. This was in August 2025; Abrego Garcia said he was willing to go.

But that proposition came with a catch. He would need to plead guilty in the criminal case, something he refused to do, as he maintains his innocence. When the Trump administration was not able to extract that win—a P.R. victory would have been helpful after it was forced to bring him back from El Salvador—it set out on a legal odyssey to instead deport him to Africa. (The indictment was ultimately dismissed altogether in May after a judge ruled it was tainted by vindictiveness.)

It is true that people here illegally are not permitted to point anywhere on a map and demand their deportation destination of choice. At a minimum, the receiving country has to agree to accept them. This is relevant here, because the African countries the Trump administration set its sights on for Abrego Garcia—Uganda, Eswatini, and Ghana—did not agree. (When news broke that the U.S. government would seek to send him to Eswatini, for example, the country's spokesperson said in a statement that the country had "not received any communication regarding this person.") The Trump administration's final attempt, Liberia, agreed only on a "temporary" basis.

Put differently, Abrego Garcia could have been gone long ago. It's defensible to portray his protracted stay in the U.S. as a reflection of America's immigration quagmire. But it wasn't rolls and rolls of red tape, or radical judges, or administrative paralysis, or that this individual simply had nowhere to go. These last many months, Abrego Garcia has been in the U.S. because the government made sure of it, explicitly barring him from self-deporting so it could attempt to send him somewhere it viewed as undesirable. It is part of the Trump administration's larger push to ramp up so-called third-country deportations, including to places where Americans are not supposed to travel for any reason.

text:
MINNEAPOLIS -- Documents about Guatemala, Mexico and El Salvador prepared for use in immigration courts, where asylum denial rates have soared to 94%, use cherry-picked data, careful phrasing and, in some cases, facts that don't stand up to scrutiny to create misleading depictions of countries that are, in fact, often plagued by violence, government corruption and police inaction.

They appear designed to make it easier for judges to deny asylum to people from those nations fleeing domestic violence and criminal gangs, painting pictures of life in their home countries that often clash with reality.

In its travel advisories, the U.S. State Department warns Americans not to visit Honduras' Gracias a Dios region, alerting them to violent crime, armed robbery, murder and active terrorist groups.

But for Hondurans, "Overall, Gracias a Dios is a low-crime, functioning department," says a State Department background report obtained by The Associated Press.

The reports have been "reverse-engineered," said Elliott Young, a professor at Lewis & Clark College who analyzed the documents for the college's Migration and Asylum Lab.

"They're trying to hit the most frequent kinds of (asylum) cases that come up and provide counterevidence to the overwhelming evidence that these are dangerous places," said Young, a scholar of Latin America and asylum law who has testified as an expert witness in more than 700 asylum cases.

In a statement, the State Department said that in line with U.S. laws and regulations it "may provide information about conditions in foreign countries" to immigration courts and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. The Justice Department, which oversees immigration courts, did not respond to a request for comment on what role the reports play in influencing asylum decisions.

Cutting back on asylum has been a centerpiece of President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown dating to his first term, when he dismissed migrants waiting in Mexico to get into the U.S. as "not legitimate asylum-seekers."

Most asylum seekers, the Republican president said, were fleeing poverty.

"Asylum is a very special protection intended only for those fleeing government persecution based on race, religion and other protected status," he said in a 2018 White House appearance.

In fact, while asylum was largely seen after World War II as a way to protect people fleeing political persecution, the definition was expanded long ago, including to encompass some people fleeing domestic and criminal violence.

Legal and illegal migration, particularly from Latin America, has exploded over the past two decades as people have sought more economic opportunity, with increasing asylum claims based on safety fears from domestic partners and criminal gangs.

Even during former President Joe Biden's years, most asylum claims were rejected.

But denials have jumped from roughly 72% at the end of that Democratic administration to 94% in June under Trump, according to the data research nonprofit Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse.

Trump was elected to a second term in part by focusing on frustrated voters who had seen illegal immigration soar under Biden, with border arrests from Mexico reaching a record 250,000 in December 2023. The asylum system, meanwhile, faced a backlog of millions of cases.

The Trump administration has reshaped immigration courts as part of its push to increase deportations, organizing mass hearings, authorizing military lawyers as immigration judges, and giving judges more leeway to summarily dismiss claims.

Immigration judges must weigh whether people seeking asylum based on domestic violence or criminal threats have a reasonable fear of persecution because of their race, religion, nationality, political views or an often-debated catch-all category, "membership in a particular social group." They also have to show that their government can't or won't protect them and that they can't move elsewhere in their home country to escape persecution.

The reports offer what can sometimes seem like travel brochure descriptions of life in these countries.

They mention good schools, low crime, quality hospitals and constitutions that protect individual rights, with brief notes that "the availability of services" can vary across each country.

Take El Salvador, where the government of President Nayib Bukele has long faced accusations of widespread human rights abuses, including torture.

The State Department report takes a far more generous view of the situation, noting the government's approach to rights abuses "is no different than that of developed countries in Europe and North America, including the United States itself," and highlighting a handful of prosecutions tied to the civil war, which ended in 1992.

"In any country, a rogue official can mistreat those under their power," it says.

For Honduras' Gracias a Dios province, violent crime rates "compare favorably with rates of violent crime in many parts of the United States," says the report.

Former officials and advocates say the six-page reports pale in comparison to traditional State Department human rights reports, lengthy dissections of more than 100 nations around the world, which under the second Trump administration have been truncated and delayed.

"These shorter reports clearly don't address the full range of human rights issues that the country reports have traditionally addressed," said Scott Busby, former deputy assistant secretary in the Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights and Labor at the State Department and now a senior adviser at the group Human Rights First.

They are "especially problematic given that the country reports themselves for last year have yet to be issued," he said.

In many ways, the reports appear aimed most directly at asylum regulations around a person's ability to escape persecution by simply moving.

Those regulations are key for anyone seeking asylum based on domestic or criminal violence.

The reports highlight specific parts of each country, mentioning places like an off-the-beaten-track tourist destination in Guatemala and a province in El Salvador that has low crime and 24-hour emergency medical care.

But those mentions only tell part of the story.

"The fact that there may be pockets of a country that are relatively safe for some people doesn't mean that everybody can just move to that part of the country," said Neela Chakravartula, an asylum attorney with the Center for Gender & Refugee Studies at the University of California College of the Law, San Francisco.

If that were the case, Chakravartula said: "We'd all be living in Malibu."

Information for this article was contributed by Joshua Goodman of The Associated Press.

"I like Kevin, but what does "bipartisan immigration reform” mean?
When I called for bipartisan immigration reform, Vice President JD Vance answered with one word: amnesty.
text:
Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt is calling on Congress to work toward immigration reform, even after being criticized by the vice president.

Earlier this month, Oklahoma GOP Gov. Kevin Stitt called for Trump to push for a bipartisan immigration reform effort.

“It’s not that complicated,” Stitt said during an interview with Politico. “But the problem is Washington, DC, each side thinks they’re winning on it. That’s why you saw this huge swing in the midterms.”

Following the interview, Vice President JD Vance took to X to ask Stitt what "bipartisan immigration reform" means to him.

"I like Kevin, but what does "bipartisan immigration reform” mean? If you mean making it harder for megacompanies to defraud our visa system, great. If you mean we should pass legislation to make it harder for employers to violate our immigration law, I'm all ears. But to a lot of people, this sounds like an effort to give amnesty to people who have broken our laws. It is morally and electorally disastrous," Vance said in the post.

Now, Gov. Stitt is doubling down on his position.

In an opinion piece published in The Oklahoman, Stitt said leaders should use President Trump's "60 Minutes" interview as an invitation to "help build what comes next."

"Not everyone in Washington has accepted that invitation. When I called for bipartisan immigration reform, Vice President JD Vance answered with one word: amnesty. He said my proposal "sounds like an effort to give amnesty to people who have broken our laws." I have never called for amnesty. But the vice president and his allies use the word like a dog whistle for an online audience. It confuses the issue and, by design, shuts down a debate that deserves rigor.

'Amnesty' has become the weapon of choice for ending a conversation our country badly needs to have. The president has opened the door to a serious discussion. Reducing a complex issue to a single word is a dangerous game, and it slams that door shut," Stitt wrote.

Stitt says he has urged the Trump administration to consider visa reform that makes state governments partners with the federal government.

"In Oklahoma, I support our farmers, manufacturers and aerospace employers. When they succeed, they create opportunity for generations of Americans, while we retool, retrain and upskill our own workers. A legal visa system that fits local economies and a firm national security posture are not in conflict. We can have both," he wrote.

Stitt says Congress has the responsibility to deliver a safe and orderly visa system to the American people.

"If our country ever drifts toward citizenship without people paying their dues, it will be because Republicans did not finish the job of reforming the system when we held a full majority," he wrote.

Recently, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that he is open to a bipartisan immigration deal where individuals under DACA can get permanent legal residence, but is against amnesty. He said that amnesty is never going to be a solution and that the Trump administration won’t allow it to happen.

text:
A United States federal judge has blocked President Donald Trump’s latest attempt to restrict birthright citizenship, delivering another legal setback to the administration’s immigration agenda.

US District Judge Christopher Cooper issued the injunction in Washington, DC, on Wednesday in a class-action lawsuit filed on behalf of children who would be denied citizenship under Trump’s executive order.

The ruling prevents the administration from enforcing the August order against children covered by the lawsuit.

Trump’s directive sought to limit automatic citizenship for children born in the United States to certain foreign parents, including those whose mothers were unlawfully present or temporarily in the country and whose fathers were neither American citizens nor lawful permanent residents.

The latest decision represents the second time a federal court has blocked the administration’s effort to implement the restrictions.

A federal judge in Maryland had issued an earlier injunction in September, also preventing enforcement of the executive order.

The administration must now successfully challenge both rulings before it can proceed with implementing the policy.

In his decision, Cooper said the legal position on birthright citizenship was clear, pointing to longstanding Supreme Court precedent.

“The merits in this case are clear-cut,” the judge said.

He added that the Supreme Court had twice confirmed that children born in the United States were citizens, except for a limited number of recognised exceptions involving people not subject to American jurisdiction.

The dispute centres on the interpretation of the Fourteenth Amendment to the US Constitution, which establishes citizenship for people born or naturalised in the country and subject to its jurisdiction.

The constitutional provision has historically been interpreted to grant citizenship to most children born on American soil, regardless of their parents’ immigration status.

Trump initially attempted to introduce restrictions on birthright citizenship through an executive order after returning to the White House.

However, the Supreme Court rejected his initial effort to impose the policy, prompting the administration to introduce a revised order in August.

The latest court ruling now presents another obstacle to that revised approach.

Cody Wofsy, a lawyer with the American Civil Liberties Union who represented the plaintiffs, welcomed the decision and argued that the president must accept the existing constitutional protections.

The legal battle is expected to remain a major test of presidential authority, immigration policy and the interpretation of constitutional citizenship rights in the United States.

text:
A man and a woman who detailed traumatic experiences while being arrested during Operation Midway Blitz have filed separate lawsuits against the federal government.

Dayanne Figueroa and Luis Jesus Acosta Gutierrez each filed lawsuits Monday in the Northern District of Illinois seeking compensation and accountability for the actions of the federal agents involved in their arrests.

Acosta Gutierrez was driving to a mechanic to get his car fixed in Elgin on the morning of Dec. 6 when an unmarked vehicle carrying federal agents cut in front of him before striking his car from the passenger side.

“The car came very close to mine and hit me from behind. My car spun around, made a 360-degree turn. I was looking right at them, face to face. I grabbed my phone and my wallet and ran,” Acosta Gutierrez told a Sun-Times reporter in Spanish. “I had never seen anything like that in my life. I wasn’t going to be arrested; I hadn’t done anything.”

He said the agents yelled “Stop, cabrón! Stop! It’ll be worse!”

“The whole process felt like psychological and mental torture,” he said.

While running, he came across a man taking out the trash and told him to flee due to the presence of agents.

The two fled into the man’s home in the 1600 block of Maple Lane, where Acosta Gutierrez stayed barricaded for hours as crowds of nearby residents, protesters and rapid responders formed.

Acosta Gutierrez, who came to the United States from Venezuela in 2023 to work and create a better life for himself and for his family, tried showing agents his work permit and Social Security card, to no avail.

Eventually, agents got to Acosta Gutierrez and struck him in the face as they detained him, he said.

“I started asking them to forgive me for the trouble,” he said. “They grabbed me with long guns pointed at me and made me feel like a criminal.”

After his arrest, Acosta Gutierrez spent several weeks at Miami Correctional Facility in Indiana before being taken briefly to Louisiana. From there, the government flew him to Venezuela. His departure was legally classified as voluntary, according to his attorney, Robert Held.

The Department of Homeland Security have previously called Acosta Gutierrez a suspected member of the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua — a claim he denies.

“I’m not the kind of person they say I am, a criminal or a gang member. This has affected my life in every way, economically and mentally,” he said. “I’m sick now. I’m not the same as before. And I want justice — not just for me, but also for people who are going through what I went through, which was unjust.”

Acosta Gutierrez is seeking $7,935 for the damage done to his car during the encounter with the federal agents.

About two months earlier, on the morning of Oct. 10, Figueroa, a United States citizen, was driving to work after dropping her son off at school when federal agents in an unmarked red van trying to drive away from a hostile crowd swerved into her vehicle in the 1600 block of West Hubbard Street in West Town, according to the complaint.

Agents forcibly dragged her from her car, handcuffed her, knelt on her body near a surgical incision and detained her despite pleas that she was recovering from kidney surgery, the complaint states.

“What happened to me is what happens to people when our government is allowed to act with impunity and trample our Constitution,” Figueroa said in a press release. “They have made a mockery of everything this country claims to stand for, and I hope this lawsuit helps hold those responsible for my attack accountable, and puts an end to this horrific abuse.”

Figueroa’s lawsuit alleges false arrest, false imprisonment, assault, battery, negligence and the intentional infliction of emotional distress .

She was one of five U.S. citizens who spoke at a congressional public forum, last December. They wanted to counter DHS claims that the department does not arrest U.S. citizens.

Figueroa also was taken to Broadview and then to a facility in Lombard. She said the blood in her urine finally prompted agents to allow her to get medical help, and she contacted her boyfriend while in an ambulance. In all, she was in custody several hours.

“Ms. Figueroa has endured one of the most horrifying experiences imaginable — having her personal safety attacked by masked ICE agents who took the law into their own hands,” said attorney Luis Carrillo.

“She is tremendously courageous for speaking out not just for herself, but for the voiceless who cannot speak. We look forward to joining the fight for justice for her,” Carrillo said.

When asked to comment on the lawsuits, DHS referred back to earlier statements made on each arrest.

text:
(CNN) - A man won $1 million playing the Massachusetts Lottery. Days later, he was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials.

The Massachusetts Lottery shared a picture of Ariel Velasquez-Morales holding a novelty check showing off his $1 million jackpot win over the weekend. He was arrested Tuesday by ICE officials in East Boston, the same neighborhood where he bought his winning scratch-off ticket.

ICE says Velasquez-Morales is a Salvadoran national who entered the United States illegally in 2013. He was ordered to be removed the following year but remained in the country.

Velasquez-Morales will now remain in ICE custody pending his removal from the U.S.

It’s not clear what will happen to his lottery winnings. He chose to accept his winnings in cash, which would give him a one-time lump sum of $650,000 before taxes, according to ICE.

The Massachusetts Lottery only requires participants be at least 21 years old and located in the state at the time they play. They are not required to be legal residents of the state.

title: 22 states are suing the feds for ending immigrant housing aid - Deseret News
description:
Britnee Dabb, deputy director of Salt Lake City’s Housing Authority, called the rule change quick, swift and scary.
Since then, ineligible noncitizens and U.S. citizens have legally lived together in subsidized housing.
This rule guarantees ONLY AMERICAN citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD-funded housing.
“HUD housing assistance is intended for U.S. citizens and a narrow list of eligible noncitizens,” the department’s press release read.
“HUD-funded housing serves only a quarter of eligible households in need,” the press release continued.
text:
Twenty-two attorneys general across the nation have banded together against a new federal rule that would eliminate federal housing assistance for families living with ineligible noncitizens — claiming it violates federal law.

The rule, which the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development finalized on Nov. 10, tightens the enforcement of the Housing and Community Development Act of 1980.

“American taxpayers will no longer foot the bill. Promises made, promises kept,” said HUD Secretary Scott Turner.

Starting Dec. 14, every member of a household receiving federal housing aid must be verified as a U.S. citizen or an eligible noncitizen — such as lawful permanent residents, refugees and asylees.

That is, if the rule isn’t stopped by the courts.

Since its finalization on Nov. 10, the rule has picked up widespread opposition. Now, that opposition is gaining momentum and has landed in the courts.

In the West, Arizona, California, Colorado, New Mexico, Oregon and Washington, all with Democratic attorneys general, have joined the lawsuit. Utah is not among them.

Britnee Dabb, deputy director of Salt Lake City’s Housing Authority, called the rule change quick, swift and scary. She said the housing authority has already let the families — about a dozen who would be affected — know about the change.

“These are our tax dollars,” she said. “We follow the rules and regulations. So with this change, we will do the same,” she said.

Taking HUD to court

A new lawsuit, filed Nov. 23 and led by New York, California and Massachusetts, argues the rule isn’t in line with the Housing and Community Development Act, which Congress amended in the 1990s to protect mixed-status families.

Since then, ineligible noncitizens and U.S. citizens have legally lived together in subsidized housing. The proration policy originated with HUD in 1995; Congress codified it in 1996. However, the government subsidizes only the eligible individuals — the household pays a higher rate to cover the ineligible renters.

The department’s new rule eliminates that option entirely.

Turner told The Associated Press on Monday, “HUD’s final rule fully implements the 1980 Housing and Community Development Act and ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars. This rule guarantees ONLY AMERICAN citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD-funded housing. This change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million which will now go to eligible Americans that are currently on a waitlist.”

The states argue that federal law bars cutting off mixed-status families who already receive prorated aid. They also argue the department’s public case contradicts its own analysis.

The numbers don’t add up

Turner said Americans should no longer “foot the bill” for housing aid to immigrants in the country illegally — but the federal department does not project any cost savings.

The official Regulatory Impact Analysis predicts the rule will cost up to $251 million when accounting for replacement households, evictions and administrative implementation costs.

“With families already struggling to afford basic necessities, the last thing our economy needs is a rule that would exacerbate the already existing housing crisis, and force citizens and noncitizens alike out of their homes and communities,” said California Attorney General Rob Bonta.

The argument echoes what Democratic senators have been saying since June, when 22 of them signed a joint letter pushing back against the rule. It argued mixed-status households receive less rental assistance and pay more in rent compared to households where every member is eligible for assistance.

Dabb agreed, saying the rule will “negatively affect” even smaller housing authorities like Salt Lake.

“If someone can’t afford to live, they might not be able to spend money in our economy ...” she argued. “They’re going to add to our already saturated market of trying to find those super affordable rents.”

Forcing an ‘impossible choice’

The states are said the rule forces an “impossible choice”: requiring mixed-status households to expel ineligible family members or face eviction. The rulemaking itself was “arbitrary and capricious” — lacking meaningful consideration of reasonable alternatives, according to the lawsuit.

“Everyone deserves a safe place to call home,” said New York Attorney General Letitia James. “Denying a child that security because of who they live with is cruel and indefensible.”

Opponents also argue the rule will affect 80,000 people across 20,000 households — many of whom, they say, are children.

Dabb said of the approximately 3,000 households receiving the subsidy in Salt Lake, a dozen or so would lose housing. “Many times it’s families with young children,” she said. “And so that’s uprooting them from the school systems. It’s uprooting the parents from their jobs that are probably close to where they live.”

But Turner argued that America’s homeless veterans, disables, elderly and victims of domestic violence stay on waitlists while illegal immigrants receive housing. This new rule, he said, makes more room for more American citizens.

With only about a dozen families losing housing, Dabb said the change doesn’t necessarily make a large dent in the waiting list.

“We would need more money to do that, not just these families removed,” she said.

What can really be verified?

The rule also requires two-step verification for citizenship, whereas previously, citizens had to sign a declaration and noncitizens had to submit immigration documents verified through the federal SAVE system.

Now, tenants might also have to submit physical, certified documentation such as a U.S. passport or a birth certificate.

“HUD housing assistance is intended for U.S. citizens and a narrow list of eligible noncitizens,” the department’s press release read. A recent audit of all HUD-assisted households found nearly 200,000 tenants without verified citizenship. “HUD-funded housing serves only a quarter of eligible households in need,” the press release continued.

James claimed using the SAVE database can lead to errors — saying naturalized citizens and older Americans are especially likely to be wrongly flagged.

The rule has already been finalized. Landlords will be given 90 days after the rule’s effective date on Dec. 14 to comply, unless otherwise decided in court.

text:
Democrats taking control of Congress in just a few weeks will have a chance to rebuild their reputation after years of Republican attacks on the party's brand.

They'll be better able to shape the narrative on the nation's top issues, including those which contributed to their fall into the minority. Republicans seized on Democratic failures during the Biden administration to communicate effectively on the economy, immigration and presidential missteps, but now, after the blue tsunami that was the midterms, the GOP is on its back foot on the very same issues.

Successful Democrats in this month's elections resisted the bait dangled by Republicans to focus on cultural issues tied to the public's top concerns. They'll likely face more of the same challenges when they take power, and they'd do well to avoid the wars the GOP's long tempted them to fight.

The sensitive issue of will be an important test. Democrats must strike a balance between defending immigrants' rights and opposing the Trump administration's mass deportation policies without falling into traps set by Republicans and the conservative media that's ready to pounce.

Representative Jamie Raskin, the Maryland Democrat, showed the dangers of entertaining right-wing fights last year, when he went toe-to-toe in an argument with a conservative X user over Kilmar Ábrego García, the immigrant involved in an illegal deportation fight. The two yelled over each other on Capitol Hill, fueling Republican attacks against sympathetic Democrats.

Raskin and other Democrats appear to have learned from their mistakes as they prepare to take control of Congress. The party's largely united around the goal of lowering prices that have concerned Americans for the past several years, brushing off Republican attempts to stir up anger over sensitive topics.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and his Senate counterpart, Chuck Schumer, pledged after their party's electoral triumph to address voters' most important issues, like the that's risen under President Donald Trump.

"The American people have forcefully rejected MAGA extremism and are demanding dramatic change in their lives," the Democrats said in a statement. "House and Senate Democrats have been given a clear mandate to aggressively address the affordability crisis, stop the reckless war of choice in Iran, meaningfully expand access to affordable healthcare and hold the crooks accountable who have unleashed unprecedented corruption on the country.

“A new day is coming on January 3rd. Democrats are united and ready to lead.”

text:
OGDEN — Weber County leaders will be scrutinizing the future of the Weber County Sheriff's Office's cooperative agreement with federal immigration authorities, focus of increasingly vocal concern by immigrant advocates pressing for its end.

"Please understand that we take your concerns and your questions very seriously. This is one of our top priorities we'll be addressing over the next two to three weeks," Weber County Commissioner Gage Froerer said Tuesday evening, after more than 20 people addressed commissioners on the issue, most of them critical of the accord.

Many of those speaking during a public hearing at Tuesday's Weber County Commission meeting said that immigrants who don't pose a threat to the community are facing detention and deportation as part of the ongoing immigration crackdown. They charged that the sheriff's office accord with Immigration and Customs Enforcement is aiding the process.

"They are not going after the worst of the worst, as the sheriff has claimed," said Amy Wicks, one of the many Weber County residents who spoke out on Tuesday. "Our decent, hardworking neighbors are being targeted. This is not making our community safer. It needs to stop."

Froerer didn't state a stance one way or another on the sheriff's office's accord with ICE, known as a 287(g) accord. But in the context of the criticism from those who spoke out, lauded the diversity of Weber County and Ogden, where Latinos account for more than 30% of the population.

"We welcome diversity in this community. That's what makes us strong. That's what, in my opinion, separates Weber County from some other counties that I see across the state," he said. "So it's my intent that we embrace that diversity and look at this policy in more detail and answer your questions."

'We're following the laws'

Weber County Sheriff Ryan Arbon, for his part, offered a strong defense of the county's 287(g) agreement with ICE. Eleven Utah counties in all have 287(g) accords with ICE, along with a handful of police departments.

"The county should absolutely not get rid of it," he said Wednesday, a day after Tuesday's meeting, which he didn't attend. The Weber County Sheriff's Office is one of several sheriff's offices and other law enforcement agencies in Utah with 287(g) accords, a tool in the ongoing immigration crackdown that's designed to aid ICE officials in locating immigrants in the country illegally.

One of the chief criticisms of 287(g) accords and the immigration crackdown in general seems to be that immigrants without criminal records are being rounded up as part of the effort. President Donald Trump had stressed the importance of the crackdown as a means of removing immigrants with serious criminal records, "the worst of the worst."

Some of those who spoke out Tuesday, though, noted the case of a Chilean couple, parents of an infant, stopped last month by Weber County Sheriff's Office officials because the car they were traveling in had canceled or suspended registration. While they didn't have criminal records, ICE officials were called in after neither could produce a driver's license. They were later detained by immigration officials for overstaying their 90-day visa by more than two years.

ICE data compiled by the Deportation Data Project, moreover, shows that 45.1% of immigrant detainees in Utah last July had convictions for violent or non-violent crimes and that 54.9% did not have criminal convictions. Just 2.6% of detainees in the period had convictions for violent crimes.

Arbon, though, argued that law enforcement agencies can't pick and choose which laws to enforce, including laws pertaining to immigration.

"When do we get to decide which laws are for us and which are not? I mean, the laws have been enacted. We're following the laws. Every single one of our stops are legal and lawful," he said. "If they're here on a visa, and they're not complying with the visa, does that mean because they haven't committed a crime while they've been here that (they) all of a sudden don't have to comply with the law?"

He said two Weber County Sheriff's Office deputies take part in the cooperative efforts with ICE under the county's 287(g) task force model agreement, distinct from cooperative efforts with corrections officials. They only contact ICE when they come across suspected immigrants in the country illegally in the normal course of their duties. They don't specifically search out immigrants.

'They are everyday people'

Whatever the case, while one speaker at Tuesday's meeting defended the sheriff's office's 287(g) accord, 20-plus people criticized it, many calling for an end to it.

Kelly Quiroz noted, with chagrin, the case of the Chilean couple. "These were not violent criminals, as we were led to believe the focus of this agreement to be. They were a young family with no criminal record," she said.

Moreover, she questioned the notion of local law enforcement working with federal immigration officials.

"I recognize that immigration laws exist and must be administered, but Weber County is not required to lend its own deputies and resources to every aspect of federal immigration enforcement, especially those that separate families. This is injustice," she said.

Read more:

C.J. Hernandez, a Democrat who won election earlier this month to a post in the Utah Senate that represents part of Weber County, said the sheriff's office's cooperative agreement with ICE is causing "a lot of stress and fear" in the community.

"I request the termination of Weber County's 2879g) agreement," she said. "Once we know better, we do better, and I ask for that from you."

Cirilo Franco warned that the county's accord with ICE has prompted some to lose trust in the sheriff's office. He also spoke of the humanity of those being detained.

"They're my family. They're my friends. They are young parents with newborn children," Franco said. "They're mothers, they're fathers. They are everyday people who are simply trying to make ends meet and provide a better future for their children and for themselves."

description:
"These Trump policies are not only illegal but also unpopular."
Trump has had a mixed record on immigration at the 6-3 conservative court since returning to power last year.
White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis dismissed Wang's assertion that the court will find Trump's immigration policies illegal.
Some Democrats have framed the recapture of Congress as a rejection by voters of the administration's immigration policies.
"Looking at the immigration cases the Supreme Court has taken this term," he predicted, "I think it's doing the same kind of cleanup."
text:
Democrats want to sideline President Donald Trump's immigration agenda when they take control of Congress next year, but the real fight may take place across the street where the conservative Supreme Court is poised to uphold several of his most controversial policies.

Video above: Kilmar Ábrego García self-deports out of the U.S.

The court will soon consider blockbuster appeals on the president's asylum ban, his vast expansion of mandatory detention of migrants and his push to send certain people in the U.S. illegally to countries other than their homeland — including some with poor human rights records.

Decisions in those cases are expected by late June.

Though those three cases and several others are less flashy than this past summer's blockbuster decision upholding birthright citizenship, the outcomes in the nuts-and-bolts disputes will have profound implications for policies the administration says are "indispensable" to its overall immigration crackdown.

"In all three of these cases, the Trump administration is trying to rewrite laws enacted by Congress, in service of a radical anti-immigrant agenda that has hurt not only immigrants, but the rule of law," said Cecillia Wang with the American Civil Liberties Union, which is opposing the administration in two of those cases. "These Trump policies are not only illegal but also unpopular."

Trump has had a mixed record on immigration at the 6-3 conservative court since returning to power last year. His unprecedented push to upend birthright citizenship was rejected. And the court limited his ability to use the 1798 Alien Enemies Act to quickly remove certain migrants from the country.

On the other hand, six-justice majorities in June allowed Trump to end a form of humanitarian relief known as Temporary Protected Status and to limit asylum claims made at the border.

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis dismissed Wang's assertion that the court will find Trump's immigration policies illegal.

"If the American Civil Liberties Union cares more about criminal illegal aliens than they do about American citizens, then they should change their name," she said.

Some Democrats have framed the recapture of Congress as a rejection by voters of the administration's immigration policies. Minnesota Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan vowed to "rip ICE apart." New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is all but certain to become the next House speaker, told CBS that Democrats would "put an end to Donald Trump's violent mass deportation machine."

But Republicans have already frontloaded funding for ICE for years. And Trump this month named Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, as White House chief of staff — a sign that the administration has no intention of slowing its immigration agenda.

"It stands to reason that hyper-aggressive immigration enforcement will continue to be one of the hallmarks of the Trump administration even as it faces Democratic majorities in both chambers of the legislature," said Steve Vladeck, CNN Supreme Court analyst and professor at Georgetown University Law Center. "Whether the extremism of these policies will be allowed to continue is therefore going to be up to the Supreme Court."

Conservatives who support the policies see a court that is prepared to back the president's program.

"Over and over, judges in the district courts and the courts of appeals have interpreted the law contrary to clear congressional intent as evidenced by the text. And as a result, those decisions keep getting overturned," Iowa Solicitor General Eric Wessan, whose state led briefs supporting the administration in two of the biggest cases, told CNN.

Wessan predicted that the justices will view lower court decisions on immigration against the administration with similar skepticism.

"Looking at the immigration cases the Supreme Court has taken this term," he predicted, "I think it's doing the same kind of cleanup."

Human rights and arrests

The showdown will begin on Dec. 9, when the justices will hear arguments in a case challenging Trump's push to remove certain migrants to countries other than their homeland. In many cases, those removals are carried out without giving the migrant an opportunity to raise human rights concerns.

Federal law allows such "third country" removals in cases when a migrant's home country refuses to accept them. The administration has used that provision to remove an Iranian national to Nicaragua, for instance, and Venezuelans to El Salvador, according to immigrants' rights groups.

In some of those cases, immigrant rights groups say, migrants were sent back to their homeland from the "third country," even when an immigration judge ordered that the administration not return to them to their native country.

Congress has also required the administration to ensure migrants won't be tortured or persecuted once they land in a third country. That determination was previously made on a case-by-case basis. Under the second Trump administration, the government now accepts blanket assurances from a foreign country that no torture will take place, and migrants are often removed to that country without notice.

The Supreme Court, on its emergency docket, three times allowed the administration to pursue the policy while the case remained pending. It has not explained its reasoning.

Increase in arrests of migrants

Next year, the court will turn to the Trump administration's decision to funnel not only recent border crossers into mandatory detention but also people who have been living within the United States for years.

That shift has permitted the Department of Homeland Security to dramatically increase the number of migrants arrested. And so if the court rejects that change, it will almost certainly jeopardize the administration's ability to carry out massive sweeps for migrants that have played out in cities like Chicago and Minneapolis.

Immigrant rights groups say no prior administration, including Trump's first, has interpreted federal law to require mandatory detention of so many migrants. But Justice Department officials told the Supreme Court that it is simply following the law that Congress enacted.

Asylum ban

And in the spring, the court will hear a challenge to Trump's asylum ban. The president argues people crossing the border are making false asylum claims as a way to enter the country then stall the deportation process, since it can take years to resolve them.

U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer, the administration's top appellate attorney, warned the court of a "vicious cycle" that encouraged "illegal entry by millions of aliens, who (quite justifiably) inferred that even if they lacked meritorious asylum claims, they would 'be released to live and work in the United States during their removal proceedings.'"

But the Immigration and Nationality Act specifically allows migrants to claim asylum, even as it leaves the decision about whether to grant safe harbor up to administration officials.

In stark language, the Justice Department has described its asylum policy as one of the "most important and effective" policies for stemming illegal immigration. A lower court order against the policy, the administration said, "threatens to revive the chaos along the southwest border that the proclamation has fended off for the past year and a half."

The ACLU, representing 13 individuals and three immigrant rights groups that challenged the policy, said that if Trump wants to change the way asylum works, he should have passed a bill in Congress during the two years the chambers were in Republican hands.

Richard Caldarone, a senior litigation attorney at the National Immigrant Justice Center, said that the policies at issue in the cases had already put tens of thousands of people in harm's way.

"These policies have been overwhelmingly rejected by lower courts across the country, and they flatly violate U.S. immigration law as it has been understood for decades," said Caldarone, whose group is fighting the administration in the asylum case.

"If the court validates the policies," he said, "it will enshrine a new generation of internment camps, all but end the U.S. asylum system as we have known it for almost half a century, and shatter our nation's commitment to upholding human rights and democratic norms."

text:
WASHINGTON — A federal judge in the District of Columbia Wednesday issued a classwide injunction to prevent the Trump administration from implementing its second attempt at redefining the constitutional right to birthright citizenship.

The order from Judge Christopher Reid Cooper will remain in effect while litigation continues. A classwide injunction blocks action affecting a defined group of individuals, as opposed to a nationwide injunction.

In a memorandum opinion, Cooper noted the Supreme Court earlier this year denied President Donald Trump’s executive order that would deny citizenship to babies born from immigrants either in the country unlawfully or on a temporary basis, in the case Barbara v. Trump.

“Yet Barbara’s ink had scarcely dried when the President issued a second executive order—Executive Order 14418, at issue here—directing federal agencies to withhold recognition of citizenship from additional categories of U.S.-born children with noncitizen parents,” he wrote. “As the Supreme Court has made clear, however, the President cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws.”

The American Civil Liberties Union, which led the first challenge against the Trump administration’s birthright citizenship order and is leading the second, welcomed the ruling.

“Enough is enough,” Cody Wofsy, deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, said in a statement. “The Supreme Court has twice rejected efforts to gut birthright citizenship, in 1898 and again earlier this year. Third time is not the charm, and the President needs to accept that birthright citizenship is the law of the land.”

The Department of Justice did not respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment.

Earlier this month, Cooper seemed skeptical of the legality of the Trump administration’s second attempt to redefine the constitutional right to birthright citizenship.

The president’s recent executive orders would deny citizenship to babies born in the United States to parents deemed part of a designated terrorist organization and to parents who purposefully came to the United States to gain citizenship in what critics call “birth tourism.”

The executive order also aimed to deny citizenship to children born to foreign diplomatic staff and children born in U.S. territories where Congress has not passed a law granting citizenship.

There is already a small carve out for birthright citizenship, extended to children born to foreign diplomats.

Abrego Garcia self-deported to Spain on Tuesday night after a year-and-a-half legal battle that included being sent to a notorious Salvadoran prison against a judge's order.

Van Hollen, who's been Abrego Garcia's most prominent backer in Congress, argued that the legal system had withstood the Trump administration's efforts to "trample" on his rights.

"They brought a malicious and vindictive prosecution against him," Van Hollen said. "They tried to force him to go to a country or countries that have records of human rights abuses. They tried… to punish him because he stood up for his constitutional rights."

"They were forced to back down from that," he went on. "He is now in a place of his choosing, a free man and living with dignity, and I think the message for all of us is that it's never wrong to stand up for our Constitution."

Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran citizen who lived in the U.S. with his family for years, was picked up by immigration agents in Maryland in 2025 and quickly deported to his home country ― even though an immigration judge had ordered that he could not be removed due to the likelihood of him facing violence at home in El Salvador.

He was sent to the megaprison known as CECOT, where he alleged he was tortured.

The Trump administration called the deportation an "administrative error," and a federal judge ordered he be returned to the U.S. The administration brought Abrego Garcia back only to pursue a human trafficking case against him ― charges a federal judge dismissed as a vindictive prosecution meant to punish him for standing up for himself.

On a call Wednesday hosted by We Are CASA, a Maryland-based immigrant rights group that championed his cause, Abrego Garcia said the government did not get to "decide where my story continues."

"I keep believing that I'm victorious ― and I've always said this ― because the United States is a country that follows the laws," Abrego Garcia said through an interpreter.

One of his attorneys, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, made a point of thanking Van Hollen for his advocacy, acknowledging "how important the senator has been in getting us to where we are today."

Van Hollen traveled to CECOT in April 2025 and tried to meet with Abrego Garcia but was turned away. Salvadoran officials instead arranged for him to meet Abrego Garcia at a hotel so he could speak with him and evaluate his condition.

text:
Immigrants facing detention by federal authorities are making hard choices about whether Thanksgiving travel is worth the risk, advocacy rights groups say.

More than 81 million people plan to travel at least 50 miles from home for the holiday, according to AAA. But the Trump administration's aggressive immigration enforcement efforts, highlighted in part by the Nov. 21 detention of two people at the Seattle-Tacoma Airport, has some people reconsidering their movements.

That includes immigrants with the legal right to live and work in the U.S. but who want to avoid being stopped and questioned, said Zachary Mueller, a senior strategist with the advocacy group States at the Core.

"Some people are terrified to leave their house," said Mueller, whose organization has trained about 75,000 people to monitor and record ICE detentions. "For some people, that fear has become so palpable in day-to-day life that this holiday is nothing new on that level."

Mueller added: "For others, they're asking 'is traveling to go see family for the holidays worth the risk of never seeing my family again?' That's a real calculation."

The exact number of people facing deportation is unclear, but roughly 350,000 Haitians and about 600,000 Venezuelans lost Temporary Protected Status in the past two years.

The Department of Homeland Security reports that in fiscal year 2026, ICE carried out more than 483,000 deportations, the most ever in a single year. President Donald Trump has promised the largest mass deportation in U.S. history, and during his second term DHS reports that more than 3 million people have already left the United States either via deportation or self-removal.

Immigrants who leave the United States voluntarily can receive a $3,000 payment and a free flight to their home country.

Administration officials said they will continue to enforce immigration laws, including those that make it harder for undocumented immigrants to fly. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers routinely check Transportation Security Administration manifests for potential immigration violators.

Last May, the Department of Homeland Security began requiring flyers to show REAL ID-compliant identification to board airplanes, a move that made it easier to detect people who lacked permission to live in the United States. People without REAL ID can fly but are subject to additional security checks and may have to pay a $45 fee.

"DHS reversed the horrendous Biden-era policy that allowed aliens in our country illegally to jet around our country. Under President Trump, DHS will no longer tolerate this," an unnamed DHS spokesperson said in a statement. "This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport."

Immigrants who are considering travel should check first with their attorney and make sure to carry copies of relevant paperwork, said Krish O'Mara Vignarajah, the president and CEO of Global Refuge. She said many refugees who sought safety in the United States are now worried about being targeted by the same government that asked them to fill out paperwork and register their home addresses.

She said many refugees, including those from Haiti and Venezuela are frustrated because Trump keeps saying ICE is targeting the "worst of the worst."

"These are people who did everything right, went through vetting, did all the paperwork," she said. "And now they're asking us whether following the rules has somehow put them more at risk."

Mueller said the harsh enforcement tactics also have impacts on travelers who witness anonymous and masked federal agents grabbing screaming people at airports. He said driving may not be a safe option for some people, particularly if they are driving through communities that have signed cooperative agreements allowing local police to help enforce immigration laws.

"It's not just the people who are first affected, but that kind of fear and trauma and concern, the wanton separation, the ability of ICE to do whatever it wants and create these chaotic scenes ... millions of Americans have been seeing this," Mueller said. "They're asking themselves when they travel, 'am I going to see something that's going to ruin my holiday because this administration wants to rip apart families?' That's the absurd reality of this moment."

Marjory Wentworth, a board member of the Haitian Support Center in Springfield, Ohio, said her family is hosting a handful of Haitians for Thanksgiving. Many members of Ohio's Haitian community lost their Temporary Protected Status in July. The Trump administration has revoked their work permission and urged them to leave the United States.

Wentworth said none of the Haitians she knows will risk flying. She said at last one local church hosted a Thanksgiving dinner for Haitian congregants over the weekend, allowing them to celebrate without traveling far from home.

"People can't go work, they've got ankle monitors," she said of her own invited guests. "I feel like people are still pretty fearful. I'm hoping we can distract them for a day."

text:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran national whose mistaken deportation became a major legal and political dispute for the Trump administration, has left the United States for Spain.

Abrego Garcia departed on Tuesday, November 24, and arrived in Madrid on Wednesday, according to reports by the Associated Press and other US media outlets.

His departure follows months of legal battles after he was mistakenly deported to El Salvador in March 2025, despite an earlier immigration court ruling preventing his removal to his home country because of fears of gang persecution.

He was arrested in Baltimore and transferred to El Salvador’s notorious CECOT prison, where he remained for months.

Following public pressure and a court order, the Trump administration brought him back to the United States in June 2025.

However, authorities subsequently pursued plans to deport him to other countries, including Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana and Liberia.

Abrego Garcia challenged those efforts in court, arguing against being sent to countries where he had no established ties.

His latest departure followed months of uncertainty over his immigration status and the possibility of another removal order.

In a statement, Abrego Garcia described the departure as a moment of freedom.

“I am leaving happy. I am leaving with my freedom,” he said.

His lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, described the move as temporary, saying his client hoped to remain abroad until the end of the current administration.

The lawyer said Abrego Garcia could seek to return to Maryland under a future administration to reunite with his American wife and child.

However, the US Department of Homeland Security presented a different account of the departure, describing it as a self-deportation carried out under an existing removal order.

The department said he received no financial incentives for leaving and would not be permitted to return to the United States.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin welcomed the development and repeated the administration’s allegations that Abrego Garcia was associated with a criminal gang.

Abrego Garcia has repeatedly denied the gang allegations.

His case became a prominent test of the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement policies after the government acknowledged that his initial deportation to El Salvador was an administrative error.

His arrival in Spain marks a new chapter in a dispute that has involved immigration authorities, federal courts and the White House, although his long-term immigration status in Spain remains unclear.

title: Jayapal Statement on ICE and SeaTac Arrest
description:
“Secretary Mullin informed me that, in what he indicated is the normal course of operations, TSA at SeaTac sent DHS a pre-flagged list of passengers on the flight that had outstanding warrants of any kind against them.
According to Secretary Mullin, ICE then notified the airport one day prior that they would be operating at the airport to arrest Ricardo.
