description:
For the shrinking share of the jailed population that does access an immigration bond hearing, the average bond denial rate has jumped.
Even when a bond is granted, freedom remains out of reach for many caught in the Trump administration’s deportation machine because median bond amounts have also increased.
“It’s a lot harder to fight your immigration case when you’re in a jail cell,” Tan told Truthout.
The Trump administration has also purged dozens of immigration judges and recruited replacements that it now calls “deportation judges,” rather than immigration judges.
Okare told Truthout that stories like these are common in the work of Envision Freedom Fund and other immigration bond funds operating nationwide.
text:
When Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 after campaigning on mass deportation, his administration got to work expanding immigration detention and reshaping the nation’s immigration courts to make it more difficult for jailed migrants to seek release. Almost two years later, data show just how successful those policies have been.

The number of people jailed in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention nationwide is up roughly 80 percent since President Joe Biden left office. The Trump administration has foreclosed most avenues through which jailed migrants have historically sought release. For the shrinking share of the jailed population that does access an immigration bond hearing, the average bond denial rate has jumped. It rose to about 60 percent in the first year of Trump 2.0, up from about 53 percent in the last year of Biden’s tenure. The denial rate has continued to rise this year.

Even when a bond is granted, freedom remains out of reach for many caught in the Trump administration’s deportation machine because median bond amounts have also increased. Those amounts have even doubled from 2024 to the first months of 2026 in some of the federal circuit court jurisdictions with the most immigration bond cases, according to data compiled and analyzed by Bklg.org.

“This is a linchpin in the administration’s deportation strategy,” Michael Tan, deputy director of the Immigrants’ Rights Project at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), told Truthout. “The primary reason they’re subjecting people to detention with no avenue for release is to coerce them into giving up their immigration cases, their claims to legal status, to remaining in the country, and to acquiesce to a deportation because they can’t stand being locked up for so long.”

Even for those who do not agree to so-called self-deportation, outcomes tend to be worse for those who fight their immigration cases while detained. Those who are released are more likely to have their immigration cases resolved with permission to remain in the U.S. than with deportation orders. Once freed, a person tends to have more resources and more time to participate in their case, gather evidence, and access other needed support. “It’s a lot harder to fight your immigration case when you’re in a jail cell,” Tan told Truthout. Especially, he added, “when ICE moves people all over the place, and so it’s not the case that you’ll be detained often in your community or near your family [and] your lawyer. Instead, ICE is routinely shipping people to far-flung locations.”

Fisayo Okare, digital communications manager at Envision Freedom Fund, told Truthout that migrant community members with whom her organization works regularly face these pressures. “Families are thinking of whether it’s worth it or not to even remain in the country or just choosing to voluntarily deport,” she said. The nonprofit Envision Freedom Fund is the largest immigration bond fund in the nation; it helps cover bonds for individuals jailed in New York or New Jersey and those who will return home to the area on release. Since the fund launched in 2018, it has provided over $15 million in bond support to help secure the release of over 1,600 people from immigration jails.

An October report from Envision Freedom Fund shows how the increase in the number of migrants jailed and struggling to access release is affecting communities in New York and New Jersey. The volume of requests for support that the bond fund receives has risen so much that it projects it will cover nine times as many bonds in 2026 as in 2024, if it can raise the funds needed to meet demand through the end of the calendar year.

“The fact is that we’re forced to bond so many more people out now because the sheer volume of the system — everything is increasing,” Ben McCoubrey, Envision Freedom Fund’s data and advocacy manager, told Truthout.

It has never been easy for those in ICE jails to access bond, a process that entails securing a bond hearing in immigration court, finding a lawyer to present the case, then convincing the immigration judge to grant a bond, and ultimately finding someone outside with U.S. citizenship or a green card and the funds needed to post the bond. But the obstacles to accessing bond are now greater than ever before thanks to what Tan characterized to Truthout as the Trump administration’s “takeover of the immigration courts.”

Since Trump returned to office, he has signed executive orders to expand detention and restrict release. Based on those directives, ICE’s lawyers have made legal arguments and issued guidance meant to subject as many immigrants as possible to mandatory detention and limit their access to bond. Those directives have become standard practice following administration-friendly decisions from the Board of Immigration Appeals, which governs the immigration courts and judges from within the Department of Justice.

The Trump administration has also purged dozens of immigration judges and recruited replacements that it now calls “deportation judges,” rather than immigration judges. Many of these new judges come from the ranks of former military lawyers, ICE lawyers, and prosecutors with little or no experience or training in immigration law.

“They’ve fired immigration judges that they think, in their view, are too friendly to immigrants and replaced them with so-called deportation judges [and] for the judges who remain, who didn’t get fired, we know that the administration is exerting pressure on them to deny relief, and to really crack down, and serve as foot soldiers in a mass deportation campaign,” Tan told Truthout. “They’ve taken an immigration court system that is supposed to be neutral and fair and made it into an arm of the immigration enforcement system.”

The ACLU has litigated the Trump administration’s mandatory detention scheme in every circuit court where it could be heard, a total of 11 of the nation’s 13. Only two circuits have concurred with the administration’s interpretation of the law. Nine have rejected it, opening the door for more individuals to access bond hearings in the 40 states covered by those circuits. The Supreme Court will hear the issue in a case arising from the Second Circuit, Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, next year; Tan told Truthout a decision is expected by the end of June. The outcome will affect access to bond hearings for those in ICE jails nationwide.

While the legal fight continues, the humanitarian crisis created by the Trump administration’s policy changes is deepening. Envision Freedom Fund’s recent report helps put a human face on the issue. “We paint a picture of what’s happening in the context of detention and deportation, how things are growing, and go beyond what we see when it’s just [the number of] people getting released on bonds,” McCoubrey told Truthout about the report’s aims.

The report includes stories of immigrants who have suffered medical neglect and other traumas in ICE jails and are navigating the lasting effects after being bonded out with Envision Freedom Fund’s support.

One man for whom the fund helped cover a $50,000 bond to secure his release in July 2026 shared that he “felt unmeasurably happy when [he] got released from the jail.” He had been jailed for over two months, and after release, said, “I believed that now everything will be okay. Because when I was in there, I was stressing a lot. I didn’t know what would happen because nowadays it’s really tough.” Just two weeks after the man’s release, his asylum case was granted — ending a more than four-year wait that began in 2022.

More recently, Okare told Truthout that Envision Freedom Fund secured release for a man in his mid-thirties who had been transferred from Delaney Hall in New Jersey to an ICE jail in Georgia. The fund then coordinated with partners to arrange transportation to bring him home in time to be with his wife and witness the birth of his child. “His wife was actually in the hospital when we got the bond request, and he got out right in time,” she said.

Okare told Truthout that stories like these are common in the work of Envision Freedom Fund and other immigration bond funds operating nationwide. For each of the tens of thousands of people jailed in the country’s ICE detention facilities, there are families missing a parent or a sibling and communities missing a neighbor.

As the Trump administration continues pulling these communities apart, Okare told Truthout that organizations like hers will keep fighting to make them whole again: “[We’re] not just paying their bond but ensuring that they get out and make it back to their community.”

SAN ANTONIO – San Antonio Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones discussed a federal immigration arrest that took place on city property during this week’s KSAT Q&A.

The conversation follows an arrest, raised publicly by Councilman Ric Galvan (D6), of a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrest at the Culebra Bulky Waste Collection Center on the West Side.

On Monday, Galvan said the arrest was the “first known instance of ICE taking action on city property here in San Antonio.” Though ICE confirmed the arrest, a spokesperson said they hadn’t chosen the site.

Based off the story gathered through city workers and video footage of the instance, Galvan told reporters an unmarked vehicle had followed a father and son onto the public driveway at the waste collection center around 9 a.m. Nov. 19.

>> ICE arrest man at city bulk waste drop-off; San Antonio councilman asks family to contact him

Jones said the location was open to the public at the time and that the man who was detained drove onto the property himself after being pulled over.

“It wasn’t like there was any cooperation between city staff or certainly (the San Antonio Police Department),” Jones said, adding that the immigration enforcement had “no city association” other than the arrest happening on the city’s property.

Jones said the city is working on its federal and state legislative agendas and met with Congressman-elect Johnny Garcia, who formerly worked with the Bexar County Sheriff’s Department before running to represent Texas’ newly drawn 35th Congressional District.

Jones said there are 100,000 undocumented people in the community and noted a “chilling effect” on people reporting crimes or abuse to law enforcement.

Asked about the coming change in Austin, Jones said she has shared the city’s priorities with newly elected state leaders. She listed Medicaid expansion and the repeal of both versions of Senate Bill 4 — which looks to prohibit “sanctuary city” policies — among the top items.

Some related bills have already been filed, according to Jones.

“We look forward to the change that our neighbors clearly said they want as a result of the recent election,” she said.

Jones, who is an Air Force veteran, also discussed the city’s push to expand housing protections for veterans.

title: Can Democrats in Congress stop Trump's deportations? - Latinoamérica 21
description:
Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress and key governorships, partly thanks to Latino voters who had supported him in 2024.
In Texas, a traditional Republican stronghold, immigration enforcement has affected school life and family security.
Miller has been a central figure in designing Trump’s restrictive immigration policy and promoting mass deportations.
Even a Congress opposed to mass deportations cannot quickly dismantle the infrastructure, personnel, funding, and international agreements that sustain them.
Trump’s immigration system extends into Latin America The international dimension is central: it makes it harder for the new Congress to reverse the crackdown.
text:
The 2026 midterm elections in the United States marked a setback for Donald Trump. Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress and key governorships, partly thanks to Latino voters who had supported him in 2024. Their shift reflects discontent primarily linked to the rising cost of living and the tightening of immigration policies.

For a large share of the Latino electorate, security at the border and within the country has become a concern: Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) operations have become increasingly visible in neighborhoods, workplaces, and communities.

In Texas, a traditional Republican stronghold, immigration enforcement has affected school life and family security. In February 2025, the superintendent of the Alice school district warned that Border Patrol agents could board school buses during extracurricular trips and question students about their citizenship and immigration status. Without proper documentation, they could face detention or deportation (The Texas Tribune, February 5, 2025). The Immigrant Legal Resource Center reinforced recommendations to prepare emergency plans and designate adults responsible for caring for children. The threat of deportation thus permeates everyday life: even at school, families must anticipate the possibility of forced separation.

Rising prices for food, housing, gasoline, diesel, and other essential goods have also put pressure on household budgets. These two experiences can compound one another: a workplace raid threatens not only rights but also families’ incomes and security.

The elections therefore raise a question that goes beyond the Democratic victory: can Congress turn this discontent into substantive change, or can it do little more than place limits on a firmly entrenched system?

The distinction matters because the immigration crackdown extends beyond US borders. Detention and deportation are linked to agreements with governments in Latin America and other regions, which face pressure to prevent people from traveling, receive deportees, and manage the consequences of US restrictions. This “externalization” of immigration control makes redirecting policy more difficult than winning control of Congress.

What changed among Latino voters?

Trump made considerable gains among Latinos in 2024; two years later, the shift toward Democrats was significant. In Zapata, in southern Texas, where Trump had won by 22 percentage points, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico prevailed by 41 points in 2026. An October 2026 Pew survey showed that 86% of registered Latino voters considered the economy very important to their congressional vote, compared with 64% who gave immigration the same priority. Sixty-two percent believed the government was going too far with deportations.

This political shift has institutional consequences. When they take control of Congress in January 2027, Democrats will be able to chair committees, demand information from federal agencies, and investigate the government’s immigration operations and policies.

ICE accountability, detention conditions, racial discrimination, due process, and the treatment of asylum seekers will likely be central to congressional oversight. Hearings can bring abuses to light, demand explanations, and increase the political cost of the most aggressive practices.

Democratic victories in Texas, Georgia, and even Mississippi could also change state-level cooperation with federal agencies. Governors can influence the priorities and resources of state law enforcement agencies, but they cannot, on their own, prevent the enforcement of federal immigration laws.

Trump, however, retains broad powers to set deportation priorities, restrict visas, and negotiate with foreign governments. He can veto legislation, while already allocated budgets, existing contracts, and administrative capacity continue to sustain enforcement operations. Controlling Congress is not the same as controlling the executive branch.

The appointment of Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff therefore takes on particular significance. Miller has been a central figure in designing Trump’s restrictive immigration policy and promoting mass deportations. His rise immediately after the elections does not suggest moderation, but rather the possibility of strengthening coordination of that policy within the executive branch in the face of a more hostile Congress. For Latin America, this matters because Washington may continue to push agreements aimed at containing migration and receiving deportees, even under increased congressional scrutiny.

Even a Congress opposed to mass deportations cannot quickly dismantle the infrastructure, personnel, funding, and international agreements that sustain them. In the short term, it could broaden political contestation and accountability rather than comprehensively reverse the policy.

Trump’s immigration system extends into Latin America

The international dimension is central: it makes it harder for the new Congress to reverse the crackdown. One of the busiest migration corridors in the Americas, running from South America to the United States through Central America and Mexico, has seen a dramatic decline in movement. In 2023, more than half a million migrants crossed the Darién Gap, between Colombia and Panama, heading north. By 2026, crossings had fallen sharply as access to the United States became increasingly restricted. But fewer arrivals at the border do not mean that forced displacement, insecurity, or the need for protection have disappeared. Nor does this eliminate the underlying causes of migration. People may become stranded, seek other destinations, or take more dangerous routes. Migration pressures have shifted southward: many people remain in Mexico and Central America, where restrictions and limited legal pathways prolong uncertainty, make their lives more precarious, or drive them to seek alternative destinations.

US enforcement increasingly depends on agreements to receive deportees, coordinate returns, and restrict movement before people reach US territory. Countries once considered transit countries are now being required to receive, detain, or return people whose movements are shaped by decisions made in Washington. In 2025, Honduras received nearly 43,000 deportees, Guatemala around 55,000, and El Salvador more than 16,000. That amounts to around 114,000 returns to these three countries in a single year, creating an immediate need for assistance and, above all, opportunities for reintegration into societies that many of these people had left because of insecurity and a lack of opportunities.

An important point is that, under so-called third-country agreements, the United States transfers people not necessarily to their country of origin, but to another state that agrees to receive them, detain them, or facilitate their subsequent removal. Between January 2025 and August 2026, more than 25,000 forced transfers to 26 countries other than the affected individuals’ countries of origin had been recorded.

In short, the elections may have challenged the legitimacy of the immigration crackdown, but they did not dismantle its structures. A Democratic Congress can examine US support for these agreements, demand that they be made public, and seek to attach conditions to some of their funding. But congressional oversight alone cannot reverse bilateral agreements or determine the policies of other governments.

The real test for Democrats will be whether they can help develop an alternative approach to migration governance. This would require not only domestic reforms but also dialogue with Latin American governments on shared responsibility for access to asylum and the protection of human rights.

text:
The family of a Maryland jockey and exercise rider is demanding answers after he was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) over the weekend on the Eastern Shore.

Charlie Munoz-Osorio, 38, was taken into ICE custody on Saturday, according to the Department of Homeland Security. His family said he was detained while driving his young son to a soccer game.

Munoz-Osorio is from Chile and has lived in the United States for about two years. An attorney for the jockey told CBS News Baltimore that his client is currently being held at a detention facility in Louisiana. His case is not listed on the ICE online database.

"This was completely unexpected, because we follow as a family all the steps necessary to stay in the United States in a legal way. This situation is really shocking because we [weren't] prepared at all," said a family member, who wishes to remain anonymous.

Munoz-Osorio's wife also told CBS Baltimore's Tara Lynch this has been a scary situation for her family.

Family wishes for transparency

The family was traveling to a soccer game near Ocean City when their car was stopped by six ICE vehicles. Munoz-Osorio was detained in front of his wife, 8-year-old son and 13-year-old daughter.

In a phone interview, the family said Munoz-Osorio entered the United States legally with a visa in 2024. The family says he applied for asylum before his visa expired.

In a statement, DHS said while he entered the country legally, he was only allowed to stay for 90 days and has overstayed his visa for two years. The department issued an order for removal for Munoz-Osorio on Saturday.

"When he entered the U.S. under the Visa Waiver Program, he agreed to waive his right to an immigration judge trial should he overstay or break the VWP rules," the DHS statement read.

The family said his immigration case is in process and he has completed all the steps needed to stay legally. They say he pays taxes and has never even received a traffic ticket. Additionally, they tell CBS News Baltimore he has a work permit that is valid through 2030.

"Nothing would tell us that we were in danger. We know this political situation is complex for all the immigrants, but we try to do everything right," the family member added.

The family added they do not think he is getting enough food while in custody.

"He wants to fight for his family and their future. The lack of clear information about his case has been extremely difficult for his family, and we are urgently seeking legal advice and representation to protect his right and ensure his case is handled fairly," the family representative added.

Jay Marks, an attorney for Munoz-Osorio, called the situation a tragedy for the family.

"Charlie's case is a catastrophe for that family, a tragedy for that family," Marks said. "We are very concerned, because when he was in the Chantilly holding room, he said that there was very little food, if any, being given out. Conditions were overcrowded."

Marks argues Munoz-Osorio can stay in the United States while the asylum application is pending. In a statement Tuesday, Marks said, "If ICE removes him without a hearing, they are acting in flagrant violation of the United States Code."

The family says they are grateful for the community's support during this difficult time. An online fundraiser has raised more than $5,000 for his legal expenses.

"Charlie is a real quiet, conscientious, hardworking guy"

Munoz-Osorio is a licensed horse trainer and jockey with the state, who primarily works at Laurel Park.

Ferris Allen, a thoroughbred racehorse trainer who works with Munoz-Osorio, said he was shocked at the arrest.

"Charlie is a real quiet, conscientious, hardworking guy. Never misses a day of work. Always on time," Allen said. "For him to be treated this way, it's as reprehensible as it gets. It makes me ashamed of our country's policies."

Allen called the exercise rider an up-and-coming jockey, who has been fighting to race horses full time after starting his career over when he moved to the United States. Once a jockey in Chile, Munoz-Osorio is now trying to race more frequently and was scheduled to race Sunday at Belmont Park. He even worked Saturday morning before his arrest.

"Our country should be way better than this. There's no person, regardless of where they're from or what their national origin is, or what their immigration status is... there's no one that should be treated this way," Allen said.

The Maryland Thoroughbred Horsemen's Association (MTHA) said it "is working closely with officials to help reunite Munoz-Osorio with his family as soon as possible." It added, "Our thoughts are with Charlie and his family during this difficult time, and we will do everything we can to support them."

In a statement, Rep. Sarah Elfreth, who represents Howard County where the family lives, said her caucus needs to restrict ICE.

"This is yet another example of ICE instilling fear in our communities and separating families – not going after the worst of the worst. When Democrats take control of the House and Senate on January 3rd, we will rein in this reckless agency," her statement read.

WASHINGTON – The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) released the following statement after bodycam footage went viral which depicted U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers being abandoned by police in Long Beach, California, as an angry mob surrounded them during an arrest.

On October 17, ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) Los Angeles conducted a targeted enforcement operation in Long Beach to apprehend a criminal illegal alien from Mexico whose criminal history includes a felony charge of inflicting corporal injury: spouse/cohabitant/date. The Long Beach Police Department (LBPD) had previously declined a detainer request for the suspect. During the operation, rioters obstructed ICE vehicles by blocking exits with their own vehicles and trash receptacles. Two of the rioters were arrested for damaging government vehicles, with one of them escaping after another rioter opened the door of the government vehicle she was in.

In bodycam footage captured by an ICE officer during the incident, an LBPD officer approaches ICE officers and says, “we’re being ordered to pull out. So you guys are going to be on your own. I’m sure you’re used to it. Good luck.” The officer later said that, “you guys are on your own, according to our watch commander.”

“The footage of what happened to our ICE officers in California is truly disturbing. As they were surrounded by an angry mob and being harassed and obstructed just for doing their job and going after dangerous criminals, the local police in Long Beach, California, were ordered to stand down and stop assisting them, leaving them to fend for themselves,” said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. “This is the end goal of the hateful rhetoric from sanctuary politicians in California and across the country. They want to see our ICE officers harmed in the line of duty, or worse. But even despite all the attacks, the patriots of ICE are committed to doing their duty and protecting the American people. title: The Supreme Court is about to take a closer look at Trump's immigration agenda | Politics
description: (CNN) — Democrats want to sideline President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda when they take control of Congress next year, but the real fight may take place across the street where
text:
(CNN) —
Democrats want to sideline President Donald Trump’s
immigration agenda
when they take control of Congress next year, but the real fight may take place across the street where the conservative Supreme Court is poised to uphold several of his most controversial policies.
The court will soon consider blockbuster appeals on the president’s
asylum ban
, his vast expansion of
mandatory detention
of migrants and his push to send certain people in the US illegally to countries other than their homeland — including some with
dubious human rights records
.
Decisions in those cases are expected by late June.
Though those three cases and several others are less flashy than this past summer’s blockbuster decision
upholding birthright citizenship
, the outcomes in the nuts-and-bolts disputes will have profound implications for policies the administration says are “indispensable” to its overall immigration crackdown.
“In all three of these cases, the Trump administration is trying to rewrite laws enacted by Congress, in service of a radical anti-immigrant agenda that has hurt not only immigrants, but the rule of law,” said Cecillia Wang with the American Civil Liberties Union, which is opposing the administration in two of those cases. “These Trump policies are not only illegal but also unpopular.”
Trump has had a mixed record on immigration at the 6-3 conservative court since returning to power last year. His unprecedented push to upend birthright citizenship was rejected. And the court limited his ability to use the
1798 Alien Enemies Act
to quickly remove certain migrants from the country.
On the other hand, six-justice majorities in June
allowed Trump to end
a form of humanitarian relief known as Temporary Protected Status and to limit asylum claims made at the border.
White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis dismissed Wang’s assertion that the court will find Trump’s immigration policies illegal.
“If the American Civil Liberties Union cares more about criminal illegal aliens than they do about American citizens, then they should change their name,” she said.
Some Democrats have framed the recapture of Congress as a rejection by voters of the administration’s immigration policies. Minnesota Sen.-elect
Peggy Flanagan
vowed to “rip ICE apart.” New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is all but certain to become the next House speaker,
told CBS
that Democrats would “put an end to Donald Trump’s violent mass deportation machine.”
But Republicans have
already frontloaded funding
for ICE for years. And Trump this month named Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, as White House
chief of staff
— a sign that the administration has no intention of slowing its immigration agenda.
“It stands to reason that hyper-aggressive immigration enforcement will continue to be one of the hallmarks of the Trump administration even as it faces Democratic majorities in both chambers of the legislature,” said Steve Vladeck, CNN Supreme Court analyst and professor at Georgetown University Law Center. “Whether the extremism of these policies will be allowed to continue is therefore going to be up to the Supreme Court.”
Conservatives who support the policies see a court that is prepared to back the president’s program.
“Over and over, judges in the district courts and the courts of appeals have interpreted the law contrary to clear congressional intent as evidenced by the text. And as a result, those decisions keep getting overturned,” Iowa Solicitor General Eric Wessan, whose state led briefs supporting the administration in two of the biggest cases, told CNN.
Wessan predicted that the justices will view lower court decisions on immigration against the administration with similar skepticism.
“Looking at the immigration cases the Supreme Court has taken this term,” he predicted, “I think it’s doing the same kind of cleanup.”
Human rights and arrests
The showdown will begin on December 9, when the justices will hear arguments in a case challenging Trump’s push to remove certain
migrants to countries
other than their homeland. In many cases, those removals are carried out without giving the migrant an opportunity to raise human rights concerns.
Federal law allows such “third country” removals in cases when a migrant’s home country refuses to accept them. The administration has used that provision to remove an Iranian national to Nicaragua, for instance, and Venezuelans to El Salvador, according to immigrants’ rights groups.
In some of those cases, immigrant rights groups say, migrants were sent back to their homeland from the “third country,” even when an immigration judge ordered that the administration not return to them to their native country.
Congress has also required the administration to ensure migrants won’t be tortured or persecuted once they land in a third country. That determination was previously made on a case-by-case basis. Under the second Trump administration, the government now accepts blanket assurances from a foreign country that no torture will take place, and migrants are often removed to that country without notice.
The Supreme Court, on its emergency docket,
three times allowed
the administration to pursue the policy while the case remained pending. It has not explained its reasoning.
Increase in arrests of migrants
Next year, the court will turn to the Trump administration’s decision to funnel not only recent border crossers into mandatory detention but also people who have been living within the United States for years.
That shift has permitted the Department of Homeland Security to dramatically increase the number of migrants arrested. And so if the court rejects that change, it will almost certainly jeopardize the administration’s ability to carry out massive sweeps for migrants that have played out in cities like Chicago and Minneapolis.
Immigrant rights groups say no prior administration, including Trump’s first, has interpreted federal law to require mandatory detention of so many migrants. But Justice Department officials told the Supreme Court that it is simply following the law that Congress enacted.
Asylum ban
And in the spring, the court will hear a challenge to Trump’s asylum ban. The president argues people crossing the border are making false asylum claims as a way to enter the country then stall the deportation process, since it can take years to resolve them.
US Solicitor General D. John Sauer, the administration’s top appellate attorney, warned the court of a “vicious cycle” that encouraged “illegal entry by millions of aliens, who (quite justifiably) inferred that even if they lacked meritorious asylum claims, they would ‘be released to live and work in the United States during their removal proceedings.’”
But the Immigration and Nationality Act specifically allows migrants to claim asylum, even as it leaves the decision about whether to grant safe harbor up to administration officials.
In stark language, the Justice Department has described its asylum policy as one of the “most important and effective” policies for stemming illegal immigration. A lower court order against the policy, the administration said, “threatens to revive the chaos along the southwest border that the proclamation has fended off for the past year and a half.”
The ACLU, representing 13 individuals and three immigrant rights groups that challenged the policy, said that if Trump wants to change the way asylum works, he should have passed a bill in Congress during the two years the chambers were in Republican hands.
Richard Caldarone, a senior litigation attorney at the National Immigrant Justice Center, said that the policies at issue in the cases had already put tens of thousands of people in harm’s way.
“These policies have been overwhelmingly rejected by lower courts across the country, and they flatly violate US immigration law as it has been understood for decades,” said Caldarone, whose group is fighting the administration in the asylum case.
“If the court validates the policies,” he said, “it will enshrine a new generation of internment camps, all but end the US asylum system as we have known it for almost half a century, and shatter our nation’s commitment to upholding human rights and democratic norms.”

A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operation resulted in the arrest of 115 people in Indiana over several weeks, according to a news release from the agency sent out on the evening of Nov. 24.

It's not clear exactly when the operation occurred or where in the state it took place, and the agency did not immediately answer follow-up questions from IndyStar.

The announcement comes a few months after a five-day operation between Aug. 30 and Sept. 3 netted more than 400 arrests in conjunction with local law enforcement agencies. While much of the operation was concentrated on Indianapolis, people were taken into custody statewide, ICE said in a prior release about the late-summer operation.

In the latest operation, the agency said there was targeted enforcement resulting in the arrests of undocumented immigrants, some who have criminal histories and convictions.

The agency identified six men who were arrested in the operation, including a 53-year-old man who the agency said has been arrested six times for firearms and battery charges and had illegally entered several times.

ICE also identified another man they said has ties to the MS-13 gang and three other men who allegedly entered the country illegally and have operating a vehicle under the influence of liquor convictions, according to the news release.

The agency, in its news release, said other people arrested in the operation have arrest records or convictions related to aggravated assault, criminal mischief, domestic violence in the presence of a child, drug trafficking, traffic offenses, licensing violations and public disturbance.

It's not clear how many of the 115 people arrested have criminal histories unrelated to immigration matters. The agency did not provide a full list of everyone who was arrested in the operation with information on their arrest records or criminal convictions. IndyStar requested this information, but in response received the same list of five people the agency has been sending to media since at least early September.

“This operation reinforces a fundamental principle: Federal immigration laws will be enforced in every American community, regardless of its size or location,” ICE Chicago Assistant Field Office Director Raymond Hernandez said in the agency's news release. “ICE officers arrested 115 illegal aliens, including many with criminal history and final orders of removal. The people of Indiana deserve the same protection under the law as residents of any major city."

text:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) is redirecting attorneys from across its civil litigating divisions to help defend the Trump administration against a surge in habeas petitions challenging immigration detention, amid the administration’s intensified deportation push.

The DOJ is digging deeper into resources to “double down on fighting the onslaught of frivolous habeas petitions used by corrupt judges to release criminal aliens back into communities and avoid deportation,” Attorney General Todd Blanche wrote on X Tuesday.

In a November 24 memo, Blanche said more than 97,000 noncitizens had filed habeas corpus petitions challenging their detention since January 2025—including roughly 10,000 since October 2026. Habeas corpus allows people in detention to ask a federal court to review whether their confinement is lawful.

Read More on Politics

Blanche characterized many of the petitions as "frivolous," arguing that the increase was partly driven by "the immigration bar's attempt to thwart President Trump's promise to the American people to prioritize their safety and security." He said the petitions had "substantially burdened" U.S. Attorneys Offices across the country.

The memo identifies roughly 2,000 litigators across the DOJ's civil components as a potential pool of additional support, though it does not specify how many attorneys will be reassigned.

The shift could have consequences beyond immigration litigation. The attorneys being tapped ordinarily handle antitrust, civil rights, environmental and other civil matters, potentially putting additional pressure on their existing caseloads.

Barbara McQuade, a University of Michigan law professor and former U.S. attorney, told Newsweek that the move will “require attorneys to put their other work on hold” while they work on immigration cases.

“This is the cost of a zero-tolerance policy,” McQuade said, adding that previous administrations had used a more targeted approach rather than pursuing all immigration cases.

“In addition, because they lack the expertise to handle immigration habeas cases, they will have to learn as they go, which is incredibly inefficient,” she added.

Blanche acknowledged that the litigating components were already carrying “a significant workload in light of personnel reduction” and said the DOJ would seek to mitigate any significant disruption to attorneys’ current dockets. The memo also says litigating attorneys will receive access to training on habeas cases.

Bridget Pranzatelli, staff attorney at the National Immigration Project, told Newsweek that “every one” of the 97,000 habeas petitions were filed by people in ICE detention seeking federal court review of their cases.

“Many of them would have gotten a bond hearing before this administration suddenly changed its interpretation of a decades-old law to fill beds that private prison companies get paid for,” she said in a statement.

The move comes as the Trump administration faces a growing number of legal challenges to its immigration detention practices. In one recent case, 41-year-old Herminio Cruz Lopez, a Mexican father detained by ICE near his home in Vista, California, is asking a federal court to order his release or grant him a bond hearing.

Cruz Lopez's attorney argues that he should not be subject to mandatory detention, saying that ICE arrested him inside the U.S. years after he last entered the country. A federal judge has ordered the administration to explain why Cruz Lopez's habeas corpus petition and request for a temporary restraining order should not be granted. The order does not rule that his detention is unlawful or require his release.

In response to Newsweek's request for comment about Cruz Lopez's detention, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) defended the arrest, saying his claims would be heard before an immigration judge and that he would receive due process.

The DHS spokesperson also criticized federal judges handling immigration-related habeas cases.

“It should come as no surprise that more habeas petitions are being filed by illegal aliens—especially after many activist judges have attempted to thwart President Trump from fulfilling the American people's mandate,” the spokesperson told Newsweek.

The DOJ memo also directs several senior DOJ offices to develop recommendations for what Blanche described as an "aggressive appellate strategy" on habeas litigation, with proposals due within 30 days.

Pranzatelli argued that if the DOJ cannot keep up with the growing number of legal challenges to ICE detention, there’s a simple fix: “Stop locking people up who never should have been detained in the first place.”

text:
The Supreme Court on Monday will hear oral argument in Wassily v. Blanche, a case on whether immigrants whose asylum protections have been terminated remain eligible to become lawful permanent residents, also known as green card holders.

Although the case will almost certainly be overshadowed by many of this term’s other immigration disputes – including Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, on the Trump administration’s suspension of access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border – it may hold considerable consequences for noncitizens and bring new significance to the Trump administration’s effort to scale back asylum.

The challengers in Wassily are two men who lost their asylum protections after being convicted of what immigration officials determined to be “particularly serious crime[s].”

Tamer Wassily was granted asylum in 2000 after raising concerns about facing religious persecution in his home country of Egypt. The Department of Homeland Security moved to terminate Wassily’s asylum protections after he was convicted in 2004 of third-degree stalking and child endangerment, beginning the process of deporting him back to Egypt.

Byron Velasquez Arreaga came to the United States from Guatemala in 1995 and was granted asylum the following year. After Velasquez Arreaga was convicted of driving while intoxicated in 2015 and for aggravated driving while intoxicated in 2018, DHS indicated that it would terminate his asylum protections and move to deport him.

Amid their removal proceedings, and after their asylum protections had been terminated, both Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga applied to become lawful permanent residents. This option is available to asylum recipients who meet certain requirements, including remaining in the United States for at least a year after receiving asylum protections, under 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b).

After many years of complicated legal wrangling before immigration judges and the Board of Immigration Appeals, the men’s cases were considered together by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit. The question before that court – and the question that is now before the Supreme Court – was whether noncitizens like Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga remain eligible for adjustment of immigration status under Section 1159(b) after their asylum protections have been terminated, because the statute refers to “any alien granted asylum” but is silent as to whether applicants must currently be asylees.

In a 2-1 ruling, a 2nd Circuit panel rejected the men’s contention that “granted asylum” addresses a past decision – in which case anyone who had ever received asylum would be eligible for status adjustment under Section 11159(b) – and concluded that noncitizens whose asylum protections have been terminated are “categorically barr[ed]” from applying for adjustment to permanent legal status.

Writing for the majority, Judge Richard Wesley emphasized the use of the word “status” in the opening of Section 1159(b), which reads: “The Secretary of Homeland Security or the Attorney General ... may adjust to the status of an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence the status of any alien granted asylum.” According to Wesley, a “natural reading of ‘the status of any alien granted asylum’ is that a noncitizen must presently be granted asylum to adjust to lawful permanent resident status under 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b).”

In January, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga asked the Supreme Court to review the 2nd Circuit’s ruling, highlighting a disagreement between the federal courts of appeals over whether the phrase “granted asylum” in Section 1159(b) “refer[s] to a completed, historical event” or “a continuing, present status.” Like the 2nd Circuit, they noted, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit has held that noncitizens who have lost their asylum protections “are categorically ineligible” “for adjustment to [lawful permanent resident] status under Section 1159(b).” The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit, on the other hand, has held that such immigrants remain “eligible for adjustment.”

In late June, the justices granted review.

In their brief on the merits, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga contend that the 2nd Circuit’s decision is out of step with the “[t]ext, context, structure, history, and purpose” of Section 1159(b). In particular, they highlight several nearby passages in which lawmakers explicitly imposed “continuing conditions” that address a termination of immigration status, asserting that Congress “could have and would have” included such a condition here if it intended to unambiguously bar former asylees from applying for lawful permanent residency.

The two men also point to Section 1159(c), which grants the DHS secretary and attorney general the authority to waive portions of the statute “for humanitarian purposes, to assure family unity, or when it is otherwise in the public interest.” Holding that adjustment to lawful permanent residency is categorically unavailable to noncitizens whose asylum protections have been terminated “would take core parts of that discretion away,” the men write. Such a limitation cuts against Congress’ purpose for allowing for discretion, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga argue. “There are many reasons why Congress would want” these officials “to retain discretion” here, they say, including that termination sometimes stems from factors “entirely outside” an asylee’s control. For example, the immigration status of the spouse and children of an asylee is often linked to the asylee’s status. If the noncitizen who was originally granted asylum loses his or her status, so does the whole family.

Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga ask the justices to recognize that, at the very least, the text of Section 1159(b) is unclear and to apply the rule of lenity, which they describe as a “well-settled and longstanding principle” under which “ambiguous provisions leading to the severe sanction of removal should be construed in favor of the noncitizen.” The Supreme Court “has repeatedly restated and reaffirmed that rule,” they conclude.

In its merits brief, the federal government counters that Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga’s interpretation of Section 1159(b) defies common sense. The text of the statute, according to U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer, describes a “transition from one status (that of an ‘alien granted asylum’) to another (that of an ‘alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence’).” If an immigrant is no longer at that starting point because his asylum status has been terminated, he can’t make the transition, Sauer asserts.

The government contends that the “statutory context” supports this interpretation, because, in nearby passages, “alien granted asylum” clearly refers to a noncitizen’s “present status.” For example, in Section 1158(c)(1), “Congress identified benefits available to an ‘alien granted asylum,’ including protection from removal and work authorization,” according to Sauer. “Those benefits undisputedly cease when asylum status is terminated.”

The government rejects the idea that barring noncitizens who have lost their asylum status from applying for a green card would interfere with the authority of the DHS secretary and attorney general to exercise discretion. Officials, Sauer writes, would remain free to intervene at an earlier point to prevent the termination of asylum status in the first place.

Sauer concludes by urging the justices to reject what he characterizes as a “last-resort appeal to lenity” – that is, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga’s claim that Section 1159(b) is an “ambiguous provision[]” and should therefore be interpreted in their favor. He argues that the rule of lenity does not apply here, not just because the meaning of the provision is clear, but also because Section 1159(b) does not directly address deportation, which is the context in which the rule of lenity arises.

The Supreme Court’s decision in Wassily v. Blanche is expected by early July at the latest.

A federal grand jury has been empaneled in Washington, DC, to consider evidence in Rep. Ilhan Omar’s immigration fraud case, The Post has learned.

The panel is hearing evidence obtained by prosecutors in DC US Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s Office and the Minnesota US Attorney’s Office related to possible immigration fraud committed by the Minnesota Democrat or her family members who fled war-torn Somalia in the 1990s, according to sources.

Pirro has also suggested federal prosecutors are looking into the finances of Omar and her husband, Tim Mynett.

It’s unclear what charges are being pursued against Omar and when the grand jury would be expected to make a decision on whether to hand up an indictment.

A heavily redacted search warrant related to the federal law enforcement raid on Omar’s DC home was unsealed Monday and revealed feds were eyeing potential crimes committed “between 1980 to the present.”

“The United States believes ILHAN has committed [redacted] crimes over decades — beginning long before she was ever in Congress,” one of the filings stated, adding that the feds’ case didn’t have “anything to do with ILHAN’s professional life.”

In another filing, prosecutors also wrote they were “in the throes of a preindictment investigation.”

Sources have previously told The Post that the immigration case has focused on multiple lines of inquiry, including whether Omar allegedly misrepresented her birth date by a year on government papers in order to become a citizen when her father naturalized in 2000.

text:
The Salvadoran migrant mistakenly shipped to his home country last year before becoming a legal thorn in President Trump’s side landed in Spain Wednesday — ending a months-long battle to keep him in the United States and avoid deportation to Africa.

Kilmar Ábrego García, whose removal to the Central American nation’s notorious CECOT prison became an early flashpoint of Trump’s immigration crackdown, was greeted by a mob of photographers at Madrid’s international airport.

The new arrival declined to speak with reporters, but raised a fist as he entered a van.

“The US government may be the most powerful government in the world, but justice can still prevail,” Ábrego García said in a statement. “In this case, despite everything they tried to say, every obstacle they put in my way, and every attempt to shame me, justice prevailed under this administration in a way that many people never thought was possible.”

The Department of Homeland Security confirmed Tuesday night that Ábrego García had left the US under a judge’s removal order and would not be permitted to return.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a X post that he was “delighted” at Ábrego García’s departure and repeated the government’s claim that the migrant was a gang member — a claim the Salvadoran has repeatedly denied.

Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, a Virginia-based attorney representing Ábrego García, claimed his client’s Spain stay would be “temporary.”

“Mr. Abrego Garcia has many options to return to the United States as the husband of a US citizen spouse and the father of a US citizen child,” the lawyer said. “We don’t expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland.”

Ábrego García was arrested in Maryland on March 12, 2025, and sent to El Salvador three days later on one of three planes carrying suspected gang members.

The administration later acknowledged that Ábrego García’s deportation was an “administrative error,” but his return to the US in June was prompted by his indictment on federal human trafficking charges out of Tennessee and followed by another protracted legal fight over his immigration status.

Federal officials subsequently sought to deport him to a series of African countries, prompting another round of legal challenges as Ábrego García fought to remain in the US.

The case became a major test of the administration’s authority to deport migrants and the ability of federal courts to intervene when deportations are challenged.

The Trump administration has made mass deportations a central promise, pledging to remove 1 million people annually as it ramped up immigration enforcement.

With the help of billions of dollars approved by Congress, the administration expanded its rank of immigration officers, increased detention capacity and accelerated efforts to remove migrants from the country.

Ábrego García’s immigration status in Spain was not immediately clear.

text:
Lawsuit Challenges ICE’s Abandonment of Longstanding Protections for Vulnerable Population

November 25, 2026 - Washington, D.C. — Human rights, immigrant advocacy, and workers’ rights organizations on Tuesday filed a lawsuit challenging the Trump-Vance administration’s unlawful decision to abandon a federal directive designed to prevent the detention of pregnant, postpartum, and nursing immigrants. The lawsuit alleges that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has made a decision to disregard its own binding policy, subjecting pregnant individuals and new mothers to prolonged detention, inadequate medical care, and GPS shackles.

Markwayne Mullin, Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS)

The lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia by the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, Venezuelan Association of Massachusetts, Workers’ Center of Central New York, Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition, Worker Justice Center of New York, and Women’s Refugee Commission.

The complaint challenges ICE’s decision to stop following a 2021 directive that prohibits the detention of pregnant, postpartum, and nursing immigrants unless detention is required by law or exceptional circumstances exist. The directive also requires weekly reviews of detention decisions, mandates monitoring of medical conditions, and prohibits using GPS monitors on covered individuals enrolled in ICE’s Alternatives to Detention program.

According to a report by the Women’s Refugee Commission, which analyzes ICE data obtained through a FOIA request, from January 2025 through March 2026, the monthly count of pregnant individuals in ICE detention has increased by 1,320%. The data also show that since 2025, more than 557 pregnant individuals have been detained for an average of 43 days or longer, with nearly 14% held for at least 90 days.

The consequences have been devastating. The complaint describes pregnant individuals who have suffered miscarriages while in ICE custody, been denied timely and appropriate prenatal care, and faced dangerous conditions during high-risk pregnancies. It also details cases in which nursing mothers have been separated from their infants, sometimes just days or weeks after delivery, and denied breast pumps, putting them at risk for mastitis and depriving their babies of critical nutrition.

“Over the past two years, Kennedy Human Rights Center has stood in court with pregnant women terrified of giving birth in a cell and postpartum and nursing mothers ripped away from their babies,” said Anthony Enriquez, VP of U.S. Advocacy and Litigation at the Kennedy Human Rights Center. “The cruelty and suffering inflicted on these women is akin to torture. It’s time for this grave human rights abuse to end.

“It’s heartbreaking that pregnant women and new mothers are being put through this. No woman should have to fear losing her baby or being separated from her newborn simply because of her immigration status,” said Ciro Valiente, Board Director and Spokesperson for the Venezuelan Association of Massachusetts. “We know how much fear and anguish immigration enforcement has created for families in our community. The government must uphold the protections already in place to prevent these women from being detained. They belong with their families, not behind bars, facing the unimaginable pain of losing a child.”

We continue to be astonished at the extent of the cruelty waged against women and families by ICE under the Trump administration. ICE has routinely targeted the most vulnerable, subjecting pregnant women and young children to detention in facilities marked by overcrowding, poor management, and a concerning lack of adequate healthcare,” commented Jessica Maxwell, Executive Director of Workers Center of Central New York. “Here in New York, ICE is now constructing a tent expansion of the Buffalo Federal Detention Facility for the purpose of holding women through Western New York’s extreme winters. The inevitable and preventable tragedies resulting from ICE violating its own pregnancy directive can not be allowed to continue. This lawsuit is a crucial step to protect our communities.”

“ICE and DHS continue to show blatant disregard not just for their own policies but for basic humanity. Ripping pregnant and nursing mothers from their vulnerable children and shipping them across state lines is almost unimaginable, yet ICE has turned a blind eye to their own directives and has done just that to too many pregnant and postpartum women,” said Spring Miller, Senior Director of Legal Strategy at the Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition (TIRRC). “Having fought and secured the release of one such mother this summer, we recognize how each of these cases demonstrates the extraordinary cruelty these agencies inflict on people every day, and the multiple points at which people in detention are denied access to due process. Together with our partners, we demand ICE and DHS reverse course, and we condemn the countless ways these agencies continue to separate families across the country.”

“Immigration detention is cruel by design and known to deprive people of adequate food, medical care, basic necessities, and access to family and lawyers. Its cruelty is starkest, and harm is most irreparable when it endangers a person’s pregnancy or separates a newborn or nursing infant from their source of love and sustenance. I urge everyone to read the complaint in this lawsuit, which reveals the extent of the tragedies occurring across the country from ICE not following its own directive. These stories will only proliferate in New York with planned extensions to the Buffalo Federal Detention Facility at Batavia—an expansion designed to hold immigrant women, including pregnant and nursing women, in tents throughout New York winters,” said Alaina Varvaloucas, Executive Director of the Worker Justice Center of New York.

“This litigation is critical to protecting the health and safety of pregnant, postpartum, and nursing women,” said Zain Lakhani, Director of Migrant Rights and Justice at the Women’s Refugee Commission. “Through a Freedom of Information Act request, WRC obtained some of the first official data providing meaningful evidence that ICE is not complying with its own 2021 Pregnancy Directive. The data also shows that ICE is detaining these women in facilities with lower medical standards and not providing them with the care they need to support safe pregnancies. We are seeking immediate enforcement of the directive so these women can protect their own health and the health of their babies.”

“Pregnant individuals and new mothers should not be subjected to dangerous detention conditions, denied critical medical care, or separated from their babies because this administration has decided to disregard its own rules,” said Skye Perryman, President and CEO of Democracy Forward. “The Trump-Vance administration cannot abandon longstanding protections while pretending they remain in place. These safeguards exist to protect people’s health, safety, and dignity, and the law requires the government to follow them. We are going to court to hold this administration accountable and ensure that pregnant and postpartum immigrants receive the protections they are entitled to under the law.”

The lawsuit also features data obtained by American Oversight through FOIA, whose ongoing investigation into medical treatment and conditions in immigration detention facilities uncovered thousands of medical claims related to pregnancy, childbirth, and postpartum complications between October 2021 and September 2025. For example, the records included 111 claims involving supervision of high-risk pregnancies from January through September 2025, raising further concerns about the health and safety of pregnant, postpartum, and nursing immigrants in federal immigration custody.

The plaintiffs argue that the administration’s conduct violates the Administrative Procedure Act and the longstanding legal principle that federal agencies must follow their own binding rules. They are asking the court to declare ICE’s decision to abandon the 2021 directive unlawful, set aside or halt that decision, and require the agency to comply with the protections established under the directive.

Read the complaint here.

text:
Immigrants facing detention by federal authorities are making hard choices about whether Thanksgiving travel is worth the risk, advocacy rights groups say.

More than 81 million people plan to travel at least 50 miles from home for the holiday, according to AAA. But the Trump administration's aggressive immigration enforcement efforts, highlighted in part by the Nov. 21 detention of two people at the Seattle-Tacoma Airport, has some people reconsidering their movements.

That includes immigrants with the legal right to live and work in the U.S. but who want to avoid being stopped and questioned, said Zachary Mueller, a senior strategist with the advocacy group States at the Core.

"Some people are terrified to leave their house," said Mueller, whose organization has trained about 75,000 people to monitor and record ICE detentions. "For some people, that fear has become so palpable in day-to-day life that this holiday is nothing new on that level."

Mueller added: "For others, they're asking 'is traveling to go see family for the holidays worth the risk of never seeing my family again?' That's a real calculation."

The exact number of people facing deportation is unclear, but roughly 350,000 Haitians and about 600,000 Venezuelans lost Temporary Protected Status in the past two years.

The Department of Homeland Security reports that in fiscal year 2026, ICE carried out more than 483,000 deportations, the most ever in a single year. President Donald Trump has promised the largest mass deportation in U.S. history, and during his second term DHS reports that more than 3 million people have already left the United States either via deportation or self-removal.

Immigrants who leave the United States voluntarily can receive a $3,000 payment and a free flight to their home country.

Administration officials said they will continue to enforce immigration laws, including those that make it harder for undocumented immigrants to fly. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers routinely check Transportation Security Administration manifests for potential immigration violators.

Last May, the Department of Homeland Security began requiring flyers to show REAL ID-compliant identification to board airplanes, a move that made it easier to detect people who lacked permission to live in the United States. People without REAL ID can fly but are subject to additional security checks and may have to pay a $45 fee.

“DHS reversed the horrendous Biden-era policy that allowed aliens in our country illegally to jet around our country. Under President Trump, DHS will no longer tolerate this," an unnamed DHS spokesperson said in a statement. "This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport."

Immigrants who are considering travel should check first with their attorney and make sure to carry copies of relevant paperwork, said Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, the president and CEO of Global Refuge. She said many refugees who sought safety in the United States are now worried about being targeted by the same government that asked them to fill out paperwork and register their home addresses.

She said many refugees, including those from Haiti and Venezuela are frustrated because Trump keeps saying ICE is targeting the "worst of the worst."

"These are people who did everything right, went through vetting, did all the paperwork," she said. "And now they're asking us whether following the rules has somehow put them more at risk."

Mueller said the harsh enforcement tactics also have impacts on travelers who witness anonymous and masked federal agents grabbing screaming people at airports. He said driving may not be a safe option for some people, particularly if they are driving through communities that have signed cooperative agreements allowing local police to help enforce immigration laws.

"It's not just the people who are first affected, but that kind of fear and trauma and concern, the wanton separation, the ability of ICE to do whatever it wants and create these chaotic scenes ... millions of Americans have been seeing this," Mueller said. "They're asking themselves when they travel, 'am I going to see something that's going to ruin my holiday because this administration wants to rip apart families?' That's the absurd reality of this moment."

Marjory Wentworth, a board member of the Haitian Support Center in Springfield, Ohio, said her family is hosting a handful of Haitians for Thanksgiving. Many members of Ohio's Haitian community lost their Temporary Protected Status in July. The Trump administration has revoked their work permission and urged them to leave the United States.

Wentworth said none of the Haitians she knows will risk flying. She said at last one local church hosted a Thanksgiving dinner for Haitian congregants over the weekend, allowing them to celebrate without traveling far from home.

"People can't go work, they've got ankle monitors," she said of her own invited guests. "I feel like people are still pretty fearful. I'm hoping we can distract them for a day."

text:
By Diane Taylor

October 26, 2026

Tasks from determining asylum seekers’ ages to border surveillance now involve AI, says Open Rights Group.

AI has been embedded across the Home Office in near-total secrecy, reinforcing the so-called hostile environment for immigration, according to research.

Tasks from the detection of potential sham marriages to determining the age of asylum seekers and checking through the contents of phones of new arrivals now involve use of the technology, according to a report by Open Rights Group (ORG).

It is also being used to conduct surveillance of borders, through live facial recognition and AI-powered drones and satellites; to summarise asylum interviews and country policy information used as evidence in those interviews; and to prioritise and assess cases through the opaque Identify and Prioritise Immigration Cases (Ipic) tool.

Information for the report has been gathered from a mix of limited information published by the Home Office, freedom of information requests and questions from MPs. The report has cross-party support from Labour’s Bell Ribeiro-Addy, the Scottish National party’s Pete Wishart and the Green party’s Siân Berry.

The report, titled Automated Discrimination: Unpacking the Digital Hostile Environment, raises concerns about the use of AI in immigration, saying it is not neutral or accurate and can replicate bias and discrimination within society, particularly when a key driver for its use is anti-immigration policies and rhetoric.

It says AI is being trialled and tested in near-total secrecy, with officials routinely invoking national security to stonewall freedom of information requests and redact disclosures. Successive governments are criticised for pushing an ideology that reduces complex human cases to a technical problem that can be fixed.

The report raises concerns about “reducing people to data points” and replicating the hostile environment first envisaged by Theresa May as home secretary in 2012. “Relying on AI to decide who gets to stay here and who gets thrown back into danger is a deeply alarming move,” it states.

Open Rights Group is calling on the government to regulate AI and ban uses that are undemocratic and risk human rights violations, such as the use of ChatGPT tools in asylum applications.

It also wants more transparency and stronger freedom of information laws, a narrower definition of national security and a robust public register of government AI tools.

Ribeiro-Addy said: “In spite of questions and requests, the Home Office has been reluctant to publish the documents that would explain how AI is used in asylum processing, what the problems are and how they are being addressed. The department has not explained how it will ensure there is accountability when they fail or justified why some of the most vulnerable people, with the least power, should bear the greatest risks.”

Sara Alsherif, a programme manager at Open Rights Group, said: “Migration is a human phenomenon and experience, not a technical problem that can be fixed by artificial intelligence. We urgently need transparency, accountability and strict regulation to restrict how AI is used and to prevent its wider rollout.”

text:
On Tuesday morning, two elected officials with distinctly different general political ideals — Del. Sam Rasoul of Roanoke and Roanoke County School Board member Tim Greenway — joined together to denounce U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity in the region.

During a press conference at Roanoke’s Williamson Branch Library, they said that policy changes on the federal level need to be made and that conversations about immigration need to happen across the aisle.

There has been a “sharp increase” in ICE enforcement in the Roanoke Valley in the past two weeks, said Jaime McGuire, a Salem immigration attorney with Amaryllis Law. She said around 50 people have been detained in the Roanoke Valley, and another 40 have been detained in Lynchburg. She said ICE has also been active in Blacksburg and Christiansburg but was not able to elaborate.

She said because these numbers are only from community members who have witnessed the detainments, she expects the numbers are actually higher.

An ICE spokesperson, in an email response Tuesday to questions from Cardinal News about the recent activity, wrote that “for operational security and the safety of our officers, ICE will not disclose or discuss law enforcement operations. Every day, DHS enforces the laws of the nation across the country, including in Virginia.”

Included in that email were pictures with convictions listed for five people identified as “criminal illegal aliens” who were detained in Virginia — none in the Roanoke Valley or its general region. The charges range from drug distribution to sexual assault to murder.

The school board is a nonpartisan office. But Greenway, who was first elected to the county school board in 2015, is a Republican who has campaigned and voted as a conservative. Greenway is a “three-time Trump-voter,” according to a press release from Rasoul’s communications team announcing Tuesday’s press conference.

Greenway said Tuesday that the policies coming from the federal government now “do not reflect the Christian Conservative values” that he has “grown up believing in.”

“This is no way to live. This is not us. These are not American values. This is the difference between keeping our streets safe and simply terrorizing some folks,” he said.

Rasoul is a Democrat who is critical of the Trump administration and has built his political career on human rights and other issues such as support of a Green New Deal.

He said that he and Greenway have had open communication on various issues over the years, and the recent spike in ICE activity prompted this conversation.

“We have students who are not going to school, people who are not going to work, taxpaying, even citizens, who are worried about what will happen to me and my family,” Rasoul said. “I just want to thank my Republican colleague Tim Greenway here for saying we need to have a broader conversation. … We’ve gotta pull it out of the partisan sphere and say, how are we going to treat people the way we want them to be treated here in America that we know and love?”

Rasoul said he encourages people to have open conversations about immigration and to reach out to federal representatives. He said he and Greenway have not spoken with U.S. Rep. Ben Cline, R-Botetourt County, but have spoken with a number of other U.S. senators and officials.

“Too many families” are not feeling safe or are being “torn apart,” Rasoul said, “and it’s because of some policies that I believe have just clearly gone too far. Enough is enough.”

Greenway said he and Rasoul have had the opportunity to sit down with some families affected, and it “becomes real. You realize that these are folks trying to become legal who are having obstacles put in their way.

“I don’t want to demonize people, whether it be immigrants or whether it be the folks that are enforcing the policy,” Greenway said. “I feel more strongly that we need to demonize the policy.”

McGuire said in the last two weeks, “working fathers” are being detained in the middle of the workday, and that families are being given no information as to how to find their loved ones. McGuire said in an email Tuesday that in the past two weeks, she has only heard of men being detained.

“This is dramatically different from what I see in my practice everyday,” McGuire said. “Normally, individuals are detained on a random basis or more sporadically. This is very organized enforcement.” In an email, McGuire said her firm does not have an answer as to why this is happening.

She said ICE actions have been more rapid than usual in recent weeks, with individuals being moved outside of the locality or the state quickly. She said due process rights have been violated, but said she was not able to specify any cases due to attorney-client privilege.

Last Wednesday, Roanoke City Councilwoman Vivian Sanchez-Jones and council member-elect Danny Clawson — both Democrats — estimated around 30 people had been detained in three days. Both were connecting with a social media group that was verifying information throughout the week.

Community groups observed and kept track of activity last week outside of an ICE facility in Salem, where large SUVs were entering and leaving the fenced gate throughout the day. Agents at the facility were fully covered and masked, and protesters said there were an unusual number of vehicles outside of the facility. Cars were parked in the grass outside of the fence.

The number of ICE detainees in the Roanoke jail more than tripled in 2025 when compared to 2024, according to the jail’s invoice documents, which Cardinal News obtained from the city.

McGuire, the immigration attorney, said Tuesday that any families who are concerned, even with legal status, should create a plan for action in case of emergency. She said those who have had loved ones detained should reach out to legal counsel as soon as possible, within 24 hours.

Cardinal News staff writer Emily Schabacker contributed to this story.
