text:
Four formerly detained immigrants said they were subjected to rape, sexual assault, anti-LGBTQ harassment and a forced labor scheme at an ICE detention center in Louisiana.

The four filed a federal lawsuit Monday against GEO Group, the private prison company behind the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center in Basile, Louisiana, as well as former assistant warden Emmanuel Reyes and former detention officer David Courvelle. The detention center is the largest in the nation for female immigrant detainees.

They “endured a months-long nightmare of rape, sexual abuse, degrading harassment, and hard manual labor that targeted primarily transgender and non-binary detained people,” according to the lawsuit.

Luis Renteria-Gonzalez, Mario Garcia-Valenzuela, Kenia Campos-Flores and Jane Doe said in the lawsuit that between 2023 and 2025 they were repeatedly abused by Reyes and Courvelle and forced to perform sex acts and hard manual labor under threats to themselves and their families. Renteria-Gonzalez and Garcia-Valenzuela are transgender men and Campos-Flores is nonbinary.

“They suffered horrific, abusive conditions at the hands of employees of the GEO Group,” Susan Meyers, the senior supervising attorney with the Southern Poverty Law Center, told NBC News.

GEO Group did not immediately respond to a request for comment. NBC News was unable to reach Reyes and Courvelle. Courvelle was sentenced to three years in federal prison in June after pleading guilty to sexual abuse of a different detainee.

“Reyes coerced plaintiffs to perform hard physical labor, sex acts, or both, threatening them with death, deportation, further sexual abuse, physical harm, and harm to their families and loved ones,” according to a statement announcing the lawsuit.

The physical labor and custodial work involved stripping floors, sanitizing housing units and facility spaces and moving heavy supplies and machinery without protective equipment, the lawsuit said, adding that the plaintiffs suffered physical injuries and exposure to toxic fumes. Reyes is accused in the lawsuit of telling Renteria-Gonzalez, “If you think you are a man, I’m going to treat you like a man.”

Reyes abused his power to sexually assault the detainees in areas hidden from surveillance cameras, stalk them, view their naked bodies on surveillance camera footage and harass people in the middle of the night, according to the lawsuit.

The lawsuit also alleges that after Doe turned down an offer to join Reyes’ “cleaning crew,” he stalked and harassed her, groped her and forced Doe to perform sex acts on him under threats to her life if she refused.

Reyes left the facility voluntarily in 2024, Meyers said. It was unclear if he was employed at another facility.

GEO Group did not immediately respond to a request for comment about Reyes’ employment status.

The lawsuit also accused Courvelle of sexually assaulting Garcia-Valenzuela multiple times and forcing Renteria-Gonzalez and Garcia-Valenzuela to stand guard outside a closet while he raped a woman who was also detained there.

“The treatment and the conditions that they had us living in, nobody should go through that,” Renteria-Gonzalez said in the statement. “It’s unbelievable that this happened under the care of the people who are supposed to protect us.”

Sarah Decker, a senior staff attorney at the Robert and Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, said the four former detainees did not suffer in silence.

“They screamed for help. They filed a complaint with every avenue that was available to them,” she said.

Meyers said that despite them coming forward with the allegations, “in many cases things got worse, because what they found was that it opened them up to retaliatory actions” such as solitary confinement.

Garcia-Valenzuela said in a statement, “We were looked down upon like the sole of someone’s shoe.”

“What we experienced there was a true nightmare,” Garcia-Valenzuela said. “For the rest of my life, I will live with the aftereffects of the torture and abuse I endured.”

There have been previous accusations of sexual abuse at the facility, including in 2022, when a Prison Rape Elimination Act audit by the Department of Homeland Security documented four sexual abuse allegations that included one staff-on-detainee allegation and three detainee-on-detainee allegations. Two of the sexual abuse allegations were substantiated, including one against a staff member who resigned the day the allegation was made, according to the audit report. All four cases were investigated and closed.

The report does not say how GEO Group responded to the four cases.

The auditor found in the report that the detention center met 36 standards, exceeded one standard, and was out of compliance with two standards: accommodating detainees with disabilities and detainees who are limited English proficient, and detainee education.

The facility entered into a 180-day corrective plan for those two standards and was later found to be in compliance.

text:
Two Georgia men are at the center of a lawsuit filed by the ACLU seeking to halt a new federal policy that allows immigrants who have previously been released by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to be re-detained for no clear reason.

Under a decades-old policy, immigrants with pending immigration cases were generally not re-detained by ICE as long as they were following all the conditions of their release, including appearing at court hearings and immigration check-in meetings. Officials would have to show that there had been a change in circumstances, such as a new criminal charge, before re-detaining someone, according to ACLU of Georgia staff attorney Raneem Ashrawi.

But a lawsuit filed earlier this month in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia claims the Department of Homeland Security reversed course on that policy in May 2025. Under the new re-detention policy, officials can take immigrants into custody without assessing whether their circumstances had changed.

The lawsuit argues the re-detention policy violates the Fourth Amendment and leaves immigrants across Georgia, North Carolina and South Carolina, where ICE’s Atlanta Field office has jurisdiction, vulnerable to being baselessly re-detained by immigration officials. The complaint also calls on the courts to block the policy, as a federal judge in California did last year.

The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to a request for comment.

Two Georgia residents are among the four plaintiffs in the class action case. Two North Carolina residents are also plaintiffs.

Alvaro Ibañez-Cardenas, a 35-year-old Venezuelan man who lives in Athens, was initially detained in 2022 upon arriving in the U.S. He was later released and was detained for a second time in September during a routine check-in at the Atlanta ICE field office, according to the lawsuit. Ibañez-Cardenas was transferred to Irwin County Detention Center before being released in October on a $20,000 bond.

In a statement provided by the ACLU, Ibañez-Cardenas said he was greatly affected by the period of detention. He lost his job at a warehouse roughly three days after being detained, the lawsuit states. His pending asylum case, which was submitted in 2023, was also cancelled as a result of his re-detention.

“I feel very paranoid and worried all the time, but I have to keep going in order to make money to take care of my family,” he said in the statement.

Ambrosio Trujillo Zavaleta, a 46-year-old from Mexico who lives in Savannah, was also detained by ICE in September along with his wife and adult son, according to the lawsuit. A plumber who has lived in the U.S. since 2004, he was arrested once in 2014 for driving without a license but was ultimately released, paid the fines associated with the charge and obtained his driver’s license. After his second arrest, he was sent to an ICE processing center in Folkston, which is located in South Georgia, where he was held for nearly a month before being released on a $20,000 bond.

Trujillo Zavaleta’s wife was also eventually released from detention, but their son is still in ICE custody. Their daughter, who is a U.S. citizen and a student at the University of Georgia, relies on him for financial support, the lawsuit said.

Though he is now back at work, Trujillo Zavaleta said the detention has left a lasting impact on him and his family.

“My wife, who was also detained at the same time as me, now lives in constant fear of leaving the house,” Trujillo Zavaleta said in a statement provided by the ACLU. “I get very nervous going out in public or driving to work because I know ICE might choose to re-detain me at any time.”

Ashrawi, the ACLU of Georgia staff attorney, said the detentions have left both men and their families feeling unsettled.

“They relied on what they were told when they were released,” she said. “They followed the conditions of their release, and so to be abruptly snatched from their family and their community has shaken them.”

text:
A former adviser to President Ronald Reagan appealed to President Donald Trump Tuesday to use his pardoning power to give relief to over a million immigrants without legal status.

In an op-ed for Fox News, Hugh Hewitt, who also served within the Nixon administration, called the potential move a "golden touch" for Trump, which would give some relief to undocumented immigrants fearing deportation.

Trump himself floated the idea of a deal with Democrats on immigration reform during an interview with CBS' 60 Minutes following the midterms, but he has faced pushback from his MAGA base and senior administration officials over their fears of an amnesty for immigrants without criminal charges or convictions.

Read More on Politics

"He can pardon undocumented immigrants for any federal crimes they might have committed. That’s different, however, from legalizing their status, which raises different issues," Ilya Somin, law professor at George Mason University, told Newsweek. "In any event, I highly doubt he would actually do anything like this. He has a history of sometimes suggesting pro-immigrant policies, but almost never actually acting on any of them. On the other hand, he repeatedly DOES act on all kinds of cruel anti-immigrant impulses."

Newsweek reached out to Hewitt and the White House for comment Tuesday afternoon.

What Is Hugh Hewitt Proposing?

Hewitt's proposal is not for a mass amnesty, but for a selective program of pardons for a particular group of people while ensuring potential immigrants did not think they could head to the U.S. and overstay their visas without facing consequences.

In his op-ed, Hewitt said that those who entered the country illegally, returned after deportation, or overstayed a visa could be eligible for a presidential pardon. Other criteria could include those who have been continuously in the U.S. before January 2020, have sustained employment and have paid taxes.

Hewitt also suggested the group could be initially narrowed to parents of U.S. citizens, and that Trump would not need to wait for Congress to act.

"Such an act of presidential mercy would be unprecedented—without a parallel mass grant of grace in American history—and it would be approved of by supermajorities of Americans and certain to be counted among his greatest achievements as president by citizens of all political persuasions who have long desired an actual breakthrough on this stalemated front," Hewitt wrote.

He suggested that White House Counsel Will Scharf write up a selection of options for the president to consider.

Jeremy Beck, co-president of the immigration reform group NumbersUSA, told Newsweek that Hewitt was seriously misreading election polling.

"Americans are concerned about how immigration enforcement has been carried out, but they want credible enforcement," he said. "You get better enforcement by shifting the emphasis to the workplace and the point of hire. That would be effective and boring -- exactly what a majority of Americans want."

Beck said midterm voters were most worried about their economic security and that an interior immigration enforcement strategy focused on workplaces, audits and the E-Verify system for checking worker eligibility was "most consistent" with that mandate.

"Offering a pardon to millions of people who are already here illegally sends exactly the wrong message to the smugglers and cartels who prey on economic migrants, especially when Congress has failed to close the loopholes they exploited during the last crisis," Beck said.

Could Trump Actually Pardon Undocumented Immigrants?

Trump has broad constitutional authority to issue pardons, but using that power to protect undocumented immigrants from deportation would likely raise more complicated legal questions.

Article II of the Constitution gives presidents the power to grant pardons for "Offenses against the United States." The Supreme Court has interpreted that authority expansively, including allowing presidents to pardon entire classes of people rather than requiring clemency to be granted individually.

That means Trump could potentially pardon federal immigration crimes committed by a defined group of undocumented immigrants.

Legal scholar Jason A. Cade previously argued in 2024 that presidential pardons raise distinctive constitutional questions in immigration cases because the pardon power comes directly from Article II and has historically been protected from congressional interference.

Cade told Newsweek Tuesday that a mass pardon would be interesting and unprecedented. "In fact, it is so unprecedented that the exact effectiveness down the road is a little hard to predict," he said.

"Arguably a broad enough pardon would remove any civil penalties related to immigration violations. However, no pardon can confer status on undocumented immigrants," Cade said.

Entering the United States illegally can be prosecuted as a federal misdemeanor, while illegally reentering after removal can constitute a felony. However, a pardon would not necessarily give its recipients legal status or an automatic right to remain in the country.

In other words, pardoning an immigrant for a federal offense does not itself grant that person a green card or another lawful immigration status—something which has been floated before and referred to as an amnesty.

"The president can certainly pardon illegal immigrants for any crimes they have committed, but that does not protect them from deportation because they still would not have any legal status, which the president cannot provide through the pardon power," David Bier, director of immigration studies at the libertarian Cato Institute, told Newsweek Tuesday.

"Illegal immigrants would still be here illegally with no right to live or work here, so the proposal protects them against criminal prosecutions for entering or reentering illegally (the punishment for which is prison) but does nothing to protect them from deportation."

Reagan's Immigration Legacy

Hewitt served within the Reagan administration, which did oversee a widespread amnesty in 1986, as part of wider immigration reforms.

The Immigration Reform and Control Act combined tougher enforcement and employer sanctions—something current policy critics have called for under the second Trump administration—with legalization for qualifying undocumented immigrants.

"The legalization provisions in this act will go far to improve the lives of a class of individuals who now must hide in the shadows, without access to many of the benefits of a free and open society," Reagan said in a statement at the time. "Very soon many of these men and women will be able to step into the sunlight and, ultimately, if they choose, they may become Americans."

While not without its issues and critics, the legislation was seen as a major milestone in U.S. immigration policy, allowing around 2.7 million immigrants to obtain legal permanent residence, or a green card.

Playing to this legacy may appeal to the current president, who has often framed himself as the most consequential resident of the White House when it comes to major policy areas—from the economy to foreign relations. With immigration one of his key focuses across both terms, it remains to be seen if he will seek to leave a lasting mark on the issue.

Would Trump See Support for a Mass Pardon?

While those within his administration and more conservative Republicans in Congress might push back against any leniency for those who once crossed the U.S. border illegally or stayed after their visa lapsed, Trump himself has mentioned on multiple occasions that he would be willing to work on a deal to help this group if they have not committed other offenses.

What could push him to act is public support for Hewitt's idea. In his 60 Minutes interview, Trump said he felt voters thought his immigration policies had been "too tough," showing he understands Americans are paying attention to how his administration tackles immigration.

Polls have also consistently shown that many Americans want to see pathways to legal status or even citizenship for long-term undocumented immigrants.

Bier said voters might support a mass pardon, but "it would not resolve the biggest issues in the immigration debate."

"In any case, the Supreme Court has already said that for as long as he is in office, the president can choose how to prioritize immigrants for deportation, how many immigrants to target, and the like, which is what Biden did," Bier said. "But Trump is not using any of his existing power to protect any immigrants from deportation, so I’m skeptical he would act on this idea.

"The alternatives are for Congress to change the law, or the president to change how he’s enforcing the law."

Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

U.S. Sen. Patty Murray is pushing for an oversight investigation into the Trump administration’s purchase of a controversial immigrant detention center in Tacoma.

In a letter sent Tuesday morning, Nov. 24, Murray requested the inspector general within the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to immediately investigate the $453 million sale of the Northwest ICE Processing Center.

Announced last week, the sale would transfer the Washington facility, with roughly 1,600 beds, from private ownership by the Florida-based GEO Group to the federal government. GEO, one of the nation’s top private prison operators, expects to net $340 million from the transaction after taxes, which will go toward stock buybacks.

The most recent assessment of the detention center site set the property’s value at $72.6 million. Earlier this year, GEO valued the detention center at $67 million, according to The Intercept.

“The Office of Inspector General must investigate this egregious waste of taxpayer dollars, which serves to enrich a private detention contractor to maintain unsafe conditions in immigration detention,” Murray wrote in her letter to Inspector General Joseph Cuffari.

Murray, a Democrat who is poised to become chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee, wants Cuffari to determine how GEO and the Department of Homeland Security landed at the hefty price.

“This waste and abuse of taxpayer dollars to pursue President Trump and Stephen Miller’s cruel and extreme immigration agenda deserves immediate attention before the sale is finalized,” Murray wrote, referring to the president’s new chief of staff and the architect of his immigration agenda.

Federal ownership could allow the Tacoma facility, which for years has faced numerous allegations of mistreatment and human rights violations, to evade oversight under a state law seeking to inspect the detention center. The state and GEO Group have been in court for years as the company has batted down the state’s attempts to investigate thousands of complaints.

The legal question has been whether the state can regulate a federal contractor, but if the feds own the facility, constitutional doctrine could bar state officials from inspecting under the 2023 law.

The Trump administration has been rumored to be looking at buying detention facilities across the country to evade oversight. Last month, GEO sold its 1,940-bed facility in Adelanto, California, to the Department of Homeland Security for $950 million.

Meanwhile, a number of Trump administration officials have worked or consulted for the company.

GEO will continue to run the Tacoma facility under a recently signed, 10-year, $1.5-billion contract with the federal government, which houses immigrants detained under the president’s crackdown.

“In short, taxpayers are sending nearly $2 billion to GEO Group to execute President Trump’s cruel immigration agenda,” Murray wrote in her letter.

Company CEO George Zoley said in a statement last week that GEO looks forward to “continuing to provide high-quality secure support services at the Northwest ICE Processing Center.”

U.S. Reps. Pramila Jayapal and Emily Randall have vowed congressional committee inquiries into the sale when Democrats retake Congress in January.

“We are going to continue to fight to do oversight, and next year in 2027, when Robert Garcia is the chair of the Oversight Committee, you better believe that we will be calling in witnesses to testify about how this deal happened, who got rich, and what the cost is for actual human beings who are being warehoused in this facility,” said Randall, a member of the committee.

Jayapal, meanwhile, is slated to become chair of the House Subcommittee on Immigration, Integrity, Security, and Enforcement.

A Homeland Security spokesperson said last week that the agency “purchased the Northwest ICE Processing Center on Nov. 18 to strengthen America’s ability to enforce its immigration laws and carry out the American people’s mandate for mass deportations.”

The “big, beautiful bill” that congressional Republicans passed in summer 2025 featured tens of billions of dollars to increase the number of immigrant detention beds by tens of thousands. But a U.S. Government Accountability Office report this fall found Immigration and Customs Enforcement has “wasted funds on unsuccessful detention initiatives and lacks important information about the long-term affordability of its investments.”

A follow-up last week from the accountability agency found ICE “has neither determined the scope and costs to purchase more facilities nor updated its spending plan to reflect its current efforts.”

“ICE also hasn’t assessed the cost effectiveness of these investments,” the report reads.

In the report, ICE officials “noted that while they do not expect the effort to result in cost savings, it will help ICE fulfill its mission in locations where state governments may resist expanded detention efforts.”

Another private prison giant, CoreCivic, offered a detention center to the state of Minnesota for $75 million, only for ICE to buy it this year for $495 million. Democrats in the U.S. Senate are investigating the purchase.

GEO said last week that the company is in active negotiations that could result in the sale of three more of its facilities by the end of the year.

text:
TUCSON, Ariz. – Abbas Ali Haider, 49, of Sialkot, Pakistan, was sentenced last week by United States District Judge Angela M. Martinez to 41 months in prison. Haider previously pleaded guilty to conspiracy to bring aliens to the United States for private financial gain and bringing in illegal aliens for profit.

According to court documents, Haider operated two fake Pakistan-based companies – Diamond TV World Productions and Multimedia Advertising Ltd. – to bring Pakistani nationals illegally into the United States. From approximately September 2019 through September 2023, Haider fraudulently obtained visas for Pakistani nationals to travel to Ecuador, Cuba, and Colombia under the cover of legitimate business travel when their real destination was always the southern U.S. border. Posing as employees of Haider’s fake companies traveling to work on films, the Pakistani nationals were admitted to countries in Latin America and the Caribbean. Haider’s network then guided them to the U.S.-Mexico border where they illegally crossed into California, Texas, and Arizona. For this, Haider charged each person as much as $40,000.

Haider was extradited to the United States from Mexico in July 2025.

This prosecution is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States.

Homeland Security Investigations Calexico led U.S. investigative efforts, working in concert with HSI’s Brasilia, Quito, Tijuana, and Caribbean attaché offices and the HSI Human Smuggling Unit in Washington, D.C. U.S. Customs and Border Protection’s International Interdiction Task Force; U.S. Border Patrol; the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Joint Terrorism Task Force in Miami; and the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Office of Enforcement and Removal Operations office in Detroit and Calexico and the United States Marshal’s Service provided substantial assistance. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs worked with law enforcement partners in Mexico to secure the arrest and extradition of Haider.

This case was also supported and prosecuted by Joint Task Force Alpha (JTFA), the U.S. Department of Justice’s lead effort in combating human smuggling and trafficking committed by cartels and Transnational Criminal Organizations throughout the Americas. In partnership with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS), JTFA investigates and prosecutes the most prolific and dangerous human smuggling and trafficking networks that impact public safety and border security. Led by the Criminal Division’s Human Rights and Special Prosecutions Section and supported by other Criminal Division components, JTFA has dedicated prosecutors from U.S. Attorneys’ Offices along the Southwest border, Southern Florida, Northern New York, and Vermont. JTFA partners with U.S. Attorneys’ Offices throughout the country and supports high-priority cases in any district. All JTFA cases rely on substantial law enforcement resources from DHS components, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Homeland Security Investigations, and U.S. Customs and Border Protection, U.S. Border Patrol, and the Office of Field Operations. JTFA also partners with FBI and other law enforcement agencies. To date, JTFA’s work has resulted in more than 486 domestic and international arrests of leaders, organizers, and significant facilitators of alien smuggling and trafficking; more than 447 U.S. convictions; and more than 377 significant jail sentences imposed and forfeitures of substantial assets.

The prosecution was led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Arizona and the Criminal Division’s Human Rights and Special Prosecutions Section.

Finance Ranking Member Demands Records Behind Flawed Memo Used to Justify Cuts to Legal Aid and Anti-Trafficking Protections

Text of the Letter (PDF)

Washington, D.C. – Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden, D-Ore., today blasted Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. over a flawed agency report being used by the Trump administration to strip legal aid and safety protections from unaccompanied immigrant children.

“The Memorandum is the clear result of a bad-faith investigation and bogus analytical foundation which lead to unsupported conclusions that call for predetermined policy changes long sought by the Trump administration,” Wyden wrote. “Children in ORR care will spend longer in federal custody, be released to fewer qualified sponsors, lose access to the counsel Congress required, and face immigration proceedings with fewer of the protections Congress enacted specifically for them.”

The report from the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), released last month, claims to show widespread fraud among adults who sponsor unaccompanied children. In his letter, Wyden detailed how HHS relied on a cherry-picked sample that represents less than 2 percent of the more than 100,000 sponsor releases. HHS then extrapolated its findings to make sweeping claims about the entire program. The report also lists three conflicting fraud rates without explaining how HHS calculated the numbers.

Wyden also called out HHS for using a backlog of 65,000 unanswered child welfare reports as a political talking point, noting that the backlog reflects ORR’s own failure to review and respond to reports from care providers. The agency simultaneously ordered providers to stop directly reporting suspected child trafficking to the Office on Trafficking in Persons (OTIP), undercutting the very protections Congress built to keep kids safe. Wyden spotlighted this OTIP directive last month.

Lastly, the letter highlights HHS’s companion “Claim vs. Reality” document, which falsely claims that having a government contractor appear as a “friend of the court,” rather than as counsel of record, satisfies the HHS’s statutory obligation to provide legal representation to unaccompanied children.

Wyden demanded that HHS preserve all records related to the report within seven business days and provide answers about how the report was initiated and produced, how the agency plans to clear the growing backlog of unanswered child welfare reports accumulating on Trump and Robert Kennedy’s watch, and the current status of legal representation for unaccompanied minors in HHS custody.

text:
The rule takes effect on Dec. 14. It would require people to verify their citizenship or eligible immigration status to receive federal housing assistance.

"No child should lose their home over a parent's immigration status," said California Attorney General Rob Bonta during a press conference. "This rule is cruel, and it's unlawful."

For over three decades, Congress has authorized prorated federal housing assistance for mixed-status families, whose members have different citizenship or immigration statuses. These families receive less assistance if a household member is ineligible because of their immigration status. The new rule would ban mixed-status families from receiving any assistance.

"Picture a mom with two kids in public housing. All U.S. citizens. Their dad is not eligible. Under this rule, all four of them lose their home," Bonta said.

One in five children in California is part of a mixed-status family, said Bonta, estimating that the rule will affect 7,000 households in his state. The new rule would also require public housing authorities and private landlords to report tenants who fail verification to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

"Congress never gave HUD the power to throw mixed-status families out of their homes or turn private landlords into immigration enforcement. But that's exactly what this rule does," Bonta said.

The new rule is the latest in a series of moves by President Donald Trump's administration targeting legal immigrants. Those moves include restricting healthcare, nutrition benefits and other subsidies while stripping legal protections from some immigrant groups to make more people eligible for deportation.

HUD Secretary Scott Turner first announced the proposed rule in January, but the department finalized it only last week.

"HUD's final rule fully implements the 1980 Housing and Community Development Act and ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars. This rule guarantees ONLY AMERICAN citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD-funded housing. This change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million which will now go to eligible Americans that are currently on a waitlist," said Turner in an emailed statement on Monday.

Earlier this year, HUD conducted an audit with DHS and identified 20,000 mixed-status households receiving federally funded housing assistance nationwide. The department said illegal immigrants were using "loopholes" to access benefits while the department struggled to provide housing for all who need it.

text:
PROVIDENCE, R.I. – Five lawfully present immigrants filed a proposed nationwide class action lawsuit today after federal Medicaid funding restrictions cost them their health coverage. All five still receive Supplemental Security Income (SSI), which helps people with very limited income and resources pay for food and housing if they are elderly or disabled. Since losing Medicaid on October 1, plaintiffs have rationed medication, missed medical appointments, and gone without treatment they cannot afford.

Read Complaint

The Lawyers’ Committee for Rhode Island, the National Health Law Program, and the ACLU of Rhode Island represent the plaintiffs. The lawsuit challenges guidance from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) implementing the so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” or “H.R. 1.” CMS told states it would stop paying its share of full Medicaid coverage for people with certain immigration statuses, including people who receive SSI. The plaintiffs argue that Congress preserved a longstanding protection entitling all people who receive SSI to the same Medicaid coverage in their state, regardless of immigration status.

“The government is stripping life-saving health coverage from some of the most vulnerable people in the country—elderly or disabled refugees, asylees, domestic violence and trafficking victims—without any authority from Congress,” said Amy Romero, Chief Legal Counsel for the Lawyers’ Committee for Rhode Island. “Our courageous clients have built new lives here lawfully. Now, they are rationing blood pressure pills, skipping heart monitoring, and putting off surgeries because the government unlawfully cut off their health care. Our suit asks the Court to restore the coverage Congress guaranteed.”

The cuts to Medicaid that Congress enacted in OBBBA are devastating. But they didn’t go this far

“The cuts to Medicaid that Congress enacted in OBBBA are devastating. But they didn’t go this far. Congress clearly kept Medicaid protections in place for immigrants who receive SSI. Federal officials went beyond what Congress allowed when they cut off funding for our clients’ care,” said Senior Attorney Sarah Grusin of the National Health Law Program. “The results are cruel. One client missed a doctor’s appointment because a single visit would have cost almost his whole monthly SSI check. Another is rationing blood pressure medicine he needs every day. They need their coverage back.”

“The Trump Administration is cruelly disregarding the real-life consequences of cutting Medicaid coverage for those who rely on it, and are entitled to it,” said Steven Brown, ACLU of RI executive director. “It is shameful that these plaintiffs, including two Rhode Islanders who are lawful refugees who fled war in their home countries, are forced to go without their medications and doctors’ appointments. We hope the court will agree with us that the Trump Administration’s actions are unlawful, and the plaintiffs’ coverage needs to be restored.”

The plaintiffs ask the federal court in Rhode Island to pause the policy while the case proceeds and permanently set it aside. They seek relief for all SSI recipients nationwide who otherwise qualify for full Medicaid and whose coverage has been or will be denied, reduced, or terminated because of the policy.

Learn more about Mahmoud v. Oz and access court documents

How losing Medicaid has affected the plaintiffs*

A.W.M., age 69, Rhode Island. He is a refugee who fled war in Sudan in 2024. He suffers from severe knee pain for which he receives pain medications and injections, which he has had to forego because the most recent visit would have cost $985.65 — effectively his entire $987 monthly SSI payment. This is only one of many health conditions that require ongoing treatment, medication and monitoring. He has also begun rationing several medications.

G.M., age 77, Rhode Island. He is a refugee who fled war in the Republic of Congo in 2024. He is stretching his supply of blood pressure medicine by taking only two or three tablets a week, although he needs it every day. He also canceled a critical eye appointment to address his vision problems because he could not afford the $150 visit.

L.K., age 89, Illinois. She was granted asylum in 2025 after leaving Uzbekistan and Russia due to threats to her life. She suffers from many heart-related conditions, requiring a number of medications, including blood thinners. But a month’s supply of her blood thinner alone costs $400 and she receives $994 a month in SSI. The manufacturer donated a 90-day supply, and the clinic where she now gets free primary care cannot provide the heart monitoring she needs. She will not be able to afford her medication once her 90-day supply runs out.

M.E., age 11, Missouri. He was born in Turkey after his parents fled the war in Syria. He came to the United States with his family as a refugee in December 2024. He receives SSI because of his disabilities, but he lost Medicaid on October 1 because of his immigration status. He needs surgery for incontinence, due to congenital malformation of genitalia but his family has had to put off the surgery, because they cannot afford the cost, now that his Medicaid has been terminated. Medicaid also covered his specialist visits, prescription medications, and diapers, which they can now no longer afford.

S.P., age 78, South Carolina. She fled the war in Ukraine in 2023 and was granted humanitarian parole and approved for SSI. But she lost Medicaid on October 1, forcing her to stop receiving twice-monthly Alzheimer’s infusions that her family could no longer afford. She also lost 80 hours of in-home care each month. Her family now pays out of pocket for some prescriptions and goes without others.

description:

text:
MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:

The Trump administration is facing protests and lawsuits for newly resurrected plans to convert warehouses into ICE detention centers. NPR's Jasmine Garsd has been digging into ICE's efforts to use these warehouses, and she's here with us now to tell us more about it. Good morning, Jas.

JASMINE GARSD, BYLINE: Good morning.

MARTIN: So why are these detention centers so controversial?

GARSD: Well, because they aren't detention centers. These are massive Amazon-style warehouses. They're not designed for housing people, and there are concerns about the money spent on them - over a billion dollars. Also there are environmental concerns.

MARTIN: Well, to that end, there were legal agreements barring the Department of Homeland Security from converting several of the warehouses into detention centers until it did environmental assessments. Did they do them?

GARSD: Well, Michel, a couple of weeks ago, DHS awarded a company $32 million for renovations and an environmental assessment in Roxbury, New Jersey. So they spent millions of dollars on a contractor for a detention center they don't have permission to build. Yesterday, the township and New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport asked a federal court to stop them. I spoke to Davenport.

JENNIFER DAVENPORT: It really does raise questions, serious questions about ICE and DHS's candor. We will continue. I am very clear on this. Our office is very clear on this. We will continue to press in court to stop ICE from violating the law.

GARSD: You know, I think the bigger picture here is the question of how DHS is spending all of this money it's sitting on. I mean, it got $45 billion last year, and a new report by the Government Accountability Office says the agency, in most cases, paid far more for these warehouses than they were worth. I asked DHS about this, and a spokesperson told me they're moving quickly to use existing detention space.

MARTIN: OK. So that's New Jersey. What about the other warehouse locations?

GARSD: Yeah. Earlier this year, ICE bought a warehouse in Surprise, Arizona, directly across from a chemical storage plant. Here's Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes back in April.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

KRIS MAYES: Let this sink in - the federal government wants to open a jail inside a documented chemical hazard zone.

GARSD: Earlier this month, DHS released its environmental assessment and found the warehouse would have no impact. Advocates call it flimsy. Mayes told NPR she's still reviewing it. Also I should add, in San Antonio, Texas, the city's fighting a warehouse detention center there on environmental grounds.

MARTIN: And, Jasmine, before we let you go, you were telling us that the rules around environmental assessments could change.

GARSD: So the National Environmental Policy Act, or NEPA, requires environmental reviews for major federal actions, but there's a bill in Congress, the bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, that would limit court challenges. In most cases, an environmental violation alone would no longer be enough to pause something like these warehouses. I will be reporting more on that in the coming weeks.

MARTIN: That is Jasmine Garsd. She covers immigration for NPR. Jasmine, thank you.

GARSD: Thanks. Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

text:
The Justice Department has directed attorneys from across its civil litigation divisions to help defend the Trump administration against a growing number of lawsuits filed by individuals in immigration detention.

More than 97,000 detainees have filed habeas corpus petitions challenging their detention since January 2025, including approximately 10,000 new petitions just since October 2026 alone, according to a Nov. 24 memo obtained by CBS News. Habeas petitions are a legal mechanism through which individuals may challenge the lawfulness of their detention.

Prior to the second Trump administration, the federal caseload for habeas immigration detention petitions tended to be much lower — closer to a few hundred in an entire year. It can take weeks or even months to resolve an immigration habeas petition.

The Justice Department says the litigation is straining resources at U.S. attorneys' offices, which have been primarily responsible for handling the cases.

"Many of the Department's U.S. Attorneys' Offices have been overwhelmed by the influx of petitions and impracticable procedures set by the courts," Attorney General Todd Blanche wrote in a three-page memo.

The memo directs attorneys from the department's Antitrust, Civil, Civil Rights, and Environment and Natural Resources divisions and U.S. Trustees Program, to assist with the litigation — roughly 2,000 litigators across its civil components. The memo doesn't specify how many attorneys will be reassigned or how many cases they will be expected to handle.

Attorneys from the offices of the attorney general, deputy attorney general and associate attorney general will also take on additional cases.

Immigration-related habeas cases have skyrocketed since President Trump returned to office, as his administration has placed record numbers of individuals in ICE detention and narrowed the avenues for them to be released, including on bond.

Blanche characterized many of the habeas petitions as "frivolous" in his memo.

"The increase in habeas petitions resulted, in part, from the immigration bar's attempt to thwart President Trump's promise to the American people to prioritize their safety and security," he wrote.

description:
Union workers, including Sea-Tac Airport employees, and community members rallied Tuesday in SeaTac against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s involvement at the airport.
Rally speakers included King County Executive Girmay Zahilay, SeaTac Mayor Mohamed Egal, Zenia Javalera, president of SEIU Local 6, and Wilson.
After Wilson left, a group of protesters broke away from the peaceful rally, exercising their constitutional rights.
The smaller group of anti-ICE protesters surrounded Wilson's car and security detail, waved signs, and accused her of being complicit with ICE.
The protest followed the Nov. 21 detention of at least two passengers by ICE agents while they were boarding an Alaska Airlines flight, according to rally organizers.
text:
Union workers, including Sea-Tac Airport employees, and community members rallied Tuesday in SeaTac against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s involvement at the airport.

But before they marched to Alaska Airlines’ headquarters from Angle Lake Park, a group broke off from a rally that was being monitored by SeaTac police and targeted Seattle mayor Katie Wilson, who was leaving after speaking at the rally.

The group marched to nearby Alaska Airlines headquarters, calling for CEO Ben Minicucci to condemn ICE and make companywide changes to protect passengers, workers, and communities from what organizers called ICE brutality at airports.

Rally speakers included King County Executive Girmay Zahilay, SeaTac Mayor Mohamed Egal, Zenia Javalera, president of SEIU Local 6, and Wilson.

"We have to wonder what this administration will do next to threaten our residents and our resources that they rely on," Zahilay said in his speech.

During her speech, Wilson thanked rally organizers and said she wanted to stand up to the chaos and cruelty, referencing masked ICE agents arresting a father and his adult daughter inside an Alaska Airlines jet bridge at the Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday morning.

“We are most powerful when we stand up together,” she said as the crowd cheered her on.

After Wilson left, a group of protesters broke away from the peaceful rally, exercising their constitutional rights.

The smaller group of anti-ICE protesters surrounded Wilson's car and security detail, waved signs, and accused her of being complicit with ICE.

The group managed to block Wilson's car, preventing her from leaving the parking lot area of Angle Lake Park.

King County sheriff’s deputies arrived, and a clash began as deputies asked protesters to move out of the way.

Officers arranged for her to back out, but then the protesters tried to block her in from the rear, according to the King County Sheriff's Office (KCSO).

Officers had to physically remove the protesters from the area so the Mayor was able to leave the park, KCSO said.

No arrests were made, and there was no reportable use of force by Deputies, and no reported damage, according to KCSO.

The protest followed the Nov. 21 detention of at least two passengers by ICE agents while they were boarding an Alaska Airlines flight, according to rally organizers.

This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.

text:
Port of Seattle officials are investigating whether federal immigration agents violated any airport safety protocols when they arrested two people Saturday morning — dragging them out the side door of a jet bridge as passengers were loading onto an Alaska Airlines flight.

“ We are preparing a comprehensive review of the incident that will draw on interviews our Port of Seattle police conducted after the incident and ongoing discussions we are having with federal officials and airport partners,” Port Commissioner Ryan Calkins said Monday.

As part of its investigation, the Port will look at federal and state policy as well as local immigration enforcement protocols in agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and airline partners. Under current agreements, federal agents have agreed to not wear face coverings and to clearly identify themselves during operations at the airport, according to Port officials.

Video of the Saturday morning arrests shows federal agents wearing surgical masks and dressed in plain clothes without any badge or uniform identifying them as ICE.

Once seen as a public safety solution at airports after the 9/11 terrorist attacks, Port Commissioner Hamdi Mohamed said ICE now compromises public safety at the airport.

“It distracts from legitimate security responsibilities and puts unnecessary stress on the very people responsible for keeping our airport running and keeping it safe, including airline workers [and] flight attendants,” Mohamed said.

At a press conference the day of the arrests, Mohamed and other officials echoed airline worker unions and the governor’s call for airlines to demand ICE stop civil enforcement at airports.

Whether that materializes or not, Mohamed said she wants to take action where possible, even as an elected official with limited power.

“One of the things… we need to consider is deactivating any Port-issued badges held by ICE that they're using through our airport,” she said. “We may not have control over federal credentials or badges that they use, but if there are badges that are under our control, we should deactivate that immediately.”

Port of Seattle officials said they’ve seen a notable increase in immigration enforcement arrests at U.S. airports, including Seattle, since August.

“The type of immigration enforcement happening at airports in America right now is new, disruptive, and needs to stop,” the Port Commission said in a statement online. “We are calling on our federal delegation to use their authority to stop ICE from making this kind of enforcement actions at U.S. airports.”

The Department of Homeland Security identified the two people arrested Saturday as Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza and Sofia Hernandez Mejia, describing both as Mexican nationals who overstayed visas.

An immigration attorney representing the father and daughter said both entered the U.S. legally more than a decade ago, hold valid work permits, and were traveling to California for a family baptism ceremony when they were detained.

DHS alleged that during the arrest, Hernandez Mejia "hurled hot coffee on the officers" and will face a federal felony charge for assaulting a federal officer. Hernandez Mejia wasn’t the subject of the initial arrest, according to DHS, until the alleged assault happened.

Hernandez Mejia’s attorney and a witness who spoke to KUOW are contesting that account.

A witness who provided video of the arrest to KUOW said, “She was holding a cup of coffee in her one hand. And they started aggressively pulling him away from her. Her coffee was spilled.”

“I didn't see any malicious intent behind her spilling the coffee or throwing the coffee,” said the source, who asked not to be identified out of concern for their safety. “It was just because the ICE agent was… ripping her father from her that her coffee spilled. That's what I saw.”

Hernandez Mejia’s lawyer also said she has a pending application for a green card through her U.S. citizen spouse.

During a Port Commission meeting Monday, Commissioner Calkins called for a major ICE overhaul, echoing sentiments shared by Gov. Bob Ferguson this week.

“The action on Saturday is just one symptom of broken trust with the public — illegitimate use of force in carrying out law enforcement actions,” Calkins said. “Ultimately, I don't believe this particular institution can be reformed. It needs to be built from the ground up.”

Calkins, who said he was making a statement as a citizen and not as a port commissioner, said ICE had crossed a red line.

“There is a point at which you are no longer able to reform an institution that has lost the public's trust,” Calkins said.

Ahead of the Thanksgiving travel rush, Port officials urged non-citizen travelers to consult with their attorneys before flying if possible. Many attorneys are advising their clients not to fly.

Officials are also urging travelers to be observant, and document and report ICE activity. Immigrant rights groups also suggest asking for people’s names and a family contact number during an arrest.

title: LGBTQ+ Rights Groups Urge Supreme Court to Block Trump Administration's 'Dangerous ...
description:
The coalition is asking the justices to uphold protections that require notice and a chance to object before such deportations.
Lower courts struck the policy down, but the Supreme Court paused that ruling while it hears the case.
The Trump administration, as part of President Donald Trump’s mass deportation scheme, has already sent queer refugees to countries where they could be put in danger.
The groups say that government policy allows the deportation of a person to countries other than the person’s home country, with little notice.
It does not stop the government from sending them somewhere else, which is the gap the groups say the policy exploits.
text:
A group of seven legal, LGBTQ+ and immigration rights organizations has filed a friend-of-the-court brief urging the United States Supreme Court to reject the Trump administration’s practice of deporting LGBTQ+ refugees to third countries, many of which criminalize LGBTQ+ people or have high levels of anti-LGBTQ+ sentiment, such as Ghana, South Sudan, El Salvador, and Cameroon. The coalition is asking the justices to uphold protections that require notice and a chance to object before such deportations.

Immigration Equality, Lambda Legal, Oasis Legal Services, the Council for Global Equality (CGE), Outright International, the Organization for Refuge, Asylum, and Migration (ORAM), and Rainbow Railroad filed the brief ahead of oral arguments on December 9 in the case Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D. The case, brought in 2025, is a nationwide class-action challenge brought by Human Rights First, the National Immigration Litigation Alliance and the Northwest Immigrant Rights Project against the Trump administration’s practice of deporting immigrants to third countries with little or no notice. Lower courts struck the policy down, but the Supreme Court paused that ruling while it hears the case.

The Trump administration, as part of President Donald Trump’s mass deportation scheme, has already sent queer refugees to countries where they could be put in danger. The groups say that government policy allows the deportation of a person to countries other than the person’s home country, with little notice.

“The Trump administration’s illegal policy of hastily deporting LGBTQ+ refugees to countries the government knows are extremely dangerous for them because of who they are – without giving them the legally required chance to object to that danger – is outrageous and cruel,” said Jenny Pizer, a co-author of the brief and Senior Director of Strategic Initiatives at Lambda Legal, in a press release.

Refugees who win “withholding of removal” cannot be sent back to the country where they would likely face persecution or torture. The status requires a higher standard of proof than asylum and offers no path to a green card or citizenship. It does not stop the government from sending them somewhere else, which is the gap the groups say the policy exploits. They argue that federal law bars deportation to any country where a person would likely face persecution or torture, including because of sexual orientation or gender identity, and that earlier administrations generally let people with this status remain in the U.S.

“LGBTIQ people from all over the world seek refuge in the U.S. when their lives are in danger because they expect to find safety, fairness, and dignity on U.S. shores. Yet the Trump administration, in flagrant violation of international law, is shipping them off to countries that its own human rights reporting has deemed unsafe for sexual and gender minorities,” said Neela Ghoshal, senior director of law, policy, and research at Outright International. “These inhumane policies must be reversed. No one should be deported to a country where they face the risk of arbitrary arrest, ill-treatment, and even death just for being who they are.”

The coalition provides several examples of those with the status who were sent to third countries. One of which is from Thelma, a bisexual Ghanaian woman whose father threatened to kill her. She fled the country after a group attacked her and her girlfriend. After an immigration judge gave her the protected status, she was sent to Cameroon, where she says she fears being sent back to Ghana.

“Going through a third-country removal was one of the hardest experiences of my life, and for a long time, it felt like no one was listening. Knowing that my truth is now being offered to protect others from going through the same pain brings real meaning to what I endured. I am hoping with everything I have that this case achieves justice—not just for me, but for every person seeking safety and a chance to live freely,” Thelma said in the brief.

text:
Source:

Read a PDF of our statement here.

On Monday, the Legal Defense Fund (LDF), Muslim Advocates, the Black Alliance for Just Immigration (BAJI), and the Haitian Bridge Alliance (HBA) filed an amicus brief in the U.S. Supreme Court case, U.S. Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D.

The brief argues that the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS’s) policy of mass deportations of immigrants to “third countries,” countries that are not their country of origin, fails to comply with the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment. The policy relies on either blanket diplomatic assurances that deportees will not be persecuted or tortured without any process at all, or, in the absence of such assurances, the policy provides a perfunctory procedure that robs people of a fair opportunity to stop their deportation. In either case, the Trump Administration is violating the Constitution’s due process requirements. As a result, people who are deported to third countries are vulnerable to persecution or torture because the Trump Administration’s policy fails to ensure their safety or prevent them from being sent to their country of origin where, because of dangerous conditions, the United States was barred from sending them back to.

The Trump Administration’s disregard for due process protections disproportionately harms and targets Black immigrants and other immigrants of color. More than half of the people deported to third countries are Black people or people of color. People deported to third countries describe inhumane detention conditions, beatings, food deprivation, and total restriction on outside contact. Many are later sent back to their countries of origin or face no other choice but to return there due to untenable conditions in the third countries.

“The Trump administration has unlawfully deported people to countries where they may face torture and death. But the Constitution is clear: people, regardless of immigration status, are afforded due process rights and cannot simply be deported to an unsafe and unfamiliar country based on the whims of the Administration and without proper procedural safeguards,” said Kacey Mordecai, Senior Counsel at LDF. “Black immigrants and other immigrants of color are more likely to be removed to third countries and face persecution and torture as a result. Permitting this unconstitutional policy will encourage this Administration’s discriminatory immigration enforcement and undermine the Constitution’s fundamental norms of equality and fairness.”

###

Founded in 1940, the Legal Defense Fund (LDF) is the nation’s first civil rights legal organization. LDF has been completely separate from the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) since 1957, though it was founded under the leadership of Thurgood Marshall while he was at the NAACP. LDF’s Thurgood Marshall Institute (TMI) is a division of LDF that undertakes innovative research and houses LDF’s archive. In all media attributions, please refer to us as the Legal Defense Fund or LDF (do not include NAACP) and refer to the Institute as LDF’s Thurgood Marshall Institute or TMI.

text:
A federal appeals court has upheld new Virginia laws restricting agreements between local law enforcement agencies and immigration enforcement.

The ruling in the Fourth Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals yesterday (Monday) kept in place legislation patroned earlier this year by Del. Alfonso Lopez (D-3) and Sen. Saddam Azlan Salim (D-37), prompting celebration from both lawmakers.

The bills, passed largely on party-line votes and signed into law by Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D), restrict the ability of Virginia law enforcement agencies to enter into or renew 287(g) agreements with the federal government, unless a slew of specific criteria are first met.

The 287(g) agreements are formal partnerships between local law enforcement agencies and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which allow deputized officers to perform functions typically undertaken by immigration agents.

The state laws restricting interactions went into effect on July 1, but in late August, U.S. District Court Judge Robert Payne issued a temporary injunction, putting the legislation on hold until the matter played out in court. On Nov. 23, a three-judge panel of the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals voted unanimously to lift the injunction.

The ruling allows the state’s restrictions on ICE interactions to stay in place while litigation moves forward. It concluded that the federal government is “not likely to succeed” on at least some of its arguments challenging the new laws.

“Just as the commonwealth’s former leaders could empower its agencies and political subdivisions to assist with federal immigration enforcement efforts in the past, its current leaders may alter the conditions of that authorization going forward,” noted the opinion.

Lopez praised the action:

“Local and state police have no obligation to assist in civil immigration enforcement, especially when their time and resources can be used keeping our communities safe. For now, Virginia will not be forced to participate in increasingly dangerous and unprofessional actions by ICE agents that disregard due process and the rule of law. If the legislation faces additional appeals, I stand ready to continue defending it.”

Added Salim: “The federal government cannot conscript our local officers into its mass deportation machine, and the General Assembly has every right to set the terms on which our own agencies cooperate.”

Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones said the ruling, while just one step in a longer process, represents a “significant victory … against federal overreach.”

The ruling “reaffirms the commonwealth’s authority to determine whether and under what conditions state and local resources may be used to assist federal immigration enforcement efforts,” said Jones, whose office is handling litigation for the state government.

Among provisions of the state legislation, agreements between local agencies and ICE cannot be authorized if federal officials act without valid judicial warrants or conduct enforcement activities at schools.

The advocacy organization We Are CASA also celebrated the ruling, saying it “protects community trust.”

“Today is a huge win for our families and the autonomy of our Commonwealth,” We Are CASA said in a press release. “For years, our members have fought to make sure Washington can’t force local police and sheriffs to do ICE’s work, and yesterday, the court backed us up. Virginia has every right to set strict rules on ICE collaboration, including requiring a judicial warrant before agents enter someone’s home.”

In the same Nov. 23 opinion, the appeals-court panel on a 2-1 vote upheld a preliminary injunction against another new Virginia law, which seeks to restrict federal agents from wearing masks or concealing their identities while operating in the commonwealth.

“There are many hard and unresolved questions” related to the mask issue, the judges wrote. “The district court did not exceed its discretion in entering a preliminary injunction.”

The decision on the mask mandate was 2-1, with Circuit Court Judge Robert King dissenting. King wrote that enactment of a mask mandate “constitutes a reasonable exercise of the commonwealth’s sovereign police powers” in arguing to lift the injunction.

text:
NEW YORK -- Children's educator and YouTube personality Ms. Rachel visited federal youth immigration court in New York City on Monday where she met children facing deportation proceedings and called attention to what advocates describe as a lack of legal representation for immigrant youth.

Among the children she met was 9-year-old Angel, who now lives in the Bronx with his mother after traveling alone from Mexico. Angel was among the children appearing in court without an attorney as they navigate immigration proceedings.

"It's heartbreaking. I care so much about every child and I just want to see every child thriving in school and my heart goes out to anyone going through this," Ms. Rachel said.

The former Bronx public school teacher toured the court alongside Congressman-elect Brad Lander, who said he wanted to see firsthand how immigrant children are being treated in the system.

"I think about how that makes a child feel whether or not you are removable...I don't want any child to hear that word associated with them," Ms. Rachel said.

Lander criticized what he described as reduced support for legal representation for immigrant youth.

"There has been an aggressive assault on the system of providing legal representation and services for young people," he said.

Nonprofit organizations such as Safe Passage Project provide pro bono legal representation to children who appear in immigration court without attorneys. Legal Director Tania Cohen said her organization has seen an increase in removal orders and a decline in funding.

"The issuance of removal orders which are deportation orders has significantly increased for immigrant children who are eligible for a green card," Cohen said.

While at the courthouse, Ms. Rachel spoke with Angel about his Christmas wish list.

"I told him to write down some things he wants for Christmas, in conversation because I wanted to get him some Christmas presents and then he came and gave me this and it says the first thing he wants is an immigration lawyer," she said.

Angel said meeting Ms. Rachel was "Good."

According to the report, a judge gave Angel's mother until Dec. 15 to obtain legal representation.

Lander said he plans to push for restored funding and increased oversight once he takes office in Congress.

"We're going to have oversight hearings and we're going to show up ourselves and we're going to push to make sure the legal funding is restored," he said.

Ms. Rachel said policymakers should focus more on the needs of children.

"I think our problems would really be a lot less if we all just focus on taking care of kids and centered kids in policies," she said.

text:
On Monday, California and 21 other states filed a lawsuit against a Trump administration policy that would deny federal housing assistance to qualifying families if one or more relatives don’t qualify because of their immigration status. This rule would affect approximately 1,700 families in L.A. with mixed immigration status that live in federally subsidized housing, and approximately 7,000 households statewide.

For the past 30 years, families with mixed immigration statuses have been allowed to live in federally subsidized housing, with proportionally reduced financial assistance for families with one or more ineligible residents. But in a Nov. 12th ruling from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, the Trump administration is trying to block all households with mixed immigration statuses from applying for and participating in Housing and Urban Development programs, like federally subsidized housing and Section 8.

According to the rule, the new restrictions will go into effect starting Dec. 14, and mixed immigration status households will have until March 14, 2027, to submit proof of continued eligibility.

The lawsuit, co-led by California, Massachusetts, and New York, argues that the Housing and Urban Development program does not have the jurisdiction to rewrite the law created by Congress. Furthermore, the lawsuit argues that the existing program expressly protects prorated assistance to families with mixed immigration status.

In addition to this lawsuit, L.A. based nonprofit Public Council has filed a lawsuit on behalf of L.A. County residents, and L.A. and San Francisco housing authorities have filed an additional lawsuit against the new rule arguing that it violates federal housing law and would increase administrative costs to cities.

In a statement on Monday, Mayor Karen Bass said, “Los Angeles is a city of immigrants. I’m proud that we have joined other cities from across the country to fight back against the Trump administration’s proposed rule change that threatens every mixed-status household with the loss of the federal housing assistance they rely on to stay afloat.”

title: LGBTQ people face stark dangers under the Trump admin's third-country removal policy
description:
This week, amicus briefs supporting the challengers’ position that the policy violates the Administrative Procedure Act were submitted in the case.
As the Justice Department argued to the Supreme Court: The Guidance also comports with due process.
The Supreme Court in Abrego Garcia blessed precisely this remedy in precisely this context.
