text:
Standing outside the federal building downtown, some of San Diego’s representatives in the House on Monday outlined their priorities on immigration when Democrats retake control of Congress in January. At the same time inside, an immigration judge ordered two children, ages 9 and 15, deported back to Guatemala.

“On Nov. 3rd, voters sent the president and they sent the nation a message: They reject President Trump and Republicans’ reckless, anti-American agenda,” said Rep. Scott Peters. “It wasn’t just about cost. It’s about the way we’re treating people.”

Top of mind was the Nov. 4 detention of an 8-year-old Haitian boy at an ICE check-in. Video of three agents leading the boy, a third grader at Fay Elementary School in City Heights, into an elevator sparked outrage and protest.

“We don’t want murderers and rapists running around. Absolutely not,” Rep. Juan Vargas said Monday. “We want them, of course, not to be in our society. I completely agree with that. That’s not who he’s going after. He’s going after a little boy, an 8-year-old boy.”

That child, who previously had Temporary Protected Status, was taken to a federal facility in Texas but has since been released to his family.

“He held me tight, so tight I had to tell him to loosen up,” said Guerline Jozef, of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, which advocated for his return. “And he said, ’Thank you, but I’m afraid. I’m afraid of what could happen again. Will they take me again?’”

Peters, Vargas and Rep.-elect Marni von Wilpert said one of their priorities in the new Congress is to pass the American Dream and Promise Act, offering legal pathways to TPS holders and DACA recipients.

They also want to bar immigration arrests within 1,000 feet of so-called sensitive locations like schools, churches and hospitals, except in the case of an emergency.

“As this administration exploits the places we trust the most and turns them into hunting grounds, protecting our schools has to be a priority,” Peters said.

“We demand safe passage for students, families and educators,” said Monique Barrett, president of the San Diego Education Association. “Advance comprehensive immigration reform. Protect due process. Prevent family separation. Use your oversight authority.”

The members of Congress said they also wanted to investigate conditions at detention centers, and institute stricter background checks and vetting for ICE agents, as well as limiting their use of force.

“ICE’s actions in our community are not law enforcement. They are chaos and violence, and they need to stop,” von Wilpert said. “Parents are afraid to take their children to school. Families are afraid to go to the doctor. Children are afraid their parents won’t come home from work. That is not public safety. And our communities deserve better.”

They also floated the possibility of clawing back billions of dollars already allocated to the Department of Homeland Security that haven’t yet been spent.

“Republicans in the Big Beautiful Bill funded ICE and Border Patrol to a level higher than the United States Marines. They got more money than the Israeli military,” Peters said. “Those dollars and those resources were turned back on our own communities. And that’s wrong. We’ve got to put an end to it.”

As they spoke, a father and his two children walked out of the federal building alongside volunteer court observers. They said an immigration judge had just ordered the children, a 9-year-old boy and a 15-year-old girl, deported back to Guatemala.

“They tried to express to the judge the problems that they felt that they had, the fear that they had, but the judge did not feel that was sufficient enough for the asylum request to be approved,” said FAITH volunteer Belinda Mayes.

“Clearly they were, in talking to the children afterwards, extremely disappointed. Very nervous, very anxious,” Mayes continued. “The father, basically at a loss not knowing what to do, because we’re only talking about an order against the children so it’s basically their future and what they’re going to be facing alone.”

Speaking in Spanish, the teenager, a freshman at a San Diego high school, said her family feared threats of violence against them in Guatemala, calling the process inside immigration court “ugly.”

The family said the judge gave them 30 days to appeal the decision, opening the window for their deportation on Dec. 23.

“They want to deport them two days before Christmas, one day before Christmas Eve,” Vargas said after speaking with the family. “Can you imagine that? How ridiculous is that? ’Merry Christmas kids, we’re deporting you.’”

title: Guantánamo Bay 2.0? The rise of legal violence inside US detention centers
description:

There has been very little pressure from legislators or the courts to dissuade the government from using legal violence—a direct failure of the very systems that allowed this kind of violence to become legal in the first place.
This violence was carried out in one of the largest detention centers in the country, located at the Fort Bliss military base in Texas.
Ending legal violence Like many who were imprisoned in Guantánamo Bay, most of the migrants in detention today have not been convicted of any crime.
If these steps are not taken, the use of legal violence and the policies of impunity that underpin them will only grow.
text:
The United States government has a long history of dehumanizing foreigners both inside and outside its borders. The treatment of prisoners in Guantánamo Bay and of migrants currently detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) provide just two recent examples of the extensive use of criminalizing language to justify targeting these groups. The George W. Bush administration routinely labeled those incarcerated in Guantánamo Bay as “terrorists” and associated them with the September 11 attacks, often without direct evidence. Today, the Donald J. Trump administration labels migrants as “animals”, “criminals”, and “rapists”. This type of dehumanizing language suggests that detainees do not deserve legal rights, and it leads to the broad erosion of the civil protections that shield people—whether or not they are US citizens—from arrest without charge and trial or harsh and unusual punishment.

The state’s curtailment of due process and other civil rights in these cases has led to a rise in legal violence: harm inflicted by a government body while enforcing state policy. Many held in Guantánamo Bay have claimed that members of the United States military physically and mentally assaulted them during their detention. Similar abuse is still taking place today against migrants in ICE detention centers. Detainees’ testimonies of violent punishments by ICE agents are all too reminiscent of the experiences of Guantánamo Bay prisoners.

The US government and military have not taken the lessons of the War on Terror to heart, and the United States is still using violence against people it detains. There has been very little pressure from legislators or the courts to dissuade the government from using legal violence—a direct failure of the very systems that allowed this kind of violence to become legal in the first place.

Mass incarceration and violence toward migrants

Since Trump took office as president of the United States for the second time, his administration has pushed ICE to detain anyone deemed to be residing in the country illegally. This has led to the mass incarceration of Latinos and other migrants all over the nation. According to The Guardian, a total of 68,400 individuals were held in detention as of December 2025. The majority of detainees have no previous criminal record. A recent Human Rights Watch report documented dozens of executive orders rolling back migrants’ right to due process, guaranteed by the Fifth Amendment, and limiting their ability to seek legal redress while detained.

These new executive orders have systematically allowed the state to punish those detained prior to legal due process or the filing of charges. The result is legal violence inflicted against migrants detained in defiance of their constitutional rights. For example, officers are now legally allowed to interrogate suspected illegal migrants using violence and make arrests without warrants.

The Supreme Court of the United States (SCOTUS) has done very little to limit the powers granted to ICE. In fact, some recent SCOTUS rulings have expanded ICE’s powers. In September 2025, SCOTUS eliminated restrictions on ICE’s use of racial profiling when making arrests. In the case of Noem v. Vasquez-Perdomo SCOTUS ruled that ICE could conduct raids in public places opening the door to using race, ethnicity, and language to determine their targets. This is unambiguously racial profiling and encourages violence toward especially Latinos regardless of their immigration status.

Several reports documenting migrant accounts of violence committed by detention officers and ICE have been released since Trump’s executive orders and SCOTUS’s legal decisions on immigration enforcement. One of many migrants who spoke with the ACLU reported that detention officers had beaten him, breaking his tooth and damaging his ear to the point that he began to lose hearing. This violence was carried out in one of the largest detention centers in the country, located at the Fort Bliss military base in Texas.

One man in a Florida detention center, speaking to Human Rights Watch, recalled officers turning up the air conditioning to intentionally freezing levels in the cells. Several people in the same location are also being denied life-saving medications needed to treat chronic illnesses.

Are detention centers the new Guantánamo Bay?

Guantánamo Bay was established in 2002 to detain individuals believed to be linked with the perpetrators of the September 11 attacks. The Center for Constitutional Rights has outlined the violent experiences of prisoners detained at Guantánamo Bay, which included practices like those used today in ICE detention centers.

The Bush administration authorized the use of violent practices in Guantánamo Bay by declaring that those imprisoned there were “unlawful enemy combatants” and thus ineligible for the protections of the Geneva Conventions. By eliminating application of the Geneva Conventions, the Bush administration removed a major barrier imposed by international law to prevent the torture of prisoners. More recently, the Trump administration has similarly rejected the Geneva Conventions by cutting funding for the United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR) and condemning their operations.

The Center for Constitutional Rights has shared the experience of Abu Zubaydah, who was subjected to waterboarding, sleep deprivation, stress positions, and confinement inside a coffin-sized box. Ahmed al-Darbi similarly reported that officers played painfully loud music for several hours and chilled his cell to extremely cold temperatures until he confessed to the crime he was accused of. The government framed these practices as interrogation, but it’s clear that they constitute torture.

Many of the prisoners in Guantánamo Bay were never formally charged with any crime. Instead, they were imprisoned indefinitely and subjected to intense and violent interrogation tactics in hopes of eliciting confessions. These abusive practices were justified by a Military Order that allowed prisoners suspected of terrorism to be held outside US jurisdiction. This was an intentional move to limit the court’s reach and provide for increased use of force against those held in Guantánamo Bay and impunity for the officers who carried it out.

Ending legal violence

Like many who were imprisoned in Guantánamo Bay, most of the migrants in detention today have not been convicted of any crime. Legal violence does not change; only its target does.

To prevent the continuation of legal violence, we must challenge the system. The executive and military orders that allowed violence and mistreatment of prisoners in Guantánamo Bay laid the foundation for the laws currently supporting ICE’s violent and indiscriminate campaign of immigration enforcement. The United States Constitution already prohibits abuse inside penitentiaries and detention centers. Cruel and unusual punishments are strictly prohibited.

The courts must consistently apply the protections provided by the United States Constitution, and they must disempower ICE. This includes protecting due process rights for migrants, firing officers who act with racial bias, eliminating officers’ rights to interrogate detainees using violence, and investigating each facility where abuse has been reported. If these steps are not taken, the use of legal violence and the policies of impunity that underpin them will only grow.

name: Human Rights
title: The Way Forward After Mass Deportation | Connecting California - Zócalo Public Square
description:
To clean up the disaster of mass deportation, the United States will eventually need more than an amnesty.
Many of those removed were legal immigrants who followed the rules and obtained visas or work authorization—and got kicked out anyway.
The 1986 amnesty law championed by President Reagan legalized nearly 3 million people—and, eventually, many of their family members.
Given the U.S. immigration and federal court systems’ complicity in the deportation campaigns, such prosecutions might have to take place overseas.
We cannot move forward while millions of our neighbors have not been compensated for harm from the deportation campaign.
text:
To clean up the disaster of mass deportation, the United States will eventually need more than an amnesty.

It will need two amnesties. One for the millions of victims of the cruel, violent, and flagrantly unlawful deportation campaign tearing through American communities. And another for those who took part in making the deportations happen.

The Trump administration is deporting people without due process, including to faraway continents and unfamiliar countries. Many of those removed were legal immigrants who followed the rules and obtained visas or work authorization—and got kicked out anyway. Families have been shattered, human rights cancelled, local economies damaged, and whole segments of society forced into hiding.

When this nightmare finally ends, California and the United States will face a monumental challenge: How do we reunite families, uncover the full scale of what was done in our name, compensate victims, restore the rule of law, and hold official perpetrators accountable?

The solution is what I am calling the Double Amnesty.

The first amnesty is straightforward: a comprehensive, unencumbered program granting permanent residency, and creating a speedy process for obtaining citizenship for everyone caught in the U.S. regime’s anti-immigrant pogrom.

This first amnesty starts with allowing readmission for deported people, with priority going to immigrants the Trump administration sent to third-party countries. Restitution must apply universally—to undocumented immigrants, long-term legal residents, migrants with temporary status, and U.S. citizens mistaken for migrants. The amnesty must also cover citizens and residents who were punished or injured for defending their neighbors against deportation. They are heroes, not criminals.

This is the only practical way to return millions of human beings to the light, stabilize our economy, and shrink the unauthorized population. The 1986 amnesty law championed by President Reagan legalized nearly 3 million people—and, eventually, many of their family members.

It also reduced unauthorized immigration to the country. Immigration restrictionists claim that relentless enforcement deters unauthorized presence. In reality, the opposite is true. When people are arrested in immigration courts or naturalization appointments, the message is: Stay undocumented, stay in the shadows.

The current administration has manufactured more undocumented immigration, not reduced it. By stripping legal status en masse—revoking Temporary Protected Status (TPS), ending protection for Dreamers, rescinding humanitarian parole, and ripping away valid visas—the government deliberately and illegally created more than 1 million so-called “illegal” immigrants.

Which brings me to the second amnesty of the Double Amnesty—in which the U.S. would offer administrative and legal relief to the government employees, ICE agents, CBP officers, and bureaucrats who participated in executing this campaign. This amnesty may be harder to swallow. Many of us would prefer to prosecute law enforcement officials who broke the law and hurt immigrants, but the scale of the lawless deportation campaign makes mass prosecutions impractical.

But the second amnesty does not offer forgiveness automatically. This amnesty must be strictly contingent on first establishing personal and institutional accountability, and on exposing violations.

The Trump deportation machine operates in the dark, with masked law enforcement personnel, secret deportations to third countries, concealed detainee facilities, and undisclosed transfers of migrants between centers and prisons to keep them from being found by families and lawyers.

As a result, deportations have been executed with staggering incompetence, shielded by bureaucratic deception, and deliberately hidden from federal courts, defense lawyers, and the public. We still do not know the true number of missing children, falsified records, or unconstitutional orders carried out in field offices across the country.

To earn this second amnesty, agents and officials must go through a process of mandatory truth-telling. They must step forward and disclose every secret directive and unwritten quota, every illegal detention and unconstitutional maneuver, and every document or record withheld from courts, defense counsel, and the public.

In addition, the top executives of private companies that knew of the immigration abuses and personally profited must report their activities—and forfeit every dollar they made, for their business and personally—to a restitution fund for the campaign’s victims.

Once perpetrators provide full, verifiable documentation of their actions, they should receive immunity. If they lie, destroy evidence, or refuse to disclose, they must face full criminal prosecution.

There is one non-negotiable exception to the amnesty:

No mercy at the top.

You Might Also Like

Architects of the deportation campaign do not get a deal. No matter how much they disclose, no matter how many documents they hand over, there can be zero amnesty for the president, for Stephen Miller, or for senior political and law enforcement leaders who designed, ordered, and directed this campaign.

Given the U.S. immigration and federal court systems’ complicity in the deportation campaigns, such prosecutions might have to take place overseas. Since the U.S. is likely to block using the International Criminal Court (which the U.S. has sought to dismantle), accountability may require holding trials in foreign courts.

Under the principle of universal jurisdiction, Germany, Spain, France, and Argentina allow their national courts to prosecute non-citizens for grave crimes committed anywhere in the world. An international tribunal might be formed by multiple countries, with Canada as the natural host, because of its strong legal system and proximity to the U.S. This is not a new idea. International tribunals have long been held outside the ICC system, from Nuremberg and the Tokyo trial after World War II to more recent tribunals examining systematic rights violations in Sierra Leone, Rwanda, Cambodia, and the former Yugoslavia.

The Double Amnesty would offer a moral and practical way forward for a broken country. It would repair the lives of millions of victims targeted by state terror, while forcing the American deportation apparatus to document its own abuses in service of accountability.

We cannot move forward while millions of our neighbors have not been compensated for harm from the deportation campaign. And we cannot fix what remains hidden. A Double Amnesty won’t be a surrender or a compromise—it is a realistic blueprint for exposing the truth, restoring the rule of law, and preventing such evils from being repeated.

Joe Mathews writes the Connecting California column for Zócalo Public Square and is founder-columnist of Democracy Local, a planetary publication. He is working on a book, One Law to Save the World, for the University of California Press.

text:
The government has been accused of a "dereliction of its duty to protect citizens" by allowing a planned asylum centre.

The shadow minister for women and equalities, Joy Morrisey, said Labour had ignored warnings raised by residents and police when it granted permission for the redevelopment of part of MoD Bicester in Oxfordshire.

She was speaking at the launch of a think tank report called Mass Immigration is a Women's Issue, attended by women from Piddington, a village near the military site.

The Home Office said other large sites had been operating for a number of years with no rising crime. The Refugee Council said "there is no evidence refugees commit crimes...more than any other groups".

But the report's author, human rights and equality barrister Dr Anna Loutfi, said the government has not disclosed data on how crime rates change when large-scale male encampments are created.

That is backed by a University of Oxford Migration Observatory report from August 2026 that said there is no published data on convicted offenders' immigration status, such as whether they are an asylum seeker, refugee, work migrant or international student.

Some villagers in Piddington - home to 350 people, including 133 women - have said they will be living in fear if 1,256 male asylum seekers are housed nearby.

Planning permission for the MoD Bicester site was approved by the Housing Secretary Angela Rayner earlier this month after the Home Office used a fast-track route for projects deemed to be urgently needed and of national importance.

It said this would allow it to continue developing the plan but that no final decision on the site had been taken.

Piddington symbolically voted to leave the UK over the planned use for the site, which has also been legally challenged by campaigners.

A government report said the decision received 3,177 representations against and one in support.

Loutfi said the concerns they were raising were common sense: "Even if this was a group of football fans it would be of concern.

"But these men often come from countries where there are culturally incompatible ways of viewing women, they're viewed as available if they are unaccompanied or dressed a certain way or drinking alcohol.

"Most of the men are single, young, excitable with nothing to do all day, it doesn't take a rocket scientist to see putting a large number of them into a population of a lot less women will be trouble."

Essex Police covers the area around MDP Wethersfield which has been used to house 800 single male migrants since 2023.

The Chief Constable of the force said in September that crime linked to the site is "very low" with 15 offences since it opened in which a member of the public was the victim and the suspect was identified as, or alleged to be, a Wethersfield "service user".

Imran Hussain, Director of External Affairs at the Refugee Council, said: "Violence against women and girls is a problem across society that needs to be addressed to ensure that people feel safe in their homes and communities.

"But public debate and narratives must reflect the fact that there is no evidence refugees commit crimes towards women and girls more than any other groups."

The Women's Policy Centre, that commissioned Loufi's report, is an independent think tank. It invited MPs from all political parties to the launch of the report and said the issue of mass immigration and women's safety is a cross party issue.

Sandra Innes, a Piddington resident of 23 years, said she felt the government was being "hugely naive" in stating that the chance of crime was negligible.

She said women in the village were "living on the edge" and said their huge frustration was the lack of communication from ministers.

"Why isn't someone coming to us engaging and talking about how they will safeguard us?" she added.

The Home Office has said it is working closely with local authorities, police, health partners and community representatives to ensure any impact is carefully managed and local concerns are addressed.

In the conditions of planning permission, it said the site would be closely managed through 24-hour staffing, controlled access, CCTV and security patrols which would "reduce" the risk.

In August, the government created a nine-page booklet for asylum seekers explaining rape, sexual harassment and domestic abuse are illegal in the UK and giving guidance on how UK laws and customs may be different from their home countries.

Reform's Fareham and Waterlooville MP Suella Braverman attended the meeting.

She is the party's spokesperson on equalities and said she was concerned to see campaigners in Piddington accused of racism on social media for voicing concerns about the development.

"It is not racist to want to keep women and girls safe. Just recently we have seen an Iranian migrant arrested in Crowborough (another former military site being used to house migrants).

"That is coming to Piddington unless the government changes course and listens to the women," she added.

text:
(CN) — A coalition of states led by California and New York sued the Trump administration Monday to block enforcement of a change in federal housing policy that would leave more than 55,000 U.S. citizens and eligible noncitizens without federally subsidized affordable housing.

Joined by 20 other attorneys general, the states say President Donald Trump’s new policy would upend three decades of federal Housing and Urban Development policy by cutting off a family’s entire housing subsidy if even one household member is ineligible, forcing mixed-status families to choose between separating from their loved ones or losing their homes.

“Despite being the federal agency charged with administering programs to provide low-income housing and reduce homelessness, HUD now seeks to implement a policy that will have the opposite effect, causing the mass displacement of U.S. citizens and eligible noncitizens from their homes,” the states write in a 56-page civil complaint filed in Massachusetts federal court.

Previously under this system, known as proration, federal housing programs have helped low-income families afford rent even when not every household member is eligible for assistance.

The new HUD rule — unveiled earlier this month and set to take effect Dec. 14 — eliminates this protection by only allowing a family to stay in HUD-assisted housing if every household member is a U.S. citizen or an eligible immigrant.

The states brings two counts of violations of the Administrative Procedure Act, accusing the policy change of lacking a rational connection between the facts it found and the decision it made.

New York Attorney General Letitia James said Monday the new rule “runs counter to our nation’s values and the very purpose of these housing programs.”

“Everyone deserves a safe place to call home. Denying a child that security because of who they live with is cruel and indefensible,” she wrote in a statement announcing the lawsuit. “With our country already in the throes of a housing crisis, it is outrageous that the federal government would push even more families out of their homes.”

James said the displacement from the new HUD policy could further strain New York City’s shelter system that already has limited capacity to support new families.

The states say Congress drafted this approach into law in 1997 and explicitly stated that families receiving prorated assistance “shall not” lose their benefits just because an ineligible family member lives with them.

California and New York are joined in the complaint by the attorneys general of Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, as well as the governor of Pennsylvania.

The coalition is asking a federal judge to declare the rule unlawful, strike it down and block HUD from enforcing it against the plaintiff states, their local governments and their public housing authorities.

The states target the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development and its secretary, Scott Turner, as co-defendants.

Shortly into his second term in office, Trump appointed Turner, a former NFL player, Texas state representative and White House senior aide, as housing secretary in February 2025.

The changes to HUD policy during Trump’s second term were explicitly laid out in the Heritage Foundation’s so-called Project 2025 policy blueprint, titled “Mandate for Leadership: The Conservative Promise.”

The conservative policy overhaul called for the HUD secretary to strip all mixed-status families of federally assisted housing.

The Project 2025 playbook suggested local welfare organizations “step up to provide welfare for the housing of noncitizens” in the absence of federal housing.

Housing advocates have criticized the changes to HUD’s policies and functions as a shift toward tax credits, mortgage boosts and regulatory cuts for property developers and owners.

The agency defended the policy change as a guarantee that “only American citizens and certain eligible noncitizens” will reside in HUD-funded housing.

“HUD’s final rule fully implements the 1980 Housing and Community Development Act and ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars," Turner wrote in a statement Monday afternoon. “This change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million which will now go to eligible Americans that are currently on a waitlist.”

title: Doing Europe's Dirty Work: Ongoing Violent Pushbacks of Migrants from Croatia to Bosnia ...
description:

Moreover, Human Rights Watch has withheld the names and other identifying information of some humanitarian workers who requested that we not publish this information.
“In the past there were broken ribs and a lot of blood,” one aid worker told Human Rights Watch.
In addition to frequent beatings and other physical violence, “verbal and emotional abuse is strong,” an aid worker with another organization told Human Rights Watch.
