text:
Members of San Diego’s Congressional delegation again called for reforms to immigration enforcement in the wake of the arrest of an Encinitas mother after dropping her kindergartner off at school.

Democratic Reps. Scott Peters and Juan Vargas were joined by newly-elected Democrat Marni von Wilpert and several local advocates at the San Diego immigration courthouse Monday.

Peters said the Encinitas arrest is one example of ICE going after the wrong people.

"This kind of stuff has got to stop," he said. "This notion that we would separate children from their families in the name of safety is perverse … people trying to follow the rules just getting abused by our own government."

Peters is the sponsor or co-sponsor of two bills in Congress that he said should be a priority when the new Democratic majority is sworn in in January.

He introduced the Stop Excessive Force in Immigration Act last year. It’s a bill he said would require immigration agents to meet the same requirements for employment as local law enforcement officers.

Those requirements include agents showing identification, wearing body cameras and using "appropriate" responses to force, he said.

The other bill would prohibit immigration enforcement in certain places, like around schools.

Rep.-Elect Marni von Wilpert said it’s one of their top priorities going into the next Congress.

"We're going to make sure that our hospitals are places of healing, not places of enforcement," she said. "Our churches are places of refuge, not places of arrest. And our schools are places of learning."

ICE told KPBS in a statement it does not target schools for enforcement and that the Trump administration "will not ignore the rule of law."

New legislation to manage ICE is one of three ways Peters said Congress will attempt to assert its oversight role next year.

Another is funding.

Last year’s Big Beautiful Bill, signed by President Donald Trump, gave billions of dollars to ICE. Peters said the agency doesn’t need it.

"We need to claw that back," he said. "It's really money turned back against our own communities by our own government. And we've got to stop that. And through the appropriations and budget process, we'll have a lot more leverage in January than we do today."

The third tool available to Democrats is their authority to conduct investigations and subpoena administration officials to testify in front of Congressional committees.

text:
Two more measles-related deaths have been reported, one each in Virginia and Pennsylvania.

The Virginia Department of Health (VDH) said late last week that the state’s first measles death of 2026 was a child aged 0 to 4 years who tested positive for measles, but did not provide any additional information, citing the family’s privacy. The state had not recorded a measles-related death since 1978.

Virginia has reported 220 measles case as of November 19, primarily in the central part of the state (195 cases). Eighteen percent of the cases have been in children aged 0 to 4 years old.

“Although anyone can become seriously ill, children younger than five years old, pregnant people, and people with weakened immune systems are at increased risk of complications,” VDH said in press release.

Ninth death in PA

The death in Pennsylvania is that state’s ninth this year. The Pennsylvania Department of Health said it was in an unvaccinated resident of Centre County but did not release any additional information. Pennsylvania, the nation’s measles hot spot and home to the largest state outbreak since the early 1990s, has recorded 1,638 cases across 46 counties.

There have now been 13 measles-related deaths reported by states amid nationwide outbreaks of the highly contagious viral disease. But the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has only confirmed six of those deaths.

The United States officially lost it measles elimination status on November 17 after Pan American Health Organization officials determined the virus has been circulating in the country for at least 12 months. The 426 new measles cases confirmed last week by the CDC represent the largest one-week jump in decades.

Deaths from fungal infections have remained elevated in the United States since the COVID-19 pandemic, despite a decline in COVID-related fungal deaths, researchers reported last week in the journal Public Health Reports.

Using death-certificate data from the National Vital Statistics System, a team led by researchers from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention analyzed any deaths from 2022 through 2025 with a fungal infection listed as an underlying or contributing cause. They used 2018-2019 and 2021 as reference points.

Fungal infection-associated hospitalizations and deaths increased significantly during the acute phase of the pandemic, the study authors note, driven by COVID-19 patients who acquired Candida and Aspergillus infections while in the hospital. But trends since then have not been well-described.

“Understanding whether fungal mortality returned to prepandemic levels or remained elevated after COVID-19–associated deaths declined could inform surveillance and prevention efforts,” the authors wrote.

Mortality rate remains similar to COVID peak

Over the 4-year period, 30,225 fungal infection deaths occurred in the United States, with an average of 7,556 deaths annually. A fungal infection was listed as the underlying cause of death in 26.9% of fungal deaths and as a contributing cause in 73.2%. The annual aged-adjusted mortality rate rose from 1.2 per 100,000 in 2018-19 to 1.5 in 2020 and 1.9 in 2021, then hovered between 1.8 and 1.9 from 2022 through 2025.

As with the acute phase of the pandemic, the most commonly specified fungal pathogens were Candida and Aspergillus, which accounted for one-quarter and one-sixth of fungal deaths. The most common underlying causes of fungal deaths were malignant neoplasms, HIV, and diseases of the heart, which the authors say more closely resembles prepandemic patterns.

The authors caution that death-certificate data likely underestimate fungal mortality, since some infections may go undiagnosed, or not be fully captured in coded records.

“Continued monitoring of fungal disease–related mortality might help identify emerging changes in pathogen-specific burden, geographic patterns, and populations at increased risk of fungal-associated mortality,” they concluded.

text:
WASHINGTON — U.S. Representatives Johnny Olszewski, Steny Hoyer, Kweisi Mfume, Jamie Raskin, Glenn Ivey, Sarah Elfreth, and April McClain Delaney and U.S. Senators Chris Van Hollen and Angela Alsobrooks (all D-Md.) are pushing the Trump Administration for answers after finding significant increases in processing delays and denials of naturalization applications at the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) Baltimore Field Office. The lawmakers point to concerning trends they have encountered that have left those seeking citizenship in the lurch – from seeing USCIS decide significantly fewer cases, to witnessing process times doubling, to learning of the frequent cancellation of citizenship ceremonies. The Maryland delegation members urge USCIS Director Joseph Edlow to take immediate corrective action to address the discrepancies and stress the need for approved applicants to promptly be scheduled for the oath ceremonies they are eligible for under law.

The lawmakers begin, “We write to raise serious concerns regarding the current state of the processing of naturalization applications (USCIS Form N-400, Application for Naturalization) pending with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services at the Baltimore Field Office.”

“A recent review of USCIS’s quarterly data revealed that the agency has decided 73% fewer naturalization cases over the past year—the lowest level over the past decade. Press Unpause, a grassroots organization that closely tracked the impacts of these policies, estimated that over 2 million filed applications were subject to USCIS’s adjudicative hold over the almost 7 months that it was in place. That is 2 million people whose lives were put on hold, which led to compounding consequences across employment, finances, health, housing, family, and legal status for so many,” they continue.

On the increased processing times in USCIS’ Baltimore Filed Office, the Maryland delegation members write, “These delays have disproportionately impacted Marylanders. Between June 1, 2026, and October 22, 2026, processing times for naturalization applications at USCIS’s Baltimore Field Office have nearly doubled: increasing from about 8 months to a year to a range of 15 to more than 20 months – more than a year and a half. The significant rise in average processing times for naturalization applications at the Baltimore Field Office is deeply concerning, especially when compared to other large USCIS Field Offices nationally. The Baltimore Field Office currently adjudicates naturalization applications slower than major Field Offices in New York City (10 to 12.5 months), Orlando (13.5 to 18.5 months), Miami (10 to 14.5 months), Dallas (13 to 16 months) and Los Angeles (10.5 to 14 months). Meanwhile, similar cases in the neighboring office in Washington, DC are adjudicated within a range of 11.5 to 14 months on average.”

“Finally, the cancellation of oath ceremonies—the last step to becoming an American citizen, when individuals swear their loyalty to the United States and receive their Certificate of Naturalization—have caused significant delays for applicants who were vetted, received full approval, and passed their required citizenship exams. American citizenship bestows critical rights and responsibilities upon those who earn it, including the right to vote and the responsibility of serving as a juror in our justice system. Needless postponement unfairly withholds those important rights and responsibilities from those who have earned them,” the lawmakers note.

“We urge USCIS to take immediate corrective action to address the extraordinary decline in the adjudication of naturalization applications at the Baltimore Field Office, examine the alarming increase in denial rates, and ensure that approved applicants are promptly scheduled for oath ceremonies. We request a written response within 30 days outlining the specific steps USCIS is taking to restore timely adjudications, address the growing backlog, and establish a reasonable timeline for returning the Baltimore Field Office to normal processing operations. The thousands of Marylanders who have fulfilled their obligations under our immigration laws deserve more than indefinite delays. They deserve a fair, timely, and transparent path to citizenship. We expect USCIS to fulfill its responsibilities accordingly,” they conclude.

The full text of the letter is available here(link is external) and below.

Dear Director Edlow:

We write to raise serious concerns regarding the current state of the processing of naturalization applications (USCIS Form N-400, Application for Naturalization) pending with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services at the Baltimore Field Office.

On June 5, 2026, a federal judge ruled that the policies set forth in U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services’ (USCIS) Policy Memorandum 602-0194, which halted the processing of key immigration benefit adjudications, were unlawful and vacated them nationwide. As a result, USCIS is legally obligated to resume standard processing of all applications that were previously paused and applications can no longer be arbitrarily held due to the applicant’s nationality.

Despite vacating these policies, many naturalization applications continue to experience a substantial delay, with no information on a timeline for final adjudication or oath ceremony scheduling. Since the aforementioned ruling in Dorcas v. USCIS, our offices have received substantial outreach from constituents whose naturalization applications continue to be excessively stalled and subject to increasing processing times. A recent review of USCIS’s quarterly data revealed that the agency has decided 73% fewer naturalization cases over the past year—the lowest level over the past decade. Press Unpause, a grassroots organization that closely tracked the impacts of these policies, estimated that over 2 million filed applications were subject to USCIS’s adjudicative hold over the almost 7 months that it was in place. That is 2 million people whose lives were put on hold, which led to compounding consequences across employment, finances, health, housing, family, and legal status for so many.

These delays have disproportionately impacted Marylanders. Between June 1, 2026, and October 22, 2026, processing times for naturalization applications at USCIS’s Baltimore Field Office have nearly doubled: increasing from about 8 months to a year to a range of 15 to more than 20 months – more than a year and a half. The significant rise in average processing times for naturalization applications at the Baltimore Field Office is deeply concerning, especially when compared to other large USCIS Field Offices nationally. The Baltimore Field Office currently adjudicates naturalization applications slower than major Field Offices in New York City (10 to 12.5 months), Orlando (13.5 to 18.5 months), Miami (10 to 14.5 months), Dallas (13 to 16 months) and Los Angeles (10.5 to 14 months). Meanwhile, similar cases in the neighboring office in Washington, DC are adjudicated within a range of 11.5 to 14 months on average.

Also concerning are the drastic changes in adjudication rates and decisions. As of September 8, 2026, USCIS quarterly data from Fiscal Year 2026 (FY26) reflected that the denial rate of naturalization applications at the Baltimore Field Office increased fivefold: rising from 7% in the second quarter (Q2) to 35% in the third quarter (Q3). This means that more than one in three applications adjudicated during this quarter was denied, compared to less than one in ten previously. It’s also a roughly sixfold increase over naturalization application denial rates in the previous fiscal year (FY25). Further, the Baltimore Field Office adjudicated only 391 naturalization applications in Q3, compared with 1,178 in Q2 which is a 67% decrease from an already low level. This amounts to only five adjudications per business day, approximately. In direct comparison to previous years, during Q2 of FY25, 5,758 applications were adjudicated, while in Q3, 5,433 applications were adjudicated. This reflects an 80% and 93% decrease, respectively, in comparable quarters from FY25 to FY26. There are now nearly 17,000 Marylanders awaiting decisions on their naturalization applications.

Finally, the cancellation of oath ceremonies—the last step to becoming an American citizen, when individuals swear their loyalty to the United States and receive their Certificate of Naturalization—have caused significant delays for applicants who were vetted, received full approval, and passed their required citizenship exams. American citizenship bestows critical rights and responsibilities upon those who earn it, including the right to vote and the responsibility of serving as a juror in our justice system. Needless postponement unfairly withholds those important rights and responsibilities from those who have earned them.

As a nation of immigrants, we believe that individuals who navigate our legal immigration system in good faith deserve timely processing of their applications. A prolonged backlog of naturalization applications after a federal court directed USCIS to resume standard processing of these applications undermines the rule of law and the integrity of our country’s legal immigration system.

We urge USCIS to take immediate corrective action to address the extraordinary decline in the adjudication of naturalization applications at the Baltimore Field Office, examine the alarming increase in denial rates, and ensure that approved applicants are promptly scheduled for oath ceremonies. We request a written response within 30 days outlining the specific steps USCIS is taking to restore timely adjudications, address the growing backlog, and establish a reasonable timeline for returning the Baltimore Field Office to normal processing operations.

The thousands of Marylanders who have fulfilled their obligations under our immigration laws deserve more than indefinite delays. They deserve a fair, timely, and transparent path to citizenship. We expect USCIS to fulfill its responsibilities accordingly.

text:
San Diego, CA – Today, Rep. Scott Peters (CA-50) hosted a press conference to discuss the legislation, oversight, and other reforms to immigration enforcement that Congress must pursue in 2027. Democrats will soon have the leverage needed to hold President Trump and his Administration accountable for its cruel, reckless, and deadly immigration enforcement tactics.

Democrats have nominated Leader Hakeem Jeffries to be the next Speaker, and under his leadership, House Democrats will work to pass the American Dream and Promise Act(link is external) for Deferred Action for Childhood Arrival (DACA) and Temporary Protected Status (TPS) recipients. Rep. Pramila Jayapal (WA-07) will Chair the House Judiciary Subcommittee on Immigration Integrity, Security, and Enforcement, and will fight to claw back the excessive funding Republicans gave Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and ensure immigrants are treated with dignity and humanity again.

Rep. Peters’ priorities mentioned include his Stop Excessive Force in Immigration Act, the Protecting Sensitive Locations Act, as well as exercising Congressional oversight authority regarding ICE detention centers, hiring practices, deportation quotas, poor training, and more.

“Immigrants are our neighbors, friends and a vital part of our economy. Under the Trump Administration, our community is under constant attack,” said Rep. Scott Peters (CA-50). “When Democrats have the majority next year, we must use it to hold the Administration accountable for the violence on our streets, trauma inflicted on our children, and the economic pain these actions have caused.”

Rep. Peters brought together members of the San Diego Congressional delegation, School Board representatives, educators, and immigrant rights community leaders who highlighted the actions Congress must take to end President Trump’s mass deportation agenda and keep our community safe.

"Under the Trump Administration, ICE has terrorized our communities. Accountability and justice are coming in this new Congress," said Rep. Juan Vargas (CA-52). "As the proud son of Mexican immigrants, I know that immigrants are integral to the fabric of our country. We'll be fighting to end ICE's cruelty and chaos, keep families together, and bring comprehensive reform to our broken immigration system."

“A few short weeks ago, the American people went to the polls and demanded change. That is exactly what we’re going to fight for in the 120th Congress,” said Rep.-Elect Marni Von Wilpert (CA-48). “We will investigate ICE abuses and demand an end to their contract with Escondido to use their firing range. We will demand answers from DHS. We will hold hearings, pursue legislation, and put an end to unchecked federal overreach to hold this Administration accountable.”

“Our moral obligation is that every child deserves stability, dignity, and an education regardless of their immigration status,” said Sabrina Bazzo, Vice President, San Diego Unified Board of Education. “Educational continuity must never be sacrificed to immigration enforcement.”

“As we are getting ready to have thanksgiving dinners with our loved ones, we must remember the immigrant farm workers, our care takers, TPS holders, and Dreamers who are part of the engine of the United States,” said Guerline Jozef, Co-Founder and Executive Director, Haitian Bridge Alliance. “We will continue to fight to protect children, like the 8-year-old boy who was taken by ICE, and families being separated by this inhumane system. We call on Congress to immediately prioritize passing S4814 and the American Dream and Promise Act.”

“Educators see firsthand the fear and trauma immigration enforcement brings into our schools and communities,” said Monique Barrett, President, San Diego Education Association (SDEA). “We stand ready to work with our Democratic Representatives to advance comprehensive reform in the next Congress. The Protecting Sensitive Locations Act is an important step, but it cannot be the finish line. Our students and families deserve due process, protection from family separation, and real accountability. We welcome partnership, but we expect action.”

"We're learning ICE has handed badges and guns to recruits with red flags in their records,” said Shawn VanDiver, Founder and President, AfghanEvac. “Think about that. We vetted our allies more carefully than we're vetting the agents arresting them. Oversight isn't partisan. It's how a country keeps its word."

A recording of the press conference and additional photos from the event, courtesy of the office of Rep. Scott Peters, can be viewed here(link is external).

title: Private Prison Told ICE Its Jail Was Worth $67 Million. ICE Bought It for Nearly Half a Billion.
description:

“ICE should explain how it arrived at $453 million and release the appraisal behind that price,” Wriston told The Intercept.
“I think this is what happens when you move too fast without sufficient internal controls,” John Roth, the former inspector general of the Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, told The Intercept.
Roth, the former Homeland Security inspector general, expects scrutiny into the nearly half-billion-dollar sale’s paper trail.
One of the cases focused on the Northwest ICE Processing Center, the Tacoma facility that GEO just sold to ICE.
text:
As it eyed a sale of a jail in Tacoma, Washington, this spring, the private prison giant GEO Group valued the facility at $67 million, according to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement records obtained exclusively by The Intercept.

This month, the federal government just paid GEO almost seven times that — $453 million — when it purchased the facility, the Northwest ICE Processing Center.

The chasm between GEO’s March 2026 asset appraisal and the sale price just eight months later represents a “massive increase,” according to Michael Wriston, co-founder of the government watchdog Project Salt Box, which tracks ICE spending and contracts.

“ICE should explain how it arrived at $453 million and release the appraisal behind that price,” Wriston told The Intercept.

“I think this is what happens when you move too fast without sufficient internal controls,” John Roth, the former inspector general of the Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, told The Intercept. “You’re going to waste a lot of money. And that assumes everyone has the best intentions and hasn’t got some sort of side deal or corrupt motive.”

Neither ICE nor GEO responded to requests for comment about the sale. Without answering questions about the sale price, the Department of Homeland Security told The Intercept the purchase was “to strengthen America’s ability to enforce its immigration laws and carry out the American people’s mandate for mass deportations.”

With Democrats set to take control of Congress, ICE’s real estate purchases are already coming under intense scrutiny on Capitol Hill.

“This new report is worthy of serious investigation and is part of a pattern of Department of Homeland Security purchases of detention facilities for hundreds of millions of dollars more than they seem to be worth,” Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., the incoming chair of the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, told The Intercept in a statement. “These deals raise serious questions about pay-to-play schemes and corruption at DHS.”

Hassan opened a probe earlier this month into ICE’s $495 million purchase of a detention center the private prison giant CoreCivic previously offered to the state of Minnesota for $75 million — a sale the state’s corrections commissioner told the news site Punch Up was being discussed for $3 million.

GEO Group’s March 2026 valuation for Northwest ICE Processing Center, which the company purchased in 2005 as part of its acquisition of another private prison firm, was submitted to the Department of Homeland Security in accordance with its contract with ICE.

According to a chart in the document, GEO calculated the current $67 million value of the detention facility, which is not the same as its market value, by subtracting annual depreciation figures from its original value of $109 million.

Roth, the former Homeland Security inspector general, expects scrutiny into the nearly half-billion-dollar sale’s paper trail.

“I’d be curious to know,” he said, “what sort of due diligence they did before they put that number down.”

Cost of Avoiding Regulations

ICE officials told Government Accountability Office investigators that their robust plans for purchasing existing immigration detention facilities was not to save money, but to avoid issues with local governments.

“Officials noted that while they do not expect this effort to result in cost savings, it will help ICE fulfill its mission in locations where state governments may resist expanded detention efforts,” said a Government Accountability Office report released this month.

Like other private prison firms across the country, GEO’s efforts to build and operate facilities it owns have met obstacles in local rules and regulations.

In some cases, state-level regulators have gone after GEO for violations of labor laws like minimum wage and occupational safety regulations. Earlier this year in California, the company paid a $100,000 fine and agreed to extend worker protections to immigrant laborers over alleged violations of California worker safety standards.

One of the cases focused on the Northwest ICE Processing Center, the Tacoma facility that GEO just sold to ICE. In 2021, a judge ordered GEO to pay $26 million to former detainees and the state of Washington for, among other allegations, state minimum wage violations. (Andrew Free, one of the authors of this article, was an attorney for the ICE detainees in the lawsuit.)

The verdict was upheld by a federal appeals court in 2025 after GEO sought the same immunity from state minimum wage laws enjoyed by the federal government. The Supreme Court is currently deciding whether it will hear GEO’s appeal.

In a May earnings call, GEO chair George Zoley noted the problem in areas with Democrats in charge of regulation.

“I think the logical solution to much of that is federal ownership of the facilities,” Zoley told the earnings call, according to the Philadelphia Inquirer.

Lucibeth Mayberry, the CEO of CoreCivic, told investors during the company’s most recent earnings call that ICE should “move quickly” to complete several more purchases before the end of the current Congress’s term.

Taking federal ownership of the facilities could lead to massive new expenses for the government — and not only due to the enormous sticker prices, according to the Government Accountability Office report.

“ICE did not manage detention facility investments in accordance with DHS acquisition practices, which include the development of life-cycle cost estimates,” the report said.

According to the Government Accountability Office, ICE violated its own guidelines by failing to update its spending plans to account for the costs of a plan to purchase warehouses to convert them into immigrations jails, as well as its acquisitions of existing detention facilities.

“In purchasing facilities like the one in Tacoma, the administration is not only sticking the American taxpayer with the massive bill — but also escalating costs for operating them for years to come,” Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss., who is slated to resume his perch atop the House Homeland Security Committee in January, told The Intercept. “DHS must answer for its actions.”

“Laughing to the Bank”

After the sale of the Northwest ICE Processing Center to ICE, GEO plans to use the $340 million net profits from the sale to buy back shares of stock, thus increasing their value, the firm told its shareholders.

“I am deeply concerned by what appears to be a gross misuse of taxpayer dollars to pad the pockets of the GEO Group, a private, for-profit company that has overseen real mistreatment and abuses of detained people across the country,” Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., the ranking member of the House Judiciary’s Immigration subcommittee, told The Intercept. “It is unfathomable that GEO has announced it intends to use the net proceeds from this sale for stock buybacks, in yet another move to put profits over the safety and health of the people it detains.”

The sale of the immigration jail is just the latest means by which GEO is extracting super-profits from public funds.

Days before announcing the nearly half-billion-dollar deal that would turn the Northwest ICE Processing Center into a federally owned property, ICE also awarded GEO a $1.5 billion contract to continue its detention services there, according to Project Salt Box.

While eye-popping ICE contracts are nothing new for major private prison firms, ICE’s purchase of the companies’ facilities at such high prices is raising eyebrows among government accountability advocates.

“Someone needs to come clean about why ICE is paying hundreds of millions for facilities that are worth a fraction of that amount,” said Scott Amey, general counsel of the Project on Government Oversight, a government watchdog.

“Who is minding the store and is anyone conducting market research or talking to commercial realtors to figure out the fair price?” asked Amey. “I don’t think so, and the public is now on the hook for years to come while the companies are truly laughing to the bank.”

— Four people filed a federal lawsuit on Monday alleging rape, sexual abuse, harassment, and forced labor while detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement at a private detention center in Basile, Louisiana.
The defendants include the GEO Group and two former GEO employees at the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center: then-assistant warden Emmanuel Reyes and former detention officer David Courvelle.
The lawsuit included instances of rape, groping, voyeurism, physical abuse, denial of medical care and retaliatory solitary confinement.

The lawsuit states they were assigned hard manual labor without proper protective equipment and were forced to work through the night.
text:
BASILE, La. —

Four people filed a federal lawsuit on Monday alleging rape, sexual abuse, harassment, and forced labor while detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement at a private detention center in Basile, Louisiana.

The defendants include the GEO Group and two former GEO employees at the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center: then-assistant warden Emmanuel Reyes and former detention officer David Courvelle.

The plaintiffs, Luis Renteria-Gonzalez, Mario Garcia-Valenzuela, Kenia Campos-Flores and Jane Doe, claim the for-profit group and its employees targeted primarily transgender and nonbinary immigrants at SLIPC.

The lawsuit included instances of rape, groping, voyeurism, physical abuse, denial of medical care and retaliatory solitary confinement.

According to the lawsuit, the plaintiffs were detained between 2023 and 2025 and were repeatedly abused by Reyes and other GEO employees.

While assistant warden, Reyes coerced plaintiffs to perform hard physical labor, sex acts, or both, and threatened them with death, deportation, further sexual abuse, physical harm and harm to their families and loved ones, according to the lawsuit.

They were also denied necessities and life-sustaining medical care and were placed in solitary confinement in retaliation for filing complaints about the abuse.

Two of the plaintiffs, Renteria-Gonzalez and Garcia-Valenzuela, who are transgender men, and another plaintiff, Campos-Flores, who is nonbinary, say they were targeted by Reyes for an off-the-books "work program," which predominantly included LGBTQ+ individuals.

The lawsuit states they were assigned hard manual labor without proper protective equipment and were forced to work through the night.

In November of 2023, Jane Doe was detained. In the complaints, she stated that she turned down Reyes' offer to join his night "cleaning crew," which led to him stalking and harassing her with aggressive, inappropriate sexual comments.

The lawsuit says that within months, he escalated his attacks, cornering Doe and forcibly groping her. She was also regularly forced to perform oral sex on him, threatening her life and family if she refused, the suit says.

In 2025, GEO detention officer David Courvelle sexually assaulted Garcia-Valenzuela three times and forced Renteria-Gonzalez and Garcia-Valenzuela to stand guard outside of the closet while he raped a woman detained at SLIPC, according to the lawsuit.

The lawsuit was filed by the Robert and Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, National Immigration Project, National Immigrant Justice Center, ACLU of Louisiana, and Southern Poverty Law Center under the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act (TVPRA) and Louisiana state law in the Western District of Louisiana, following prior complaints in September 2025.

text:
Denmark's Supreme Court on Monday ruled in favor of a housing association that terminated 91 leases in order to prevent the label "hard ghetto" being applied to their housing complex. The decision align's with Copenhagen's hardline approach to immigration.

The court on Monday upheld Denmark's 2018 "ghetto law," which allows for the relocation of "non-Western" residents from minority-heavy neighborhoods in order to foster integration. The Danish court ruling diverges from a top EU court decision last year that found application of the law could amount to discrimination.

The Danish laws requires social housing estates to rebuild, renovate and adjust their social mix if these become minority heavy, stipulating that 60% of apartments be rented to "Westerners" at market value by 2030.

Denmark's hardline immigration policies making it a role model in the EU

Denmark's pioneering role in spearheading tougher immigration rules has made it a model for some in the EU. Denmark was also one of five countries that last week announced its intent to set up an asylum seeker deportation hub in Rwanda.

Danish Housing Minister Jacob Mark welcomed Monday's decision, saying it "strengthens security, social cohesion and integration."

The court's decision upheld a 2022 lower court ruling against seven tenants who fought their evictions in Nojsomhed, Helsingor, just north of Copenhagen.

In Monday's ruling, the law was found to be non-discriminatory when it comes to the eviction of "immigrants and descendants from non-Western countries" as it is not broadly based on ethnicity. The EU ruling focused on this particular aspect, saying the law would be discriminatory if criteria were race based, while ultimately allowing national courts to have the last say in the matter.

"The Supreme Court notes that applying the criterion of the law involves dividing people into two groups [immigrants and descendants from non-Western countries, and all other persons]. Both groups include a very large majority of different ethnic origins, and there will simultaneously be persons with the same ethnic origin in both groups," read the Danish court's ruling.

Who is a 'non-Western' resident?

Tenants' associations estimate that 11,000 people across Denmark will have to be relocated to comply with the law.

The housing association in question issued a written statement saying that it was aware that the evictions would impact those affected, adding that it undertook measures to insure that residents found new homes.

title: California sues to block Trump rule denying aid to families with mixed immigration statuses
description:
California, along with 21 other states and Washington D.C., filed a lawsuit on Monday challenging a Trump administration rule that would bar tens of thousands of low-income households from receiving federal housing assistance, including more than 7,000 in California.
The new rule would terminate aid for all of these households on Dec.14.
Undocumented immigrants have been banned from receiving federal housing subsidies for decades.
“California won’t stand idly by while the Trump administration forces families to choose between staying together and keeping a roof over their heads,” said Attorney General Rob Bonta in a press conference announcing the suit.
They also warn that housing agencies will be squeezed financially as they evict lower-cost mixed status households and replace them with households entitled to full benefits.
text:
California, along with 21 other states and Washington D.C., filed a lawsuit on Monday challenging a Trump administration rule that would bar tens of thousands of low-income households from receiving federal housing assistance, including more than 7,000 in California.

Earlier this month the Trump administration finalized a rule to bar all households with “mixed” immigration status — meaning, those with some members who are citizens or legal residents and others who live in the country illegally — from receiving housing vouchers or living in public housing.

The new rule would terminate aid for all of these households on Dec.14. The states’ lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for Massachusetts argues that the Trump administration overstepped its authority in overriding a congressional statute and asked the federal court to freeze the new rule from going into effect.

Undocumented immigrants have been banned from receiving federal housing subsidies for decades. But starting during the Clinton administration, Congress has required the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development to provide assistance in proportion to the share of members who have legal status. A family with two undocumented parents and two citizen children, for example, would receive half the eligible aid.

“California won’t stand idly by while the Trump administration forces families to choose between staying together and keeping a roof over their heads,” said Attorney General Rob Bonta in a press conference announcing the suit.

In a written response, the HUD press office said the rule “ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars.”

“This rule guarantees ONLY AMERICAN citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD-funded housing,” the statement, attributed to Secretary Scott Turner, continued. “This change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million which will now go to eligible Americans that are currently on a waitlist.”

Since the Trump administration published the final version of the rule earlier this month, local public housing agencies have been racing to figure out how to comply while minimizing the eviction of residents and financial collateral damage for the agencies themselves. Some warn that many U.S. citizens and legal residents may struggle and ultimately fail to comply with the more stringent requirements to prove eligibility. They also warn that housing agencies will be squeezed financially as they evict lower-cost mixed status households and replace them with households entitled to full benefits.

The new rule would terminate aid for all of these households on Dec.14.

text:
California, along with 21 other states and Washington D.C., filed a lawsuit on Monday challenging a Trump administration rule that would bar tens of thousands of low-income households from receiving federal housing assistance, including more than 7,000 in California.

Earlier this month the Trump administration finalized a rule to bar all households with “mixed” immigration status — meaning, those with some members who are citizens or legal residents and others who live in the country illegally — from receiving housing vouchers or living in public housing.

The new rule would terminate aid for all of these households on Dec.14. The states’ lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for Massachusetts argues that the Trump administration overstepped its authority in overriding a congressional statute and asked the federal court to freeze the new rule from going into effect.

Undocumented immigrants have been banned from receiving federal housing subsidies for decades. But starting during the Clinton administration, Congress has required the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development to provide assistance in proportion to the share of members who have legal status. A family with two undocumented parents and two citizen children, for example, would receive half the eligible aid.

“California won’t stand idly by while the Trump administration forces families to choose between staying together and keeping a roof over their heads,” said Attorney General Rob Bonta in a press conference announcing the suit.

In a written response, the HUD press office said the rule “ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars.”

“This rule guarantees ONLY AMERICAN citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD-funded housing,” the statement, attributed to Secretary Scott Turner, continued. “This change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million which will now go to eligible Americans that are currently on a waitlist.”

Since the Trump administration published the final version of the rule earlier this month, local public housing agencies have been racing to figure out how to comply while minimizing the eviction of residents and financial collateral damage for the agencies themselves. Some warn that many U.S. citizens and legal residents may struggle and ultimately fail to comply with the more stringent requirements to prove eligibility. They also warn that housing agencies will be squeezed financially as they evict lower-cost mixed status households and replace them with households entitled to full benefits.

title: California and other states sue to block Trump housing rule that could split up immigrant families
description:

The federal housing department’s new rule also requires all residents receiving federal housing assistance, including U.S. citizens, to verify their citizenship or immigration status and provide additional documentation.

text:
The new rule is scheduled to go into effect on Dec. 14. Mixed-status households would have until March 14, 2027, to submit proof of eligibility, according to the rule.

In Los Angeles, about 1,700 families with mixed immigration status live in publicly-funded housing managed by the city’s housing authority, according to a recent L.A. City Council motion.

Statewide, California Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office said more than 7,000 mixed-status households could be affected.

"This rule is cruel and it's unlawful,” Bonta said in a press conference Monday. “California won't stand idly by while the Trump administration forces families to choose between staying together and keeping a roof over their heads.”

Scott Turner, HUD secretary, responded to the lawsuit in an emailed statement.

“HUD’s final rule fully implements the 1980 Housing and Community Development Act and ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars. This rule guarantees ONLY AMERICAN citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD-funded housing. This change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million which will now go to eligible Americans that are currently on a waitlist,” the statement said.

California is co-leading the suit with New York and Massachusetts.

What the rule does

The federal housing department first proposed the changes in February, sparking concerns from housing advocates and state officials. HUD received more than 11,000 public comments, according to the legal complaint.

The federal housing department’s new rule also requires all residents receiving federal housing assistance, including U.S. citizens, to verify their citizenship or immigration status and provide additional documentation. Critics warn that the requirements could increase costs and administrative burdens for housing authorities across the country.

After the rule was finalized in November, Turner said the federal government was closing a “decades-old loophole” that has been exploited.

“We’re closing that loophole,” Turner told Fox News. “From this time forward, anyone that is receiving taxpayer-funded housing from HUD has to verify that they are a legal citizen or an eligible tenant in this country.”

Bonta rejected that framing Monday. “That's not a loophole or an oversight,” he said. “That is what Congress intended.”

What the lawsuit argues

The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Massachusetts, argues HUD has no authority to rewrite a system Congress wrote into law. The states say the statute expressly allows prorated aid to mixed-status families and protects them from losing benefits because an ineligible person lives with them.

They also argue the new citizenship verification requirements go beyond what Congress allowed. In the complaint, they say the rule is arbitrary under the Administrative Procedure Act, a federal law that governs how agencies develop and implement regulations, because HUD failed to justify it or weigh the potential harm to families, housing providers and states.

The states are asking the court to strike down the rule and block HUD’s enforcement of it.

“No child should lose their home over a parent's immigration status,” Bonta said.

Other lawsuits

The states’ lawsuit filed Monday is not the only legal challenge to the rule. Los Angeles-based nonprofit Public Counsel filed a separate lawsuit Nov. 16 on behalf of two community organizations and three L.A. County residents whose families receive federal housing assistance.

The city of Los Angeles has also joined a coalition of cities and housing authorities led by San Francisco in a separate lawsuit filed Monday in federal court in Massachusetts. The cities argue the rule violates federal housing law and increases costs to cities.

L.A. Mayor Karen Bass issued a statement Monday, saying the federal rule change would push more vulnerable L.A. families into homelessness.

“Los Angeles is a city of immigrants,” Bass’ statement said. “I’m proud that we have joined other cities from across the country to fight back against the Trump administration’s proposed rule change that threatens every mixed-status household with the loss of the federal housing assistance they rely on to stay afloat.”

text:
New York Attorney General Letitia James and the city of New York sued the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development Monday over a new rule that would strip federal housing assistance for families with mixed immigration status.

The state lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts alongside a coalition of 21 other attorneys general across the country, argued that the proposed rule change — which could strip assistance for 20,000 mixed-status families or around 78,100 people, many of whom are children — exceeds HUD’s authority and violates the Administrative Procedure Act.

The city lawsuit included a coalition of more than a dozen local governments and housing agencies.

The existing rule allowed families to live together in “HUD-assisted” housing if at least one family member is a U.S. citizen or an eligible non-citizen, such as a visa holder. The new rule states that every family member in that household must be a U.S. citizen or eligible non-citizen and each member must demonstrate their eligibility or risk losing their housing.

James said the new rule means that HUD will require people in federal housing programs to prove their citizenship through an “unreliable” process or even risk eviction.

“Everyone deserves a safe place to call home. Denying a child that security because who they live with is cruel and indefensible,” James said in a statement. “With our country already in the throes of a housing crisis, it is outrageous that the federal government would push even more families out of their homes. This rule runs counter to our nation’s values and the very purpose of these housing programs.”

The state's lawsuit also argues that the federal rule change harms the states that signed on as plaintiffs in at least three ways: an increase in administrative costs for state agencies that report to HUD, increased spending on state social safety nets like right-to-shelter programs, and a reduction in income for state-financed housing developments that host tenants with federal subsidies.

The city lawsuit argued that tens of thousands of people would be removed from the program, including public housing and Section 8.

And as a result of removing people from their homes supported by federal assistance, the lawsuit argued the new rule would increase homelessness and shift much of these costs to house people to local governments.

In a statement, HUD Secretary Scott Turner said the rule change “ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars.”

“This rule guarantees only American citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD-funded housing. This change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million which will now go to eligible Americans that are currently on a waitlist,” Turner said.

The existing rule, called “proration,” was written into law by Congress in 1997, which helped reduce a family’s subsidy so it only covered the payment for eligible household members. The law explicitly specified that families “shall not” lose their benefits if an eligible family member lives in the same household.

James also said the rule would make it harder for millions of U.S. citizens to keep the housing they already qualify for because they’d have to provide their Social Security number and authorize a citizenship status check through a database.

title: San Diego members of Congress will fight Trump on immigration - inewsource
description:

“Our children cannot wait for Congress to find its courage,” Monique Barrett, president of the San Diego Education Association, said at Monday’s news conference.

text:
Joined by community leaders outside of the federal building in downtown San Diego on Monday, three members of the next Congress announced their plans to carry out what they called a clear mandate from voters to push back against the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

U.S. Reps. Scott Peters and Juan Vargas and newly elected Marni von Wilpert, all San Diego Democrats, said they will focus on bringing more oversight to immigration agencies, addressing aggressive arrest tactics and protecting children and families.

Just as the news conference was winding down, a volunteer who had accompanied immigrants to their court hearings that day was helping two children — ages 9 and 15, from Guatemala. An immigration judge had just ordered them deported, and they had not been represented by an attorney, the volunteer said.

Rep. Vargas, upon learning of the situation, spoke with the children and their father after the news conference.

“We’re going to try to help them every way we can,” Vargas told reporters. “I know it’s going to be difficult.”

The father said the kids were ordered out of the country in one month. After getting the decision from the judge, the father of the children said he felt “powerless.” He just wanted his family to be OK, he told reporters.

“Under the Trump administration, this community is under constant attack,” Peters said at the beginning of the news conference, before news of the children’s deportation order had been shared publicly.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrested an 8-year-old boy from Haiti in the same building earlier this month, before the government returned him to his family in San Diego 13 days later after congressional intervention.

These incidents with children illustrate what will be at stake when a newly empowered Democratic congressional majority gets sworn in and begins working to curtail the immigration crackdown that was one of several reasons behind Republicans’ staggering loss in the Nov. 3 election.

Despite controlling both chambers of Congress, questions remain over exactly how Democrats can overcome President Donald Trump’s veto power in order to pass legislation on immigration.

Meanwhile, immigration and education advocates say time is of the essence.

“Our children cannot wait for Congress to find its courage,” Monique Barrett, president of the San Diego Education Association, said at Monday’s news conference. “Our humanity shows up in what we do for our children when the cameras are gone.”

What’s next in Congress?

Peters pledged to reintroduce a bill he brought to the House floor a year ago, the Stop Excessive Force in Immigration Act. Peters said the bill would raise the standard for use of force immigration agents can deploy in the field to force that is “commensurate to the threat.”

The bill would also require additional de-escalation training for immigration officers, the use of body-worn- and vehicle cameras while conducting enforcement and place limits on using rubber bullets, tear gas, pepper balls and flash bangs and wearing masks.

Democrats also support the Protecting Sensitive Locations Act, which would bar immigration enforcement within 1,000 feet of schools, healthcare and childcare facilities, places of worship and domestic violence or emergency shelters, among other locations.

Numerous ICE arrests of parents near schools, including two Haitian parents in City Heights earlier this year, have generated sharp backlash against the immigration crackdown. Last week, a parent was arrested near an Encinitas elementary school after picking up food in a food drive.

Barrett said education leaders demand greater protection surrounding schools, including a “one-mile safe perimeter” around San Diego owned, leased and operated properties and “safe passage” for students, parents and educators.

School leaders like Sabrina Bazzo, San Diego Unified School Board vice president, worry of the ripple effect of this crackdown from families to communities.

“When families are afraid that a parent might not be there when their child comes home from school, that fear follows children into our classrooms,” she said.

Since the election, Trump has chosen the architect of his immigration agenda, Stephen Miller, as his new chief of staff and repeatedly emphasized that he can stop legislation passed by a simple majority in Congress.

Assuming everyone voted, overcoming a Trump veto would require some Republican votes to reach the necessary two-thirds majority in the House and Senate. As it stands, there are 56 Democrats in the Senate and at least 258 in the House, with a few House seats still undecided.

Peters told inewsource last week that the new Congress will be limited somewhat by the president’s authority.

“All we can do is provide oversight, make sure that he understands this is unpopular, make sure that we get both Republicans and Democrats to speak back to these abuses and keep working at it,” he said.

Other speakers Monday morning included Guerline Jozef, co-founder and executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, and Shawn VanDiver, founder and president of AfghanEvac, an advocacy group for Afghans who helped the U.S. military abroad.

Speakers also pledged support for the American Dream and Promise Act, proposed legislation that would provide a pathway to citizenship for immigrants who came to the U.S. as children and citizens from certain countries who were previously eligible for temporary protection in the U.S. due to dangerous and unstable situations in their home countries.

Peters also said Monday that Democrats plan to investigate conditions inside ICE detention centers and “ensure that every person has access to quality medical care, proper nutrition and legal counsel to which they’re entitled by the Constitution.”

He also said they will subpoena Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and others to find out who authorized some of the more controversial tactics in the immigration crackdown.

Uncertainty for two siblings

Belinda Mayes, a volunteer with a faith group that accompanies immigrants to their court hearings, stood in the hallway outside the courtroom as the siblings from Guatemala and their father attended the hearing Monday in which the kids were ordered deported.

“Basically, the court found that there was no basis to stay here, such as asylum or anything else, and as a result, they’re now facing a removal order,” she said.

Attorneys and advocates for immigrants have railed against the Trump administration’s decision to stop funding attorneys for migrant children who are in the U.S. alone. They say, as a result, children as young as 1-year-old have faced immigration proceedings without an attorney.

In San Diego on Monday, the 9-year-old boy, in an oversized camouflage Gap hoodie and reading glasses, stood next to his 15-year-old sister, who wore jeans with pink flowers, and news cameras towered above them when the news conference ended.

Rep. Vargas spoke with the father and said his office would try to get him legal representation before the children are supposed to leave the U.S. on Dec. 23, just two days before Christmas.

“Honestly, how heartless is that?” Vargas said. “That is utterly ridiculous.”

title: Seattle airport arrests renew protests over ICE enforcement tactics | PBS News
authors: Geoff Bennett, Karina Cuevas, Amalia Huot-Marchand
description:
Geoff Bennett: The incident comes as The New York Times reports new findings from an upcoming investigation by the Homeland Security Department's inspector general.
Joining us now is Hamed Aleaziz, who covers immigration and the Department of Homeland Security for The New York Times.
Geoff Bennett: What does this investigation reveal about how ICE is preparing agents to carry out immigration enforcement?
Hamed Aleaziz: Well, for the past year, ICE has undertaken this really unprecedented enforcement spree at American airports.
Geoff Bennett: Hamed Aleaziz of The New York Times, thank you for joining us this evening.
text:
Geoff Bennett:

New questions are being raised tonight about ICE's training and enforcement tactics after officers arrested a father and daughter as they were boarding a flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport this weekend. The confrontation was captured on video by several passengers.

The daughter, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, and the father, Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, say they were traveling to California for a family baptism when officers forcibly removed them from the jet bridge. Their attorney says the two have been seeking asylum since 2015. ICE says both had overstayed their visas and alleges that Sofia threw hot coffee at officers. That's not captured on video, and her lawyers say the coffee spilled.

Woman:

We have a work permit.

Geoff Bennett:

The incident comes as The New York Times reports new findings from an upcoming investigation by the Homeland Security Department's inspector general. The report details sweeping changes to ICE's training program under former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, including allowing thousands of new recruits to complete basic training online and sharply reducing the number of hours of instruction they receive.

Joining us now is Hamed Aleaziz, who covers immigration and the Department of Homeland Security for The New York Times.

Thanks for being with us.

Hamed Aleaziz:

Thanks for having me.

Geoff Bennett:

What does this investigation reveal about how ICE is preparing agents to carry out immigration enforcement?

Hamed Aleaziz:

Yes, what this investigation reveals is that, as the Trump administration undertook a massive hiring blitz in the last year, hiring thousands of new officers, they cut down on training substantially, not only for those new recruits who did not have past law enforcement experience.

They cut training for those folks by nearly 50 percent. But also for those individuals who had past law enforcement experiences, that training changed substantially. They went from a in-person one-month training program to allowing these individuals to do their training virtually.

And what that led to was a lot of officers actually zooming through their training, some of them within a day.

Geoff Bennett:

And as we have seen in this incident and others, these agents are given enormous authority, including the authority to detain people and use force. What did investigators find about whether these recruits were actually prepared to exercise that force?

Hamed Aleaziz:

Yes, I actually ended up speaking with some of the instructors, some of the ICE instructors who were teaching these new recruits, to get their sense of how they felt this new training regimen was going.

And many of them were very concerned. One of them called it a catastrophic failure. Another said that this could be a potential liability for the agency down the line.

Geoff Bennett:

Were there any internal warning signs, based on your reporting? Did anyone inside ICE raise concerns about the training changes?

Hamed Aleaziz:

Well, earlier this year, there was a ICE whistle-blower who actually had left the agency and came out and said that the recruits were getting substantially less training than necessary.

And he basically protested this idea that what ICE had done here was appropriate. That is probably the most significant ICE official to actually come out and say this. Otherwise, what was happening was really unclear inside of the agency. There wasn't any type of explanation that these investigators found as to why these changes were being made the way they were.

In fact, the head of training, when they went to go interview him, he said that his decision was -- he was basically he insinuated that he was told by the deputy director of ICE to make these changes and that those changes were supported by Kristi Noem her adviser, Corey Lewandowski.

Geoff Bennett:

Meantime, the current DHS secretary acknowledges that some of these decisions need to be reversed. Can additional training realistically close the gaps?

Hamed Aleaziz:

Yes, that's what these -- that's what the DHS I.G. wants. The I.G. wants ICE to go back and to essentially retrain these officers, to put them through extensive training to allow them to do their job competently.

But the main issue with that is that ICE right now is under pressure, as they have been the entire Trump administration, to arrest thousands of people. They want major -- this White House wants major arrest numbers, deportation figures. And so if you take these officers off of the streets and into training programs that will last weeks, months on end, that could really put a dent in those numbers that this administration wants.

Geoff Bennett:

Major numbers. And do they also want major spectacles like what we saw at this airport, the Seattle-Tacoma Airport? I mean, why else would someone be detained while they were boarding a plane like that?

Hamed Aleaziz:

Well, for the past year, ICE has undertaken this really unprecedented enforcement spree at American airports.

It started last year, where they essentially created this plan alongside the TSA, to share information so that ICE would know when individuals who they wanted to arrest would be flying in American airports. They started with individuals with deportation orders, and they graduated to individuals who had overstayed their visas.

And so that's why we have been seeing so many of these videos of arrests in American airports, is because ICE has started to expand their enforcement inside of these airports. And so it's led to not only incidents like this, but we have seen these types of videos inside American airports for the last year.

And I think that, while the DHS secretary, Mullin, Markwayne Mullin, has really emphasized wanting to lower the temperature, kind of do the work under the radar, these types of incidents continue to happen.

Geoff Bennett:

What does accountability look like at this point? What consequences, if any, could follow from the inspector general's findings?

Hamed Aleaziz:

Well, I think some of that remains to be seen. Obviously, we have a Congress coming in, Democrats taking control of the Senate and the House. They have already said that ICE and DHS is going to be a main target of their investigation.

So what I imagine will come is that these congressional staffers will be putting a target on ICE, specifically what happened during the tenure of Kristi Noem with the hiring, the training, and everything that happened.

Geoff Bennett:

Hamed Aleaziz of The New York Times, thank you for joining us this evening.

Hamed Aleaziz:

Thank you for having me.

Legal fight over 20,000 California ballots ends as appeals court approves DOJ dismissal

A federal appeals court today approved the Justice Department’s bid to dismiss its own lawsuit that sought to stop California from counting roughly 20,000 ballots until officials could verify the immigration statuses of recipients it alleged were noncitizens.

The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals decision marked the official end to a flurry of litigation in California immediately preceding the competitive and high-stakes November midterms. Federal prosecutors who brought the lawsuit previously said that their efforts would become moot after Election Day, since local officials would no longer be able to prevent ballots from being counted.

The contested ballots were at the heart of a protracted legal battle between the Trump administration and California over the eligibility of voters in the heavily Democratic state, and came amid broader federal scrutiny of local elections nationally.

Appeals court gives Trump another chance to move his hush money conviction case to a federal venue

An appeals court today opened the door to moving to federal court President Trump's New York state criminal case that resulted in a felony conviction.

In a brief two-page order, the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals found that a lower court judge had “erred” when he ruled Trump’s legal team had waited too long to raise a presidential immunity defense.

Democratic Rep. Jimmy Gomez to resign after Ethics Committee finds he engaged in sexual misconduct

Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., said today he will resign next week after the House Ethics Committee found that he engaged in sexual misconduct with a House staffer and said that his behavior could constitute criminal sexual assault.

“I recognize the seriousness of the Ethics Committee’s report, and as I previously stated I take full responsibility for the personal mistakes I committed outside of my marriage,” Gomez said in a statement.

He said he cooperated with the Ethics investigation but added he has “strong disagreements with the Committee’s report and its conclusions.”

Trump walks offstage to 'YMCA' after emotional event with families of murder victims

Trump finished his remarks at the Justice Department, where he brought onstage several relatives of victims, some of whom became emotional while speaking.

The president walked off the stage to his campaign anthem "YMCA," despite the somber tone of the event.

Trump brings up relatives of victims killed by commuted felons

Speaking at the Justice Department, Trump brought up several relatives of victims who were killed by people whose sentences Newsom is commuting.

“Governor Newsom, under the cloak of darkness, unilaterally makes a decision to commute the sentences of the most heinous criminals in our society. I am disgusted and frustrated. My brother did not die in vain,” said Police Lt. Jason Davis, whose brother was killed by Luis Enrique Monroy Bracamontes.

Marc Klaas, whose 12-year-old daughter Polly was abducted and killed by Richard Allen Davis, said nothing could bring her back, but “her life mattered.”

“The pain inflicted on our family was real, and the pursuit of justice should not become a political exercise,” Klaas said, adding his advocacy was about “whether one politician should have the power to nullify the decisions of judges, juries, and the citizens who enacted these laws, all to advance a political agenda.”

Sandy Friend, whose 8-year-old son Michael Lyons was killed by Robert Boyd Rhoades, became emotional when speaking. Friend called on Newsom to “face” her, saying sentences had been commuted with the “swipe of a pen,” without speaking to families.

“Governor Newsom, we deserve to be heard. You never heard what my child endured, or lived with the emptiness of having an empty chair at every holiday and milestone, yet you took the only justice we had, and left families feeling abandoned by the state that promised to protect us. You’ll never understand the unimaginable pain that you’re putting these families through,” Friend said.

Trump says 'we're not going to let' Newsom commute California death sentences

Speaking at the DOJ, Trump criticized California Gov. Gavin Newsom for commuting all death sentences in the state.

“After the juries delivered their verdicts and the justice system returned a much-deserved sentence of death, Newsom, a terrible governor in so many other ways, came along and stole away the only closure those families might ever have,” Trump said.

“He stood with the murderers and the child slayers, but today we say the American people stand with you. We stand with you. We’re not going to let this happen,” he added.

Trump delivers remarks at the Justice Department

Trump is delivering remarks at the Justice Department in Washington and is expected to speak about “protecting American families.”

The White House said he will focus on Gov. Gavin Newsom’s plan to commute all death sentences in California.

White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement today that Newsom was failing “innocent victims and their families by refusing to carry out justice against these heinous murderers.”

“He is playing politics with public safety,” Bis added.

It is rare for a president to speak at the DOJ. The last time Trump delivered remarks there was March 2025.

Trump postpones planned detonation of toxic drums at Iowa army facility

President Donald Trump said Monday he had ordered the Army not to go forward with the planned detonation of a Iowa bunker filled with drums of lead azide until the courts weigh in.

The detonation, which was planned for Wednesday, would send a plume of lead dust across Iowa and likely into neighboring states, which has raised fear and concern from local residents who said they had not had enough time to prepare.

First lady welcomes arrival of White House Christmas tree

This year's tree is an 18-foot concolor fir from Silent Night Evergreens in Endeavor, Wisconsin.

How Huang's reinstatement came to be

Trump and Vance were personally engaged in talks over the weekend with key parties to ensure Jensen Huang was reinstated as the CEO of Nvidia this morning, according to a person familiar with the conversations.

Trump and Vance were briefed on national security elements of the Nvidia situation, including allegations that Alice Huang was tapped by China to gather intelligence on Jensen Huang. The person said Trump and Vance did not see evidence to suggest Jensen Huang had engaged in anything illegal or untoward related to U.S. national security.

Nvidia said in a statement this morning that it had “received input from senior levels of the United States government.”

Trump and Vance were convinced that Huang is best positioned to protect open source AI models and preventing closed source model companies from gaining too much power, the person added. Open source models give the United States more control over AI technology and allow Americans more privacy and cost options than closed source models do.

Vance’s relationships in the business community — and, in particular, Silicon Valley, where he worked in venture capital before entering politics — were helpful in bringing about a swift resolution, this person said.

Judge orders East Potomac golf course to remain open through mid-December

In the litigation over East Potomac golf course, U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes is extending her order that blocks the administration from closing the course through Saturday, Dec. 12. The judge's temporary restraining order was previously set to expire this coming Saturday.

This mean the Trump administration is still barred from closing the course, although it has made it difficult for anyone to actually use it by removing flags, tees and pins around the course.

Reyes is also ordering the acting director of the National Park Service, Jessica Bowron, to testify at a Dec. 8 hearing on the D.C. Preservation League’s motion for a longer-term preliminary injunction that would block the closure of the course indefinitely while litigation continues.

Congress reacts with anger and skepticism to Huang’s reinstatement

The stock market was thrilled with the announcement that Jensen Huang was returning as CEO of Nvidia, but lawmakers on both sides of the aisle reacted with shock — and said they still expect him to answer questions next week on Capitol Hill.

“You gotta be kidding me,” Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, told MS NOW when he learned of Huang’s reinstatement 11 days after he resigned in the wake of revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese spy.

Earlier this month, CVS announced it planned to split into CVS Health and CVS Pharmacy. Warren, D-Mass., and Hawley, R-Mo., said in the letter that the "breakup of CVS is good news," but added that "it does not go far enough to address the concerns about the company’s anticompetitive behavior."

"Whether your intent is to try to head off regulatory pressure, or to cast free less profitable parts of the business, we are concerned that the new entity will still be a vertically integrated healthcare conglomerate with costly implications for patients and providers," the senators wrote.

They requested that CVS respond to a series of questions about the company's plans and provide further information about expenses and profits of its subsidiaries. They asked the CEO to respond by Dec. 9.

Warren and Hawley also teamed up earlier this year to introduce the "Break Up Big Medicine Act" to push against health care industry consolidation. The bill has not advanced.

Democrats calling on their party to invest in the South after historic victories this year won’t have to wait until 2028, with races for governor in Mississippi, Louisiana and Kentucky coming up in 2027.

These contests will come just one year after Democrats flipped Senate seats in Mississippi and South Carolina, governorships in Texas and Georgia, and House districts across the South for the first time in decades. And Southern Democrats are confident their party has taken notice.

Alice Huang, the woman at the center of the Nvidia scandal, kept in contact with China’s top spy agency from the spring of 2025 until fall 2026, according to The New York Times. The picture is a takeoff of the famous Trump "fight, fight, fight" picture following the attempt on his life in Butler, Pennsylvania, during the 2024 campaign, where Trump pumped his first in the air after the shooting.

White House turkeys to live large after pardon ceremony

Expected presidential pardon recipients Freedom and Feathers gobbled up attention at a press conference today, ahead of their scheduled appearance at the White House.

The beefy birds — Freedom is 42 pounds and Feather 40 pounds — were introduced at the Willard InterContinental hotel in Washington.

They are headed tomorrow to the White House South Lawn, “where President Donald Trump will hopefully grant them a presidential pardon,” National Turkey Federation Chair Christy Puffenbarger said.

People can vote for which of the two will receive the traditional ceremonial pardon on the White House’s website until midnight, but both will be spared, Puffenbarger said.

The two hail from West Virginia, where turkey farmer Scott Reitzel said they were raised to be accustomed to people and photographers.

After the ceremony, the turkeys will be taken to their new home at Texas A&M University’s Poultry Science Department, where they’ll live out their days in a “brand new climate controlled home with a front porch and outdoor access,” the school’s Audrey McElroy said.

Schumer says Congress must investigate Trump's role in bringing Huang back to Nvidia

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said the White House's involvement in Huang's reinstatement at Nvidia "underscores the need for Congress to act."

“Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he’s learned nothing from his resounding election defeat," Schumer said in a post on X.

The senator added that "Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain."

Democrats will become the majority in both houses of Congress in January.

Huang’s reinstatement 'changes nothing' for House panels set to interview him, committee spokesperson says

Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO “changes nothing” for the three House committees that are set to conduct a closed-door transcribed interview with Huang on Dec. 1, a spokesperson for the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence told NBC News.

“When Jensen was CEO, our three committees were demanding answers. When he was removed and no longer CEO, we were still pursing the facts. The fact that he was been reinstated as CEO, changes nothing. There are serious questions on national security implications that still need answers. Seems like the only thing that is consistent these days on this issue is our three Committee’s commitment to oversight,” the spokesperson said in a statement.

Huang is scheduled to appear before the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party for a transcribed interview Dec. 1. Nvidia's general counsel is also set to also appear Dec. 2 for transcribed interviews.

Last week, a spokesperson for the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence said there is a “good chance” that transcripts of the interviews will be released after they are conducted.

Trump says he spoke ‘directly and indirectly’ with Nvidia’s board about reinstating Huang

Trump said he spoke with Nvidia’s board about reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO in an interview on CNBC this morning, where he sought to provide assurances to address the concerns of lawmakers and others about national security.

“I’ve been speaking to the board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it,” Trump said today. “And I felt more strongly as I saw what was happening with the company, because that was, to me, a very important part of our country.”
